entries.definition: Appearance or luminosity. Munidatta pairs a moon-appearance and a sun-appearance, which he equates with the grasped and the grasper (cp.14.m2), and speaks of three appearances, the moon, the sun and the pulinda, which make and unmake saṃsāra and which practice stops (cp.14.m5).

Nonbeing, absence, a non-thing (Sanskrit abhāva, Old Bengali abhāba; Tibetan dngos po med pa): the lack of being, which Madhyamaka thought no more asserts of reality than being itself. Song 29 says nonbeing does not go (1a); Munidatta says nonbeing too is not reality, since it has the form of the unreal (cp.29.m2).

The higher knowledges: extraordinary capacities that Buddhist texts ascribe to advanced practitioners, usually six (magical powers, the divine ear, knowing others' minds, recalling past lives, the divine eye, and the ending of the defilements). Munidatta says the poet raised his mark to display them (cp.04.m6).

forms.translit: shes rab ye shes kyi dbang

entries.definition: A tantric rite by which a teacher admits a disciple to a practice. Munidatta describes a yogin, consecrated in due order and having pleased the true guru with offerings of pledge substances, receiving the wisdom-knowledge empowerment at midnight (cp.01.m3).

Attachment, clinging (abhiṣvaṅga). Usually a fault, as when Munidatta calls attachment to māyā delusion; in his comments on yogic union it is positive: the lord of yogis is attached day and night to lovemaking with the jñānamudrā (cp.19.m4), whom the yogins never give up (cp.19.m5). Tibetan: mngon par 'grogs pa, mngon par chags pa.

Practice (abhyāsa): repeated application to a meditation or instruction until it becomes second nature. Munidatta introduces couplet 4 of song 20, his 'third verse', as stating 'the fruit of practice' (abhyāsaphala) (cp.20.m5), after a verse on examination (vicāra) and before one on direct realization.

Inconceivable (acintya): beyond the reach of thought. In song 22 the poet calls himself an acinta yogin (2a) and says 'that dhāma is acinta' (6b). Munidatta renders it acintya: through knowing the true nature of things by the guru's grace, 'we are inconceivable yogins' (cp.22.m3). The Tibetan has bsam med, which can also mean 'without thought'.

No-mind, the state of being without mind (Sanskrit acittatā; Tibetan sems med pa). In Munidatta's comment on song 31, the king of mind goes to no-mind and enters clear light, and its conceptual thoughts dissolve there, as moonlight into the setting moon (cp.31.m4). Siddha writings often speak of going beyond ordinary mind in this way.

forms.lemma: me long lta bu'i ye shes

entries.definition: Mirror-like wisdom (Sanskrit ādarśajñāna, Tibetan me long lta bu'i ye shes), one of the five wisdoms of a buddha, which tantric schemes pair with the aggregate of form. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, lists 'the mirror-like' with the aggregate of form, the earth element and the eye faculty among the five objects he reads in the five people (cp.23.m2).

A wonder or marvel (Old Bengali adabhūā, Sanskrit adbhuta; Tibetan ya mtshan): something astonishing; in Sanskrit poetics also the mood (rasa) of the marvellous. The refrain of song 30 says a wonder has risen in the middle of the sky. Munidatta's paraphrase speaks of the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union, in clear light (cp.30.m3).

symbolic.image: a wonder risen in the middle of the sky

readings.referent: the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union (adbhutayuganaddhaphalodaya), in clear light (prabhāsvara): his paraphrase of the refrain puts clear light where the song has the middle of the sky; the Tibetan comment agrees ('od gsal ya mtshan che ba zung 'jug gi 'bras bu shar ba)

entries.definition: Resolve or firm conviction (Sanskrit adhimukti, verb adhi-muc): settled, devoted confidence; in the tantras also the conviction that one is the deity. Munidatta says Kukkurīpāda speaks having resolved on himself as that very meaning, the Blessed Lady Nairātmā yoginī (cp.20.m1), so that in his reading the 'I' of the song is Nairātmā (cp.20.m2). The Tibetan has lhag par mos.

Nondual, nonduality (advaya): the absence of two, as of subject and object or of wisdom and means, a key word of the siddhas. Line 3b opens with ādaadiṭi, whose first part may stand for advaya, though the division is uncertain; Munidatta's gloss has 'coupled union' (yuganaddha) and the Tibetan 'two' (gnyis).

Scripture, authoritative tradition (āgama). Munidatta uses the word when he quotes a verse without naming its work ('and so the scripture': tathā cāgamaḥ); in song 16 it introduces a verse saying that whatever is conceptualized is false (cp.16.m6). The Tibetan has lung.

forms.translit: dar byed pa dang bdag tu byed pa

entries.definition: I-making and mine-making (ahaṃkāra, mamakāra): taking things as 'I' and as 'mine', the grasping at self that Buddhist teaching places at the root of attachment. Munidatta says the suchness-mind elephant strikes down this 'ornament' of the five sense objects (cp.12.m4); the Tibetan has dar byed pa dang bdag tu byed pa.

forms.translit: rgas pa dang 'chi ba nyid med pa

entries.definition: Free from old age and death (Sanskrit ajarāmara): a body that neither ages nor dies, a goal shared by the siddhas' yoga and Indian alchemy. The refrain of song 3 speaks of becoming ageless and deathless; Munidatta says this is gained through a special practice once bodhicitta is bound with the noose of imperishable bliss (cp.03.m3).

The letter a, first of the Sanskrit alphabet and the vowel inherent in every consonant, and so treated in tantric thought as the root of all speech. Munidatta calls a the essential syllable among the letters of āli and kāli, and quotes the Nāmasaṃgīti: a is the foremost of all letters (cp.17.m3). The Tibetan has snying po'i yi ge a.

A letter or syllable (akṣara); the word also means 'imperishable'. Munidatta speaks of the four syllables of 'Śrī Heruka' (cp.17.m2) and calls a the essential letter among the letters of āli and kāli (cp.17.m3). Where he speaks of the true nature of that letter, the Tibetan has 'unchanging nature' (mi 'gyur ba'i ngo bo nyid).

Imperishable or unchanging bliss: bliss that does not decline because the vital essence is not lost (akṣara, ‘not flowing away’); the term is central in the Kālacakra tradition. Munidatta says bodhicitta gone to self-blessing is bound with the noose of the bliss of imperishability (cp.03.m3); the Tibetan has mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba, ‘unchanging bliss’.

forms.translit: mtshan nyid med la mtshon du med

entries.definition: The defining mark (lakṣaṇa) of what cannot be marked or pointed to (alakṣya); in Indian thought lakṣaṇa is a thing's defining mark and lakṣya the thing so defined. Song 15 says it 'does not go' when self-awareness is examined. The Tibetan has 'without characteristics, it cannot be indicated'; Munidatta calls examining it conceptual thought (cp.15.m2).

An ornament (Old Bengali ābharaṇa, Sanskrit alaṃkāra), here the regalia of a tantric yogi: earrings, anklets, necklaces, ash and the like. Munidatta says the couplets he counts second and third (couplets 3 and 4 of song 11) describe the yogi's ornaments, yogikālaṅkāra (cp.11.m3, cp.11.m4). The Tibetan has rgyan.

The series of Sanskrit vowels. Munidatta glosses the dhamaṇa of song 1 as āli, with the purification of the moon, and quotes the Dvikalpa: the union of āli and kāli is Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6). In song 7 Munidatta reads the pair differently: āli with (ā)lokajñāna and kāli with (ā)lokābhāsa, apparently the light and the spreading of light of the completion stage (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan there has 'jigs byed and dus mtshan ma.

Light (āloka): in the Guhyasamāja completion stage, the first of three ever subtler luminous experiences (light, spreading of light, culmination of light) in which the winds and concepts dissolve. Munidatta glosses the song's āli as lokajñāna (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan, ye shes kyi snang ba, suggests reading ālokajñāna, 'the knowledge that is light'.

Spreading of light (ālokābhāsa): in the Guhyasamāja completion stage, the second of three ever subtler luminous experiences, following light (āloka). Munidatta glosses the song's kāli as lokabhāsa (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan has snang ba mched pa, 'increase of appearance', the usual rendering of ālokābhāsa.

A phrase of uncertain sense in song 21 (4b): what the mouse, risen into the sky, grazes on. Dhāṇa may be 'paddy, grain' (Sanskrit dhānya) and amaṇa the name of a rice crop, or amanas, 'mindless'; the Tibetan line has yid kyi chos, 'the mind's dharma'. Munidatta's paraphrase has the honey of ultimate bodhicitta in its place (cp.21.m4).

symbolic.image: what the mouse grazes on when it rises into the sky

readings.referent: the drink of the honey of ultimate bodhicitta (paramārthabodhicitta), which the mouse tastes after going, through the guru's lineage, to the lotus grove of great bliss and coming back (his paraphrase puts this where the song has it graze amaṇa dhāṇa; there is no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: Deathlessness (amaratva): freedom from death, the aim of alchemy and of yogic practices for immortality. Munidatta's gloss on the song's 'ageless and deathless' (5b): novice yogins who roam the world, or reach the heaven of the gods by mantras and herbs, do not attain deathlessness, since they lack the guru's path (cp.22.m6). The Tibetan has 'chi ba med pa nyid.

Nectar (Old Bengali amia, Sanskrit amṛta, 'deathless'; Tibetan bdud rtsi): in Indian myth the drink of immortality, and in tantric writing a name for bodhicitta and other vital essences. In song 21 the mouse makes its meal of nectar; Munidatta speaks of the taste of the nectar of bodhicitta (cp.21.m2).

symbolic.image: the nectar the mouse eats as its meal

readings.referent: the nectar of bodhicitta, whose taste the mouse, the mind-wind, itself makes its meal in the union of vajra and lotus, through the joys beginning with the joy of the body in the moments beginning with vicitra; the Tibetan agrees (byang chub kyi sems bdud rtsi'i zas)

entries.definition: Fibre, the filaments of cotton (Old Bengali ām̐su; compare Sanskrit aṃśu, 'filament', and Bengali ā̃ś, 'fibre'). In song 26 cotton is carded down to fibre, and fibre to fibre, until nothing is left (1a, 1b). The Tibetan line has cha shas, 'part', as if reading Sanskrit aṃśa; Munidatta's comment speaks of parts (avayava) instead (cp.26.m2).

symbolic.image: fibre carded out of fibre

readings.referent: the parts (avayava) of the whole, down to the atoms of the heap that makes up the parts, until the whole is shown to be partless: his paraphrase speaks of parts where the song has ām̐su, with no explicit gloss; the Tibetan line itself has cha shas, 'part'

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in the first couplet: those who went by the straight road 'became anābāṭā'. It may mean 'off the road' or 'roadless', playing on bāṭa, 'road'; the Tibetan has 'their road went elsewhere', as if reading āna, 'other'; Munidatta's paraphrase has anāvarta, 'no return', in its place (cp.15.m2).

symbolic.image: those who went by the straight road becoming anābāṭā

readings.referent: no return (anāvarta): the lords of yogis who went by the excellent path of the avadhūtī are fixed, never to return, in the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss (his paraphrase puts anāvarta where the song has anābāṭā; no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: Unstruck (anāhata): in Indian yoga, the inner sound heard without one thing striking another. In song 11 an unstruck ḍamaru plays; Munidatta speaks of the unstruck sound of the ḍamaru (cp.11.m2). The Tibetan has gzhom med, 'indestructible'.

symbolic.image: the unstruck sound

readings.referent: the sound of emptiness (śūnyatāśabda, śūnyatānāda), on hearing which the Māras are broken

entries.definition: Joy. The tantras Munidatta cites count four joys arising in yogic union; the order of the last two, the joy of cessation (viramānanda) and innate joy (sahajānanda), differs between systems. Munidatta calls great bliss 'the fourth joy' and speaks of knowing innate joy in the joy of cessation (cp.01.m3).

readings.referent: supreme joy, understood in the joy of cessation

entries.definition: Darkness (Sanskrit andhakāra, Old Bengali andhakārā; Tibetan mun pa). The last line of song 30 says Bhusuku the yogin dispels it. Munidatta reads it as the darkness of the afflictions, dispelled by the rising of the fourth joy (cp.30.m6), and in the previous comment has the moon of innate joy destroy the darkness of delusion (cp.30.m5). Compare night (rajanī).

symbolic.image: the darkness that Bhusuku the yogin dispels

readings.referent: the darkness of the afflictions (kleśāndhakāra), which the siddha master Bhusukupāda dispels by the rising of the fourth joy, apart from which there is no other means in the three worlds; the Tibetan comment agrees (nyon mongs pa'i mun pa bsal ba)
the darkness of delusion (mohāndhakāra), destroyed by the moon of innate joy (sahajānandacandra); said in his comment on couplet 4, where the song names no darkness; the Tibetan has gti mug gi mun pa

entries.definition: An embrace (Sanskrit aṅkapālī; aṅka is 'lap' or 'flank'), which the poet asks the yoginī to give. Munidatta explains the word as if it were aṅka, 'mark', and pāl-, 'protect'. The Tibetan translation has yan lag 'khyud, 'embrace of the limbs'.

symbolic.image: the embrace the poet asks the yoginī to give

readings.referent: she gives her own mark (aṅka, svacihna) to the practitioner and protects it (pālayati)
or else, through union marked by the moments beginning with vicitra, she gives the sequence of joys

entries.definition: A ring worn round the ankle, often hung with small bells (Old Bengali neura, from Sanskrit nūpura). In song 11 bell and anklet are on the poet's feet, named together with āli and kāli. Munidatta counts them among the yogi's ornaments (cp.11.m3); the Tibetan has rkang gdub, 'ankle ring'.

symbolic.image: an anklet on the poet's feet, named with āli and kāli

readings.referent: one of the yogi's ornaments (bell, anklet and the rest), which the lord of yogis makes with the moon, the sun and the rest, purified by vajra recitation; the gloss does not say how āli and kāli fit

entries.definition: The two sides or edges (Old Bengali duānte, 'at both ends'): in song 5, the two banks of the river of existence, both muddy. Munidatta renders it antadvaya and explains it as the near and far banks, left and right. Sanskrit anta and Tibetan mtha' also mean 'extreme', as in the two extremes the Middle Way avoids.

symbolic.image: the two muddy sides of the river

readings.referent: the near and far banks (pārāvāra), left and right, smeared with the mud of the faults of nature

entries.definition: The existence between death and the next birth, which many Buddhist schools say a being passes through before rebirth. In a scriptural verse Munidatta quotes, it is named with arising, abiding and ceasing, and all conceptual thought is called the work of wind and mind (cp.04.m3).

forms.translit: chos thams cad mi dmigs pa

entries.definition: Non-apprehension (anupalambha): finding nothing to take as an object, since nothing exists by its own nature; a Madhyamaka term. Munidatta speaks of the non-apprehension of all things, with grasped and grasper absent (cp.06.m2). The manuscript's anulambha is apparently a slip: the Tibetan dmigs su med pa supports anupalambha.

Praise or commendation (Sanskrit anuśaṃsā; in Buddhist Sanskrit also ‘benefit, blessing’). Munidatta uses it to introduce couplets in which the poet speaks of what he has attained: ‘his own praise’ (cp.07.m5), ‘praise of himself’ (cp.07.m6). The Tibetan translation has rjes su bsngags pa, ‘praise’.

Unsurpassed, having none above (anuttara): a standard epithet of the highest awakening and of what leads to it. In the last line of song 5 it qualifies the lord (sāmī) to be asked; Munidatta has 'the lord of the unsurpassed Dharma' (cp.05.m6), and the Tibetan translation 'unsurpassed awakening' (bla med byang chub).

Midnight (Old Bengali adharātī, Sanskrit ardharātri, 'half of the night'). In the refrain of song 2 the thief takes the earring at midnight. Munidatta sets it beside 'the fourth juncture' (caturthī sandhyā); the empowerment entry records a midnight empowerment in his comment on song 1.

symbolic.image: midnight, when the thief takes the earring

readings.referent: the fourth juncture (caturthī sandhyā), named in apposition to midnight: the time, in the house of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation, when the thief, innate joy, steals the 'wealth' of the faults of the winds

entries.definition: Imputation or superimposition (āropa): attributing to something a nature or existence it does not have. Munidatta sets 'false imputation' (asadāropa) beside Ḍombī's bhābhariālī (cp.18.m3); elsewhere he speaks of imputing a dwelling of one's own (cp.07.m3). The Tibetan has sgro 'dogs pa, here 'imputing impermanence'.

An arrow (Old Bengali bāṇa; śara in śarasandhāna, 'fitting the arrow'). In song 28 one's own mind is the arrow, shot with a single aim from the bow of the guru's word to pierce supreme nirvāṇa. The Tibetan has mda'.

symbolic.image: the arrow of one's own mind, fitted once to the bow

readings.referent: one's own mind as bodhicitta (nijamanobodhicitta)
the single arrow: 'the arrow of one taste' (ekarasa), the two made one

entries.definition: The name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 4 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody skya rengs, 'dawn', as if the name were Sanskrit aruṇa, 'dawn-red'; whether aru is a shortened form of that word is uncertain.

Liquor (Sanskrit āsava), a fermented or distilled drink. In the refrain of song 9 Kāṇha plays, drunk on it (āsabamātā). The Tibetan translation renders it sbrang gi chang, 'honey liquor, mead'. Munidatta speaks of drinking the liquor of non-apprehension (cp.09.m2). A different word from vāruṇī, the liquor of song 3.

symbolic.image: the liquor Kāṇha is drunk on as he plays

readings.referent: the liquor of the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of 'these three', by drinking which Kṛṣṇācārya, the knowledge-elephant, is intoxicated; the three are not named

entries.definition: Ash (Old Bengali chāra, Sanskrit bhasman), which Śaiva and kāpālika ascetics smear on the body, often ash from the cremation ground. In song 11 passion, hatred and delusion are the ash the poet smears on; Munidatta says they are burned by the fire of the passion of great bliss (cp.11.m4). The Tibetan has thal ba.

symbolic.image: ash smeared on the body, made of passion, hatred and delusion

readings.referent: what remains when passion, hatred and the rest are burned by the fire of the passion of great bliss; with that ash the yogi's limbs are smeared

entries.definition: The eight powers that Indian yoga traditions ascribe to accomplished yogis, such as becoming minute, becoming light, and lordship over others. Munidatta names them as part of the mark of the lord of yogis that the poet raises (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan has 'the eight qualities, beginning with lordship'.

The eight great accomplishments (aṣṭamahāsiddhi): a set of eight worldly powers promised to tantric adepts, commonly the magic sword, the pill, eye-salve, swift feet and the like; lists vary. Song 15 says they are gained by going the straight road. Munidatta says they arise again for one who meditates on the self-blessing mind purified by clear light (cp.15.m5).

Grasping at a self (ātmagraha; Tibetan bdag tu 'dzin pa): taking a person or thing to have a real, independent self, which Buddhist teaching places at the root of saṃsāra. Munidatta says the form of self-grasping, as object of meditation and meditator, is refuted (cp.26.m3). Compare I-making and mine-making (ahaṃkāra, mamakāra).

The self (Old Bengali apā, apparently from Sanskrit ātman through Prakrit appā): what 'I' refers to, which Buddhist teaching denies is a lasting, independent entity. In song 31 (1b) the poet does not know where the self has gone and entered. Munidatta reads it as the king of mind (cp.31.m2); the Tibetan has bdag, 'I, self'.

symbolic.image: the self, gone and entered somewhere the poet does not know

readings.referent: the king of mind (cittarāja), whose whereabouts the poet does not know once objects, winds, senses and the rest have been made without intrinsic nature in clear light: he cites apā and paraphrases with cittarāja; the Tibetan comment, citing bdag gis ('by me'), likewise speaks of the king of mind (sems kyi rgyal po)

forms.translit: rang gi rkyen nyid du byed pa

entries.definition: Self-conviction (ātmapratyayitā): certainty that rests on one's own experience, not on another's word or on outer means. Munidatta introduces couplet 3 of song 32, his 'second verse', as stating it: by the vajra guru's grace one is to know the true nature of bodhicitta with one's own mind (cp.32.m4). The Tibetan renders pratyaya literally, rkyen, 'condition'.

Inexpressible, not an object of speech (Sanskrit avacana, avacanatva; Tibetan smrar med): beyond the reach of words. Song 29 asks to whom, and saying what, it could be imparted (4a); Munidatta ends his comment on that couplet with 'because it is inexpressible' (cp.29.m5). Compare 'inconceivable' (acintya).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: yongs su ma dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI pa

entries.definition: Literally ‘she who has shaken off’: in tantric yoga, the central channel of the subtle body, running between a left and a right channel, into which the yogin draws the vital energies. Munidatta distinguishes a purified avadhūtī, which he equates with Nairātmā, from an unpurified one.

An obscuration (Tibetan sgrib pa, regularly for Sanskrit āvaraṇa): whatever veils the mind and blocks liberation, above all the afflictions. Munidatta says that by the guru's word the obscurations of delusion and the rest flee (cp.24.m3), and that for one who bows to the true guru's feet those of delusion, hatred and the rest go far away (cp.24.m5).

A part (avayava), as against the whole (avayavin) that parts make up; Buddhist and Brahmanical schools disputed how the two relate. In his comment on song 26 Munidatta speaks of proving that the part has six parts, of the heap of atoms that make up the parts, and of drawing out the parts by examination (cp.26.m2, cp.26.m3).

The whole (avayavin, 'that which has parts'), which Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realists held to be a single entity over and above its parts. Buddhist critics answered that one part moves while another does not, so the supposed whole is many. Munidatta alludes to both, speaking of moving and unmoving and of a whole established by a single valid cognition (cp.26.m2).

Ignorance: the basic misapprehension of how things are, which Buddhist teaching places at the root of saṃsāra as the first link of dependent arising. In song 10 Munidatta says the lotus-place has the form of ignorance.

An axe (Old Bengali ṭāṅgī; compare Sanskrit ṭaṅka, 'axe, chisel'), used in song 5 in building the bridge. Munidatta's gloss has paraśu, 'axe'. The Tibetan translation of the line has gzong gnyis, 'two chisels'; its comment has sta re, 'axe'.

symbolic.image: the axe used in building the bridge

readings.referent: the axe of coupled union (yuganaddha), with which the work is made firm in order to show its fruit

entries.definition: Bark (Sanskrit valkala). In song 3 the liquor-seller uses fine bark to make her liquor; a fermenting starter made from bark, roots and herbs may be what is meant. The Tibetan translation has phabs, ‘yeast’, in this line (cp.03.1b).

A post or pillar (Old Bengali bākhoṛa, a word of uncertain origin), which in song 9 is wrenched or crushed once the evaṃkāra is made firm; in a song about an elephant it may be the post the animal is tied to. Munidatta renders it 'a pair of pillars' (stambhadvaya); the Tibetan translation has ka gnyis, 'two pillars'.

symbolic.image: a post, or pair of posts, crushed once the evaṃkāra is made firm

readings.referent: the pair made of the moon-appearance (the syllable e) and the sun (the syllable vaṃ), 'the knowledge of day and night', crushed and made free of appearance by the process of vajra recitation; the gloss sets the pair beside 'vākhoṛa, the pair of pillars' without an explicit equation, and the Tibetan assigns moon and sun to the syllables the other way round

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in song 17 (1b), between the unstruck stick and the avadhūtī. It may come from Sanskrit vakra, 'bent', or name a part of the vīṇā. The Tibetan line has drang, 'straight' or 'drawn', in its place; Munidatta does not gloss it. The source form is kept for now.

The tip of a hair (Old Bengali bālāga; Sanskrit vālāgra), a stock measure of the smallest amount. Song 26 (4b) says not even a hair's tip enters; the Tibetan line has skra rtse'i cha, 'a hair-tip's portion'. Munidatta first reads bāla as 'fool', then as 'like a hair': not even the joint of a line is there (cp.26.m4).

symbolic.image: not even a hair's tip enters

readings.referent: the fool, the ignorant one (bāla, ajña), who does not enter this dharma and stays far from it: a play on bāla, 'hair' and 'child, fool'; he then offers 'like a hair' as an alternative, and the Tibetan comment keeps the hair in both readings (skra'i rtse mo)

entries.definition: A beginner in yoga. Munidatta addresses the novice yogin (bālayogin) where the song calls out "fool" (mūḍha), and says the ocean of illusion has no end for him (cp.15.m3, cp.15.m4).

A bond or fetter (Old Bengali bāndhaṇa, Sanskrit bandhana). In song 9 the poet breaks bonds 'of many kinds, pervading'. Bondage and release are a constant theme of Buddhist teaching; Munidatta elsewhere quotes the Hevajra: the world is bound by passion and freed by passion. The Tibetan translation has 'ching ba.

symbolic.image: bonds of many kinds, pervading, which the poet breaks

readings.referent: the binding of various kinds that pervades the avadhūtī, broken once the moon and sun have been made free of appearance; the grammar of the gloss is loose, and the Tibetan has 'the obstruction ('gog pa) pervading the avadhūtī'

entries.definition: Old Bengali bāpuṛā, 'poor wretch, wretched' (Sanskrit varāka), a word of pity or contempt. In song 20 (3b) it closes the examination of the channel. Munidatta renders it varākī, qualifying vāsanā (cp.20.m4); Shastri notes the feminine bāpuṛāi as the expected form, and the Tibetan transliterates it. Not bāpa, 'father'.

symbolic.image: that same poor wretch, set against the examination of the channel

readings.referent: the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) themselves, 'that very wretched vāsanā', which is not found at all when the body's channels, the thirty-two goddesses, are examined

entries.definition: Old Bengali baṛiā, apparently the pawns of a board game like chess (compare modern Bengali boṛe, 'pawn'); in song 12 they are broken up and killed first. Munidatta cites the word as vaṛikā and calls it twilight language for the hundred and sixty natures; the Tibetan translation has mi reng, whose exact sense is unclear.

symbolic.image: the pawns, broken up and killed first

readings.referent: the hundred and sixty natures (prakṛti), which are first made without intrinsic nature by the process of vajra recitation; vaṛikā is twilight language for them

entries.definition: A bed: a cot or bedstead (Old Bengali khāṭa, from Sanskrit khaṭvā) and the bedding spread on it (seji, Sanskrit śayyā). In song 28 a bed of the three worlds is laid and its bedding spread with great bliss, where the Śabara and Nairātmā pass the night. The Tibetan has khri, 'seat, bed', and nyal sa, 'sleeping place'.

symbolic.image: a bed of the three worlds, its bedding spread with great bliss

readings.referent: a bed made 'with that great bliss' once the three realms, body, speech and mind, have been spread out in the clear light of bliss, shared with the Śabara's mind-vajra; a paraphrase rather than an explicit gloss of the bed

entries.definition: A bell (ghaṇṭā). In song 11 bell and anklet are on the poet's feet, named together with āli and kāli, among the regalia of a kāpālika yogi. Munidatta counts them among the yogi's ornaments (cp.11.m3). The Tibetan has dril bu, also the word for the ritual hand-bell.

symbolic.image: a bell on the poet's feet, named with āli and kāli

readings.referent: one of the yogi's ornaments (bell, anklet and the rest), which the lord of yogis makes with the moon, the sun and the rest, purified by vajra recitation; the gloss does not say how āli and kāli fit

entries.definition: Old Bengali beṇi, "both, the two", standing after a pair: dhamaṇa and camaṇa (cp.01.5b), sin and merit (cp.16.3a), āli and kāli (cp.17.3a). Munidatta has dvau, "the two", at cp.16.m4, and the Tibetan gnyis. It is a different word from veṇī, "braid", though the two look alike; in song 4, cāndasujabeṇi may be either (the Tibetan has gnyis there too).

Betel: areca nut with lime and spices wrapped in a betel leaf (Sanskrit tāmbūla), chewed as a stimulant and shared between lovers and guests; camphor was one of its flavourings. In song 28 the heart is the betel and camphor is eaten in great bliss. The Tibetan line has so rtsi, literally 'tooth medicine'; the commentary has go la.

symbolic.image: the heart as betel, chewed with camphor

readings.referent: the heart, the clear light (prabhāsvara), resolved upon (adhimucya) as the betel; the Tibetan has 'the clear light of the heart'

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in the refrain of song 18: the poet asks Ḍombī what kind of bhābhariālī is hers. Munidatta cites it as bharbhariālikā and sets 'false imputation' (asadāropa) beside it (cp.18.m3). The Tibetan has skra yags, apparently 'fine hair', in the line and in the comment.

symbolic.image: Ḍombī's bhābhariālī, which the poet asks about in the refrain

readings.referent: false imputation (asadāropa): the gloss sets asadāropeṇa beside the cited word, without an explicit equation, in a question put to Ḍombī as the avadhūtī; the Tibetan comment has 'imputing impermanence' (mi rtag par sgro 'dogs pa)

entries.definition: The female organ (the word also means ‘good fortune, share’), a frequent term in the yoginī tantras and their commentaries. Munidatta equates the cord Ḍombī sells with the bhaga, ‘the place of the lotus’, which he says has the form of ignorance (cp.10.m6).

Bhairavī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 12 is sung, given in its heading; the word is also a name of a goddess. The Tibetan translation calls the melody rnga bo che, 'great drum', perhaps reading the name as bherī, 'kettledrum'; the reason is uncertain.

Existence or becoming (bhava): the round of repeated birth, often a synonym of saṃsāra and set against nirvāṇa. Song 5 opens with the river of existence (bhavaṇai). In the verse of Saraha that Munidatta quotes, bhava stands beside nirvāṇa (cp.05.m3). The Tibetan has srid pa.

readings.referent: conventional bodhicitta, made steady

forms.translit: dngos po dang dngos po med pa

entries.definition: The pair being and nonbeing, or things and their absence (Sanskrit bhāva and abhāva), the two poles that Madhyamaka thought says cannot be asserted of reality. Song 9 names the pair in its fourth couplet; Munidatta comments that all things (bhāvāḥ) are pure by nature (cp.09.m4). The Tibetan has dngos dang dngos med, 'things and non-things'.

Being, an existent thing (Sanskrit bhāva, Old Bengali bhāba; Tibetan dngos po): whatever is there, set in Madhyamaka thought against its absence, nonbeing (abhāva), and no more true of reality than nonbeing is. Song 29 opens by saying being does not come to be (1a); Munidatta says being is not reality, since examination finds no apprehension of it (cp.29.m2).

forms.lemma: 'khor ba dang mya ngan las 'das pa

forms.translit: srid pa dang mya ngan las 'das pa
forms.lemma: srid pa dang mya ngan las 'das pa

entries.definition: Existence (bhava), the round of rebirth, paired with nirvāṇa, its cessation; siddha poetry often calls the two one. In song 19 they are the drums of Kāṇha's wedding. Munidatta explains the pair as the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest, to be purified in sequence (cp.19.m2); the Tibetan comment has 'saṃsāra and nirvāṇa'.

symbolic.image: existence and nirvāṇa, which the song makes the paṭaha and mādala drums of Kāṇha's wedding

readings.referent: the conceptual thought (vikalpa) of mind, wind and the rest, spoken of before, which is to be purified in sequence and is imagined (utprekṣya) as the instruments beginning with the paṭaha; the Tibetan has 'nonconceptual' (rnam par mi rtog pa) where the Sanskrit has vikalpa

entries.definition: The forces, or army, of existence (Old Bengali bhababala: bhava, 'existence', and bala, 'strength, troops'), which Kāṇha says he has conquered in lines 1b and 4b of song 12. The Tibetan translation has srid pa'i stobs, 'power of existence', and srid pa'i dpung, 'army of existence'. Munidatta reads it as the sense objects.

symbolic.image: the forces of existence, defeated in the game

readings.referent: the force of the appearance of sense objects (viṣayābhāsabala), which Kṛṣṇācārya conquers as he plays in the union of vajra and lotus
the force of the host of things (bhāvagrāma), the sense objects beginning with form; the Tibetan has 'the power of the town of things'

entries.definition: Meditation or cultivation (bhāvanā, literally 'bringing into being'): the repeated practice by which an understanding becomes one's own. Munidatta introduces couplet 4 of song 13, his 'third verse', as teaching the purification of meditation, so as to establish the point beyond doubt (cp.13.m5). The Tibetan has sgom pa.

The pair 'what is meditated on' (bhāvya) and 'the one who meditates' (bhāvaka). Munidatta says the form of grasping at a self as object of meditation and meditator is refuted (cp.26.m3), and quotes the Dvikalpa (Hevajra): there is no meditator, nor anything to be meditated on. The Tibetan has bsgom par bya ba and sgom pa po.

A raft or float for crossing water (Old Bengali bhelā, Sanskrit bhelaka). In song 15 the fool sees neither boat nor raft ahead on the ocean. Munidatta says there is no means of crossing apart from the true guru's raft; where his Sanskrit has vāhya, the Tibetan has 'the true guru's word', as if reading vākya (cp.15.m4).

symbolic.image: a raft, not seen ahead on the ocean

readings.referent: the raft of the true guru (sadguruvāhyabhelaka), apart from which there is no other means, such as a boat, of crossing the ocean; the Tibetan has 'by the true guru's word' (bla ma dam pa'i gsung)

entries.definition: Confusion or error (bhrānti): taking a thing for what it is not, as a rope for a snake; Buddhist epistemology's word for mistaken cognition. Song 15 twice speaks of the fool's confusion. Munidatta tells the novice yogin to shake it off, and not, in confusion, to take clear light as empty and so fall into annihilation (cp.15.m4, cp.15.m5).

Bhujaṅga, literally 'snake', also a lover, paramour or gallant, the sense its pairing with dārī, 'courtesan', suggests in song 28, where the Śabara is the bhujaṅga and Nairāmaṇi the dārī. The Tibetan takes it as 'snake', sbrul in the line and ltos 'gro, 'belly-crawler', in the commentary.

symbolic.image: the Śabara as bhujaṅga

readings.referent: the Śabara's mind-vajra (cittavajra), with whom the bed of great bliss is made

entries.definition: Old Bengali biāṇa, taken here as 'birth, bringing forth' (compare Bengali biyāna, used of animals giving birth). In song 20 (3a) the speaker's first biāṇa is wrapped in habitual tendencies. Munidatta's paraphrase has 'this body was born' (prasūta) (cp.20.m4); the Tibetan line reads rnam shes, 'consciousness', as if the word were vijñāna.

symbolic.image: the speaker's first birth, wrapped in habitual tendencies

readings.referent: this body (kāya), born at first as a casket of conventional habitual tendencies (saṃvṛtivāsanāpuṭa); his paraphrase puts it where the song has 'my first birth', without an explicit gloss

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense, addressed in the vocative in the refrain of song 2 ('listen, O biātī'). The Tibetan translation renders it rigs ngan, 'low-born woman', which suggests Sanskrit vijātī, 'of other (low) birth'; other derivations are possible. Munidatta writes viātī.

symbolic.image: the woman addressed as biātī in the refrain

readings.referent: the purified avadhūtī, which the lord of yogis, having resolved on its form in himself, addresses: 'O purified avadhūtī, listen'

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense and derivation in the first couplet of song 20: the speaker says her bigoā cannot be told. The Tibetan line has nyams myong, 'experience', and Munidatta's paraphrase puts 'my experience of the imperishable bliss of distinguished union' in its place (cp.20.m2). Whether the Old Bengali meant this, or something like 'plight', is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the speaker's bigoā, which cannot be told

readings.referent: the speaker's experience of the imperishable bliss of distinguished union (viśiṣṭasaṃyogākṣarasukhānubhava), which cannot be known through speech in any way (his paraphrase puts it where the song has mohora bigoā; there is no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: A drop: in tantric yoga, a drop of the vital essence, bodhicitta, which in its bodily form is semen and is guarded and moved through the channels of the subtle body. Munidatta speaks of the drop of bodhicitta at the opening in the tip of the vajra-jewel (cp.03.m2).
A river boat, one of the commonest images of the songs, with its ferryman, oars and crossings. In this song Kāṇha asks Ḍombī in whose boat she comes and goes.

symbolic.image: the boat in which Ḍombī comes and goes

readings.referent: the path of conventional bodhicitta, on which she comes and goes (he adds that in fact she does not)
what lies in the middle: the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā) in the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (the syntax of the gloss is loose)
the path of the joy of cessation, purified by the innate
purified bodhicitta, which the yogī is told to row
the body of great bliss (mahāsukhakāya), in which body, speech and mind dissolve into the fourth refuge
the means of the fourth joy (caturthānandopāya), on which Kāṇha crosses the ocean of existence
the path of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, with the mind set at the helm
great bliss itself (mahāsukhanaukā, "the boat of great bliss"), with one's own body as the oar

entries.definition: Awakening (bodhi): the realization that makes one a buddha. In song 5 the poet says awakening is near and one should not go far. Munidatta speaks of the accomplishment of bodhi-Mahāmudrā, very near through practice (cp.05.m5). In the last line the Tibetan translation has byang chub, 'awakening', where the Bengali has 'lord'.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems
kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems

entries.definition: 'Mind of awakening'. In the Mahāyāna, the resolve to reach awakening for all beings; in the tantras also a subtle bodily essence whose loss must be prevented. Munidatta speaks of 'the moon of conventional bodhicitta' drying up, and quotes the Rativajra: once bodhicitta has fallen, how can there be flawless accomplishment? (cp.01.m2).

The physical body (Old Bengali and Sanskrit deha, also kāya; Tibetan lus). The songs often picture it as a place or thing: a town, a tree, a forest, a pool. In song 11 Kāṇha wanders in the town of the body, which Munidatta repeats as dehanagarikā (cp.11.m2).

A code word of the yoginī tantras; in ordinary Sanskrit bola is gum myrrh. In the Hevajra Tantra's list of code words bola (bolaka) names the vajra, the male organ, as kakkola names the lotus. In the verse Munidatta quotes on song 18, 'dear bola' meets kakkola (cp.18.m5); he does not explain it. The Tibetan transcribes it po la.
A string of bone beads or carved bone ornaments, part of the regalia of kāpālika ascetics and tantric yogis. Kāṇha says he has put one on for Ḍombī's sake.

symbolic.image: a garland of bones

entries.definition: A bow. In song 28 the guru's word is the puñcaā and one's own mind the arrow with which supreme nirvāṇa is pierced. Munidatta renders the word dhanus, 'bow', and the Tibetan line has gzhu, 'bow'; the derivation of the Old Bengali puñcaā is unclear.

symbolic.image: the bow of the guru's word

readings.referent: the true guru's word (sadguruvākya), which is made the bow

entries.definition: A bracelet or bangle (Old Bengali kāṅkāṇa, Sanskrit kaṅkaṇa; Tibetan lag gdub, gdu bu). Song 32 (3a) says not to take a mirror to look at the bracelet on one's hand, apparently a proverb: what is in plain sight needs no instrument. Munidatta repeats the question (cp.32.m4), spelling the word kaṅkāṇa.

A member of the priestly caste at the head of the caste order, bound by rules of ritual purity that forbid contact with untouchables. The first couplet of this song sets a shaven-headed brahmin beside Ḍombī's hut outside the town.

symbolic.image: a shaven-headed brahmin

readings.referent: the mind as a restless young brahmin (cittavaṭuka, ‘mind-lad’), born from the seed syllable HŪṂ called brahma

entries.definition: A branch or bough (Old Bengali ḍāla, ḍālī). In song 28 the branches of the various fine trees touch the sky; Munidatta repeats the word (ḍāla) in his Sanskrit. The Tibetan has yal ga.

symbolic.image: the branches of the fine trees, touching the sky

readings.referent: the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), touching the sky, the clear light

entries.definition: Breath (Tibetan dbugs). Munidatta's comment on the refrain of song 23, surviving only in the Tibetan, distinguishes the entering, the outgoing and the abiding breath, joined with the syllables oṃ, hūṃ and āḥ as in vajra recitation, and reads the refrain's living and dead as the first two (cp.23.m3). Compare wind (vāyu).

A young wife living in her husband's family home (Old Bengali bahuṛī, from Sanskrit vadhūṭī); the Tibetan translation has mna' ma, 'bride, daughter-in-law'. In song 2 she stays awake while her father-in-law sleeps, is afraid by day, and goes to Kāmaru at night.

symbolic.image: the young wife of the household

readings.referent: the yoginīs, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, who keep awake day and night

the avadhūtī, which in its conventional aspect, as semen, creates the three worlds and then, producing the knowledge of day, is afraid; at night, as the naturally purified avadhūtī, it empowers the five aggregates and goes of itself, free of concepts, to its own place in the wheel of great bliss

entries.definition: A bridge or crossing (Old Bengali sāṅkama, Sanskrit saṃkrama). In the refrain of song 5 Cāṭila builds a bridge over the river of existence, from the planks of a split tree, so that people bound for the far shore can cross; whoever climbs onto it is not to go right or left.

symbolic.image: the bridge Cāṭila builds over the river of existence

readings.referent: the unity of self-blessing (svādhiṣṭhāna) and clear light (prabhāsvara), the Jina's bridge for carrying beings across the ocean of saṃsāra; the Sanskrit reads sthādhiṣṭhāna, evidently for svādhiṣṭhāna, as the Tibetan rang byin gyis brlab pa confirms
the unity of the conventional and the ultimate, which Cāṭila joins through the guru's lineage; the Sanskrit word glossed here, śatrumam, looks corrupt, and the Tibetan has zam pa, 'bridge'

entries.definition: 'Awakened one': one who has reached full awakening (bodhi); with a capital, the historical Buddha, Śākyamuni. In the Rativajra verse Munidatta quotes, Śākyasiṃha and the other buddhas broke Māra's army (cp.16.m2); the Tibetan there has mkhas rnams, 'the wise', perhaps reading budha, 'wise', for buddha.

A universal monarch (cakravartin, 'wheel-turner'): in Indian and Buddhist tradition, the ideal king whose rule extends over the whole world. In Munidatta's simile, as a universal monarch enters his pleasure garden by the golden road, so the lord of yogis playfully enters the lotus garden of the wheel of great bliss by the path of the avadhūtī (cp.15.m3).

A word of uncertain literal sense in the last line of song 1, paired with dhamaṇa; the two appear as the seat on which the poet sits. It may be related to Sanskrit camana, 'sipping'. Munidatta spells it cavaṇa.

symbolic.image: camaṇa, one of the pair that serves as the poet's seat

readings.referent: kāli, the consonant series, with the purification of the sun

entries.definition: Camphor (Old Bengali kāpura, Sanskrit karpūra), a white, fragrant substance that vanishes into the air if left exposed. In the line Munidatta quotes from 'the Caryā masters' on song 18, camphor fallen into a ditch is lost; he cites it after the destruction of the moon, conventional bodhicitta, without explaining the image (cp.18.m4). The Tibetan has ga pur.

readings.referent: coupled union, in the relation of fruit and cause

entries.definition: A woman of the Caṇḍāla, the community caste society ranked lowest and treated as untouchable. In the last couplet of song 18 Kāṇha says he has sung the kāmacaṇḍālī, 'the Caṇḍālī of desire'; the next line names Ḍombī. The Tibetan has 'dod pa gtum mo; gtum mo is also its word for the caṇḍālī fire of tantric yoga.

symbolic.image: the Caṇḍālī of desire, whom Kāṇha sings

readings.referent: such a Caṇḍālī, 'the means of practice for one who abides in action' (karmasthasādhanopāya), whom Kṛṣṇācārya alone sings and no one else; the compound is obscure, and the Tibetan has 'the means of accomplishing the place of action' (las kyi gnas sgrub pa'i thabs)

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: thod pa can gyi spyod pa

entries.definition: Tantric conduct: the outward way of life of an adept, including dress, ornaments, song and behaviour that defies convention. The word gives the Caryāgīti, ‘songs of conduct’, their name. Munidatta speaks here of conduct ‘with elaboration’ (saprapañca).

A sandhyā is a juncture of the day, such as dawn or dusk, at which rites are performed. Munidatta sets the wisdom-knowledge empowerment 'at midnight, at the fourth juncture' (cp.27.m2), naming the two together. The Tibetan has nam phyed kyi thun mtshams bzhi, which could also mean 'the four junctures of midnight'.

A chain (Old Bengali sikala, from Sanskrit śṛṅkhalā); in song 16 apparently the chain that tethers the elephant, which is twisted apart. The Tibetan line makes it 'the iron chain of the two, virtue and sin'. Munidatta's comment does not gloss the chain; it speaks of cutting sin and merit, the two nooses of saṃsāra (cp.16.m4).

Old Bengali chiṇālī: an unchaste or wanton woman, a term of abuse. The last line of song 18 says there is none beyond Ḍombī. Munidatta explains it as a woman whose nose has been cut off (chinnanāsikā), a traditional punishment for an unchaste woman, or as a woman of the town (nāgarikā). The Tibetan has dmangs rigs, 'low caste'.

A sign or mark (Sanskrit cihna). In song 3 a sign is seen at the tenth door and a customer comes, perhaps like the sign that advertised a liquor shop. Munidatta speaks of the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion seen at the door of Vairocana (cp.03.m4). The Tibetan translation has rtags.

symbolic.image: a sign seen at the tenth door

readings.referent: the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion (mahārāgasukhapramodacihna), which the gandharva being sees at the door of Vairocana before it enters

entries.definition: Mud or mire (Old Bengali cikhila), which in song 5 lies on both sides of the river of existence. Munidatta repeats the word and explains it with paṅka, 'mud'. The Tibetan translation has rab 'dred, 'very slippery', in the line and in the comment.

symbolic.image: mud on both sides of the river

readings.referent: the mud of the faults of nature (prakṛtidoṣa) with which the two banks, near and far, left and right, are smeared; the Tibetan translation instead has 'not stained by the mud of the faults of nature' and applies it to the middle

entries.definition: A strip of cloth or rag (Sanskrit cīra), here raised like a flag: the poet says he has raised it among men and women. The Tibetan translation renders it rtags mtshan, 'sign, emblem'.

symbolic.image: the cloth the poet raises among men and women

readings.referent: the mark of the lord of yogis (yogīndracihna), the eightfold mastery and the rest, raised to display the higher knowledges

forbiddenInLine: mark of the lord of yogis

entries.definition: Mind: the stream of thought and awareness. Song 1 speaks of the restless mind. In a verse Munidatta quotes, the mind clouded by concepts, restless as windblown lightning and stained by passion is called saṃsāra (cp.01.m2).

readings.referent: one’s own mind as bodhicitta

entries.definition: Mind and wind taken as one (Sanskrit cittapavana): in tantric yoga the mind is said to ride on the vital wind, so that the two move, and are stilled, together. Munidatta reads the mouse of song 21 as the mind-wind (cp.21.m2), and speaks in song 6 of the pair's dwelling; the Tibetan has sems dang rlung, 'mind and wind'.

Cloth or a garment (Tibetan gos). In song 25 the poet, weaving five times, makes a stainless cloth (1b). Munidatta's gloss on the stainless cloth speaks of making wholly pure by natural clear light, and he quotes the Hevajra: the conventional is like jasmine, the ultimate has the form of bliss (cp.25.m2).

symbolic.image: the stainless cloth, woven five times

readings.referent: what is made wholly pure by natural clear light (rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal); the Hevajra verse he adds likens the conventional to jasmine and gives the ultimate the form of bliss; the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation

entries.definition: Coming and going (Old Bengali abaṇāgabaṇa, apparently a pair of verbal nouns; compare Sanskrit āgamana, gamana). In song 7 Kāṇha is downcast 'in coming and going', after the couplet on whatever came and went. The Tibetan translation seems to parse the word differently, as bdag nyid 'ongs nas, 'having come himself'.

symbolic.image: coming and going

readings.referent: the arising and perishing (utpāda, bhaṅga) of things, in which, knowing the nature of conventional truth by the guru's grace, Kṛṣṇācārya becomes of distinguished mind (the paraphrase puts utpādabhaṅgeṣu where the song has abaṇāgabaṇe; there is no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: A companion, or company (Old Bengali saṅga; the edition prints sa(su)ṅgā, marking a doubtful vowel). In the last line of song 8 the rower meets great bliss on the road as companion; the Tibetan translation has grogs, 'companion'. Munidatta speaks of obtaining the embrace of Nairātmā-knowledge, the companion of great bliss (cp.08.m5).

symbolic.image: the companion met on the road with great bliss

readings.referent: the knowledge of Nairātmā (nairātmājñāna), the companion of great bliss, whose embrace the poet says he has obtained on that path; the Tibetan has 'the knowledge of selflessness'

entries.definition: The open yard of a house (Sanskrit aṅgana), the first word of the refrain of song 2. The Tibetan commentary has sgo mdun, 'in front of the door'; its quotation of the song reads sgo bdun, 'seven doors', probably a slip for the same words.

symbolic.image: the courtyard of the house, in the refrain

readings.referent: the wind of emergence (vyutthāna) and entering; the wording of the gloss is obscure, and the Tibetan has 'entering, with reference to the wind of arising'
the sky-Gaṅgā, the lake of the wheel of great bliss; his paraphrase puts gaganagaṅgā where the song has 'courtyard of the sky', without an explicit gloss

entries.definition: A crocodile (Sanskrit kumbhīra, the broad-snouted crocodile of Indian rivers); the Tibetan translation has chu srin, a water monster. In song 2 it eats the tamarind of a tree. Munidatta reads it through kumbhaka, breath retention, a word it resembles.

symbolic.image: a crocodile that eats the tamarind of the tree

readings.referent: the absorption of kumbhaka (breath retention) purified by vilakṣaṇa, which, with the stages of one's own experience, 'eats' bodhicitta, that is, makes it without intrinsic nature

entries.definition: What the young wife fears by day in song 2. The rendering 'crow' rests on the Tibetan translation, which has bya rog, 'crow', in the song and the commentary; the Old Bengali kāṛai is otherwise uncertain and might be parsed differently. Munidatta quotes the word without a Sanskrit equivalent.

symbolic.image: the crow the young wife fears by day

readings.referent: the kāyakālapuruṣa, the 'Man of Time' of the body (Tibetan dus kyi skyes bu, 'person of time'), of whom she is afraid and terrified

entries.definition: Old Bengali dāha, what Kāṇha says he gives well in the last couplet of song 12. In the game it most likely means a move or turn (compare Bengali dān, Hindi dā̃v); Munidatta renders it dāya, 'gift', explained as the intention of an exceptional offering, and the Tibetan translation has bde mchog, 'supreme bliss'.

symbolic.image: the good move Kāṇha makes

readings.referent: a gift (dāya), meaning the intention of an exceptional offering (prābhṛta)

entries.definition: A small two-headed drum shaped like an hourglass, sounded by beads on cords when the hand twists it; Śiva, kāpālika ascetics and tantric deities carry it. In song 11 Kāṇha's ḍamaru is unstruck and yet sounds. The Tibetan keeps the word (Da ma ru).

symbolic.image: the unstruck ḍamaru that sounds with a hero's sound

entries.definition: A stick or rod (Old Bengali dāṇḍī, Sanskrit daṇḍa, diminutive daṇḍikā); in song 17 the long body of the vīṇā, which carries the gourd and the strings. Line 1b calls it unstruck (aṇahā); Munidatta has Vīṇāpāda attach to 'the unstruck stick' (anāhatadaṇḍikā) what he has made one with the avadhūtikā (cp.17.m2). The Tibetan has dbyig and dbyig pa, 'staff'.

symbolic.image: the stick of the vīṇā, named with the unstruck

readings.referent: the unstruck (anāhata): Vīṇāpāda attaches to 'the unstruck stick' (anāhatadaṇḍikā) what he has made one with the avadhūtikā, 'the one with the wheel of objects' (viṣayacakrī; the sense is unclear); the Tibetan has 'attaching the unstruck sound to the staff' (gzhom du med pa'i sgra dbyig pa la sbyar te)

entries.definition: Old Bengali dārī, apparently a courtesan or harlot, paired with bhujaṅga, 'paramour'; the Tibetan has gzugs 'tshong ma, 'courtesan'. Munidatta glosses it dārikā and derives it from dārayati, 'tears apart', since she tears apart the afflictions (cp.28.m5). Sanskrit dārikā usually means 'girl' and dāra 'wife', so the sense is not certain.

symbolic.image: Nairāmaṇi as the dārī

readings.referent: Nairātmā, called dārikā because she tears apart (dārayati) the afflictions

entries.definition: The ten powers (daśabala) of a buddha: ten kinds of knowledge, among them knowing what is possible and impossible, how actions ripen, and that the defilements have ended. 'Possessor of the ten powers' is a title of the Buddha. Song 9 speaks of the jewel of the ten powers; Munidatta names them with the fearlessnesses (cp.09.m5).

The ten directions: the four cardinal and four intermediate points, with the zenith and the nadir; that is, everywhere. In song 9 the jewel of the ten powers is in the ten directions, and Munidatta says it pervades them (cp.09.m5). The Tibetan has phyogs bcu.

The tenth door or opening of the body: yogic traditions count nine bodily openings and add a hidden tenth, often placed at the crown of the head. In song 3 a sign is seen at the tenth door. Munidatta calls it the door of Vairocana (cp.03.m4).

symbolic.image: the tenth door, at which a sign is seen

readings.referent: the door of Vairocana (vairocanadvāra), where the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion is seen, and by which the gandharva being enters

entries.definition: A deer or antelope (Old Bengali hariṇā, Sanskrit hariṇa, mṛga), the central figure of this song: its own flesh makes it an enemy, it touches neither grass nor water, and its hooves are not seen as it bounds away. Munidatta says the poet speaks in the twilight language of the word 'deer' (cp.06.m1), and calls it 'the mind-deer' throughout.

symbolic.image: a deer, an enemy through its own flesh, that touches neither grass nor water and whose hooves are not seen as it bounds away

readings.referent: the mind, which Munidatta calls 'the mind-deer' (cittahariṇa) throughout his comment
with the doe, the pair 'mind and wind' (cittapavana), whose dwelling is not understood through the door of the senses (the gloss does not say which animal is which)
the body's wind (in the Tibetan comment, "the deer of body-wind"); in song 6 the deer was the mind

entries.definition: Deśākha, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 32 is sung, given in its heading, where Shastri prints dveśākha. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name (de sha kha) instead of translating it, which supports the reading Deśākha.

Devakrī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 8 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody lha rnams rol pa, 'play of the gods', as if the name were Sanskrit devakrīḍā, 'divine play'; whether krī is a shortened form of that word is uncertain.

Meditation in which practitioners visualize themselves as the deity of a tantra, the foundation of tantric practice. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes firm the vajra of body, beginning with deity yoga (cp.04.m5).

A goddess (Sanskrit devī, Old Bengali debī). In the last couplet of song 17 a goddess sings while someone dances. Munidatta identifies 'their goddess' with the yoginīs, Nairātmā and the rest, who perform the auspicious rite of singing together (cp.17.m5). The Tibetan has lha mo.

symbolic.image: the goddess who sings in the last couplet

readings.referent: the yoginīs, Nairātmā and the rest, who perform the auspicious rite of singing together; the Tibetan has them make auspiciousness with vajra song (rdo rje'i glus)

entries.definition: A word of uncertain literal sense in the last line of song 1, paired with camaṇa; the two appear as the seat on which the poet sits. It may be related to Sanskrit dhamana, 'blowing'. Munidatta spells it dhavana.

symbolic.image: dhamaṇa, one of the pair that serves as the poet's seat

readings.referent: āli, the vowel series, with the purification of the moon

entries.definition: Dharma: the Buddha's teaching, and also any phenomenon. In song 5 Cāṭila builds the bridge for the sake of dharma. Munidatta takes the word as 'phenomenon': a dharma holds its own characteristic, like a pot or a cloth, and has no form by its own nature (cp.05.m3). The Tibetan of the line has chos dbyings, 'sphere of phenomena'.

The heaps or sections (skandha) of the Buddha's teaching, traditionally counted as eighty-four thousand; skandha here does not mean the five aggregates. In the tantra verse Munidatta quotes, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit for those who do not know reality (cp.06.m6).

'Source of dharmas' (Tibetan chos 'byung, regularly for Sanskrit dharmodaya): in the yoginī tantras a triangular figure, the matrix from which phenomena arise, often identified with the female organ. Song 25 opens with it. Munidatta explains it in twilight language as the dharmodaya of wisdom, or else as the source of dharmas as they truly are (cp.25.m2).

symbolic.image: the dharmodaya named in the first line

readings.referent: in twilight language, the dharmodaya of wisdom (shes rab kyi chos 'byung)
or else the source of the dharmas that, through ultimate awareness, have become just as they really are

entries.definition: Elements (dhātu): in the tantras usually five, earth, water, fire, wind and space, which with the aggregates and the senses make up the person; Abhidharma also counts eighteen elements of perception. In the Sūtaka verse Munidatta quotes, aggregates, elements and senses are each fivefold and each blessed by a tathāgata (cp.13.m4). The Tibetan has khams.

The refrain of a song, usually its second couplet, sung again after each later couplet. Munidatta names it when commenting on it. The abbreviation ধ্রু in Shastri's edition is only a cue to repeat the refrain and is not translated.

Carding: beating or combing raw cotton to loosen and separate its fibres (Old Bengali dhuṇi, 'having carded'; compare Bengali dhunā, 'to card', and Sanskrit dhū, 'shake'). Song 26 cards cotton, then fibre, again and again (1a, 1b, 3a). Munidatta renders it dhūtvā, 'having shaken' (cp.26.m2); the Tibetan line has brtags, 'examined'.

symbolic.image: carding the cotton again and again

readings.referent: examination by valid cognition: after citing tuladhuṇi he speaks of 'the valid cognition of that examination' (vicārapramāṇa) drawing out the parts and the rest (dattvā; the Tibetan has 'byin pa, 'extracting'); the Tibetan line itself has brtags, 'examined'

shaking (dhūtvā dhūtvā) the atoms that make up the parts until the whole is shown to be partless (niravayava): a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment has phye zhing phye ba, 'dividing again and again'

entries.definition: Sound or resonance (Sanskrit dhvani, Old Bengali dhani). In song 17 the sound of the string plays, and the sound of the thirty-two strings pervades everything. Munidatta speaks of 'the sound of emptiness' (cp.17.m2) and explains 'by the sound' as the unstruck knowledge of Nairātmā (cp.17.m4). The Tibetan has sgra.

symbolic.image: the sound of the vīṇā strings, which pervades everything

readings.referent: the sound of emptiness (śūnyatādhvani), as he sums up the refrain

the unstruck knowledge of Nairātmā (anāhatanairātmajñāna), which has the nature of wisdom and means and pervades being and nonbeing; the Tibetan has 'the knowledge of the unstruck Nairātmā' (gzhom du med pa bdag med ma'i ye shes)

entries.definition: Dimness of sight (Tibetan rab rib, regularly for Sanskrit timira): an eye disorder in which one sees hairs, specks or a double moon that are not there, and so a stock Buddhist image of false appearance. In song 24 the sun clears the dim sight of delusion in the ocean of existence; Munidatta's comment does not single the word out.

A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the unfit (abhavya) is called ḍiṇḍima and the fit 'great kāliñjara' (cp.04.m3). As an ordinary word a ḍiṇḍima is a kind of drum.

symbolic.image: ḍiṇḍima, in ordinary use a kind of drum

readings.referent: the unfit (abhavya)
readings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

entries.definition: A doe, the female deer (Old Bengali hariṇī). In this song her dwelling (or that of the pair) is not known, and she tells the deer to leave this forest. Munidatta calls hariṇī twilight language for the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), Nairātmā, and derives the word from harati, 'takes away' (cp.06.m5). The Tibetan translation has ri dgas ma.

symbolic.image: the doe, who tells the deer to leave this forest

readings.referent: the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), Nairātmā: hariṇī is twilight language for her, 'she who takes away' (harati) the graspings of existence; as the meditator's practice matures she comforts the mind-deer and tells it to leave the body-forest for the lotus grove of great bliss
with the deer, the pair 'mind and wind' (cittapavana), whose dwelling is not understood through the door of the senses; the gloss implies that the doe is the wind but does not say so

entries.definition: A woman of the Ḍom caste, a community that caste society treated as untouchable and kept at the edge of towns and villages. In Kāṇha's songs she is the woman the poet addresses and desires; in this song her hut stands outside the town, she dances on a lotus, and he says he will kill her.

symbolic.image: a Ḍom woman whose hut stands outside the town

readings.referent: Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess), the purified avadhūtī; she is called Ḍombī because she cannot be touched
Nairātmā, whom he addresses in place of Ḍombī (‘O Ḍombī, Nairātmā’)
the unpurified avadhūtī, for one who lacks the guru's lineage
the yoginī of those without the teaching lineage (asampradāyayoginī), who wrecks conventional bodhicitta
the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā), the unpurified avadhūtī, whose flow Kāṇha sets out to break
wind in form (vāyurūpā)
the jñānamudrā: the purified avadhūtī, luminous by nature

entries.definition: The name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 24 is sung, known only from the Tibetan heading. dpa' bo is the regular Tibetan for vīra, 'hero'; ti la looks like a transcription, perhaps of tila or tilaka. The Indian name behind it is not identified, so the Wylie is kept.

A large kettledrum (Sanskrit dundubhi, Old Bengali dunduhi), beaten in war and at festivals; in Buddhist stories gods sound it in the sky at great events. In the refrain of song 19 its sound rises with cries of victory as Kāṇha sets out to marry Ḍombī. The Tibetan line has rnga chen, 'great drum', and places it in the sky.

symbolic.image: the sound of the kettledrum rising, with cries of victory, as Kāṇha sets out to marry Ḍombī

readings.referent: one of the omens (nimitta) that appeared in abundance in the sky, with cries of 'victory, victory' and a rain of flowers, when Kṛṣṇācāryapāda set out to break the flow of Ḍombī, the unpurified avadhūtikā

entries.definition: The bad destinies or lower realms of rebirth (Sanskrit durgati, Tibetan ngan 'gro): usually the animal realm, the hungry ghosts and the hells, the unhappy half of the six realms. Munidatta says the mind-mouse itself brings about the fall into them, naming animals and hells (cp.21.m3).

Wicked people (Old Bengali dujjaṇa, Sanskrit durjana). Song 32 (4b) says that in their company one abasari jāi, apparently 'goes to ruin'; the Tibetan line has 'dies' and calls them sdug pa'i skye bo, perhaps for gdug pa'i, 'harmful', as in its comment. Munidatta reads them as delusion and the like (cp.32.m5).

symbolic.image: the wicked, in whose company one goes to ruin

readings.referent: delusion and the like (mohādi), 'the wicked, delusion and the rest' (mohādidurjana), through association with which ordinary people sink in the ocean of saṃsāra; the Tibetan comment agrees (gti mug la sogs pa gdug pa'i skye bo)

entries.definition: Hard to discern or to mark out (Sanskrit durlakṣa, Old Bengali dulakkha): not picked out by any sign. The refrain of song 29 says biṇāṇā, apparently consciousness, is hard to discern (2a); Munidatta says reality, being hard to discern, cannot be discerned by a novice yogin (cp.29.m3). The Tibetan line has mtshon du med, 'cannot be indicated'.

Duality, a pair of opposites (Old Bengali dvandala, apparently from Sanskrit dvandva, 'pair, opposition'). Song 30 (1b) speaks of splitting being and nonbeing, dvandala. Munidatta's paraphrase sets 'the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest' beside being and nonbeing in its place (cp.30.m2); the Tibetan line has no clear equivalent. The sense is uncertain.

A dual aspect (dvayākāra): appearance as two, above all as grasped object and grasping subject. Munidatta says that on this excellent path, being nondual, the dual aspect does not exist (cp.26.m4); his paraphrase puts it where song 26 has dui māra (4a), and the Tibetan line has rnam pa gnyis, 'two aspects'.

Hatred or aversion (dveṣa), with passion and delusion one of the three root afflictions. Song 11 writes deśa, which the Tibetan zhe sdang and Munidatta's rāgadveṣādika (cp.11.m4) show stands for dveṣa; the same spelling is the ordinary word for 'country, place'.

Gambling, play at dice (Sanskrit dyūta, dyūtakrīḍā). Munidatta introduces song 12 as Kāṇha setting out the same meaning again through the contemplation of a game of dice (cp.12.m1); the Tibetan has rgyan po 'gyed pa, 'gambling'. The song's own words (a king, pawns, an elephant, sixty-four squares) suggest a board game like chess.

Eight young women (kumārī): so Munidatta, who cites the words as aṭhakumārī, and the Tibetan translation (gzhon nu ma rnams brgyad) read the end of the first line of song 13. Shastri divides it aṭhaka mārī, which might instead mean 'having struck (or killed) the eight'. The song does not say who the eight are.

symbolic.image: eight maidens, named with the boat of the three refuges

readings.referent: the bliss of the Buddha's lordship (buddhaiśvarya) and the rest, which is experienced; the Tibetan comment agrees (sangs rgyas kyi dbang phyug)

entries.definition: Having one form or aspect (ekākāra). In the refrain of song 11 Kāṇha wanders in the town of the body ekārem̐, which Munidatta renders ekākāratayā, 'in oneness of form' (cp.11.m2). The Tibetan has rigs gcig, 'of one kind'. Whether the Old Bengali simply means 'alone' is uncertain.

Having one mind, the mind made single (Old Bengali ekumaṇā; compare Sanskrit ekamanas). In song 23 (1b) Bhusuku will become one-minded on entering the lotus grove; the Tibetan line has 'make the mind one'. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, explains making the mind one as becoming free of conceptual thought (cp.23.m2).

symbolic.image: becoming one-minded on entering the lotus grove

readings.referent: becoming free of conceptual thought (rnam par rtog pa med pa), oneself rightly calling to oneself (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘One taste’: the realization that all things share a single nature, so that apparent opposites are not experienced as separate; a key term of siddha and Mahāmudrā teaching. Munidatta says Kṛṣṇācārya dances on the lotus with Nairātmā ‘in one taste’.

An elephant, one of the recurring images of siddha poetry. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya's Dohākoṣa that Munidatta quotes, the great elephant (karivara) dwells far away (cp.06.m4); Munidatta does not explain the images of the verse. The Tibetan translation has glang chen mchog, 'best of elephants'. In song 9 Munidatta names the elephant as twilight language for the mind (cp.09.m1, cp.09.m3).

symbolic.image: the elephant, the lord of elephants (karivara, gajendra)

readings.referent: the mind: in twilight language the elephant is the mind (cittagajendra, the mind as lord of elephants), and Kāṇha himself is that elephant
the mind of suchness of the lord of yogis, as lord of elephants (tathatācittagajendra)
the mind as lord of elephants (cittagajendra), in whose twilight language Mahīdhara teaches

entries.definition: The syllables e and vaṃ, which open the formula ‘Thus (evaṃ) have I heard’ at the head of the sūtras and tantras; in the yoginī tantras they stand for the female and male, wisdom and means, joined. In a verse of Kāṇha that Munidatta quotes, the lotus blossoms taking evaṃkāra as its seed (cp.03.m4). In song 9 Munidatta makes e the moon-appearance and vaṃ the sun (cp.09.m2); the Tibetan comment has them the other way round.

The eye (Old Bengali ākhi, Sanskrit akṣi, locana). The last line of song 15 says to go the road with eyes closed (ākhi bujia); the Tibetan line has 'the road known by the eye'. Munidatta has the yogi see coupled union with eyes fixed and open, and quotes a verse on the eyes of those who gaze at emptiness (cp.15.m6).

symbolic.image: going the road with eyes closed

readings.referent: seeing coupled union (yuganaddha) with eyes fixed and open; the Tibetan comment has 'with the pair of eyes half-closed and unmoving' (a paraphrase where the song has eyes closed; no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: The father (Old Bengali bāpa, modern Bengali bāp). In song 20 (4b), after the root is cut, the father is destroyed (saṃghārā), a violent paradox like the killing of the mother in song 11. Munidatta's comment does not mention him, and the Tibetan line has no father. Not to be confused with bāpūṛā, 'poor wretch', in 3b.

The husband's father (Old Bengali susurā, Sanskrit śvaśura), who in song 2 falls asleep while the young wife stays awake. The Tibetan translation has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law', both in the song and in the commentary. Munidatta cites the word as sasurā.

symbolic.image: the father-in-law who has fallen asleep

readings.referent: the breath, beginning with the 'swift' (tvarita), led into yogic sleep, the fourth joy

entries.definition: A fine weave, finely woven cloth (Tibetan thags bzangs; the line spells thag bzangs). In couplet 4 of song 25 the unstruck fine weave is not apart from the guru's word. Munidatta says the phrase is twilight language and explains it through prāṇa and āyāma, the unstruck sound and the two winds (cp.25.m5).

symbolic.image: the unstruck fine weave, not apart from the guru's word

readings.referent: in twilight language: through prāṇa and āyāma, which have the nature of means and wisdom, fully imagining the unstruck sound and the image (gzugs brnyan) in the two winds; the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation

entries.definition: A footrest or foot support (Tibetan rkang rten). In the first line of song 25 it stands between the dharmodaya and the vajra's place; in a weaving song it may name part of the loom, but that is a guess, and the Old Bengali word is lost. Munidatta says the four feet become the support of the four joys (cp.25.m2).

symbolic.image: the footrest of the first line

readings.referent: the four feet (rkang pa bzhi) that have become the support of the four joys; he adds a verse of the Hevajra (Tibetan comment only)

entries.definition: A forest or wood (Old Bengali baṇa, Sanskrit vana). In this song the doe tells the deer to leave this forest. Munidatta reads it as the body, 'this body-forest' (kāyavana) (cp.06.m5). The Tibetan translation has nags, 'forest', in the line and lus kyi nags, 'forest of the body', in the commentary.

symbolic.image: this forest, which the doe tells the deer to leave

readings.referent: the body, 'this body-forest' (kāyavana): the mind-deer is to give up its grasping at the body (kāyagraha) and go to the lotus grove of great bliss

entries.definition: The full moon (Tibetan zla ba gang ba). Song 24 opens with the full moon risen, when the king of mind is stainless. Munidatta explains it as the moon-disc of bodhicitta, complete with its sixteen digits, which rises by the guru's kindness (cp.24.m2). Compare the entries for the moon and the sixteen digits.

symbolic.image: the full moon, at whose rising the king of mind is stainless

readings.referent: the moon-disc (zla ba'i dkyil 'khor) of bodhicitta, endowed with sixteen digits, which rises by the guru's kindness; at that time the lord of yogis, the king of mind, becomes utterly stainless

entries.definition: Sky; open space. The sky is a common image in siddha poetry and in Buddhist tantric language. In this song it forms the first half of gaaṇadukhola, the vessel used to bail the boat; Munidatta repeats the compound (gaganadukholaka) without explaining it.

symbolic.image: the sky, in the compound 'sky-scoop' used to bail the boat

readings.referent: the instruction of the fourth joy: Munidatta sets 'the instruction of the sky' and 'the instruction of the fourth joy' side by side
form and the rest, all sky, where the fleeing deer dissolves into clear light (Tibetan comment)
filling the sky: being wholly joined with purified clear light (Tibetan comment)
clear light: his paraphrase of the refrain puts prabhāsvara where the song has the middle of the sky
clear light: the sky the branches of the tree touch

entries.definition: The Gaṅgā of the sky (gaganagaṅgā), in Indian myth the heavenly course of the Ganges. In Munidatta's comment on the last couplet of song 16, where the song has 'the courtyard of the sky', the mind-elephant goes to the sky-Gaṅgā, which he identifies with the lake of the wheel of great bliss (cp.16.m6). The Tibetan comment lacks it.

symbolic.image: the Gaṅgā of the sky

readings.referent: the lake of the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), which the mind-elephant, driven by the fire of the passion of great bliss, reaches and merges with

entries.definition: In Buddhist doctrine, the being of the intermediate state between death and rebirth, said to feed on smells and to enter the womb at conception; in Indian myth also a celestial musician. Munidatta reads the song's customer as the gandharva being (gandharvasattva), who enters by the door of Vairocana and does not come out (cp.03.m4, cp.03.m6).

A buyer or customer (Sanskrit grāhaka, a word that also means ‘grasper’). In song 3 a customer comes to the liquor-seller, and one who has gone in does not come out. The Tibetan translation renders ‘beer-buyer’ (chang nyo) and ‘beer-drinker’ (chang 'thung).

symbolic.image: a customer who comes to the liquor shop and, once inside, does not come out

readings.referent: the gandharva being (gandharvasattva), who, seeing the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion at the door of Vairocana, comes of itself, enters by that door and drinks the juice of the lotus of great bliss

the gandharva being, which enters from the blazing fire of great passion and whose entry has no coming out; Munidatta calls this couplet the stopping of the gandharva being's going (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Gauḍā, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 18 is sung, given in its heading; Gauḍa is also an old name for part of Bengal. The Tibetan translation calls the melody glu dbyangs chen po, 'the great melody', as it calls that of song 2 chen po; whether Gauḍā and Gavaṛā are one rāga is uncertain.
Gavaṛā, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 2 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) instead names the melody chen po, 'great'; why it does so is unclear.

A toll station (Old Bengali ghāṭa; Sanskrit ghaṭṭa, a landing place or toll station on a river or road), where travellers paid dues. Song 15 says there is none on the road it describes. Munidatta lists the toll-house (ghaṭakuṭī, for ghaṭṭakuṭī) among the dangers absent from this path (cp.15.m6); the Tibetan has khral sa, 'tax place'.

Disgust or revulsion (Old Bengali ghiṇa, Sanskrit ghṛṇā; Tibetan skyug bro, 'nausea'): the aversion that caste purity attaches to impure people, places and substances, which tantric conduct sets out to overcome. Song 31 twice pairs it with fear as what the poet has given up (4a, 5b); Munidatta has shame (lajjā) in its place (cp.31.m5). Compare 'without disgust'.

Gold (Old Bengali sonā). In the first line of song 8 the boat of compassion is filled with gold, leaving no place for silver; the Tibetan translation has gser. Munidatta's paraphrase has the boat filled with the essence of the true guru's grace, through identity with emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (cp.08.m2).

symbolic.image: the gold with which the boat of compassion is filled

readings.referent: the essence (rasa) of the true guru's grace, with which the boat, bodhicitta, is filled through its identity with emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (his paraphrase puts this where the song has 'filled with gold'; he gives no explicit gloss of the gold)

entries.definition: A gourd (Old Bengali lāu, from Sanskrit alābu), dried and hollowed to serve as the resonator of a vīṇā. In song 17 the sun is the gourd, with the moon attached as the string. Munidatta has the sun-appearance imagined (utprekṣya) in the form of a gourd (tumbinī) (cp.17.m2); the Tibetan has ku ba.

symbolic.image: the gourd of the vīṇā, which the song says is the sun
