readings.referent: the sun-appearance (sūryābhāsa), imagined as having the form of the gourd; the song itself names the sun as the gourd, and the Tibetan comment agrees (nyi ma'i snang ba ku ba'i rnam par bltas nas)

entries.definition: The pair 'what is grasped' and 'what grasps', object and subject. Buddhist thought, especially Yogācāra and the tantras, treats their apparent separation as the root of delusion. Munidatta applies the pair to the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and says Nairātmā accepts nothing in the manner of grasped and grasper.

Wife, mistress of the house (Old Bengali ghariṇī, Sanskrit gṛhiṇī, from gṛha, 'house'). In the refrain of song 28 the Śabara is told that his own wife is named Sahaja Sundarī. The Tibetan has khyim mi mo, 'woman of the house'.

symbolic.image: the Śabara's own wife

readings.referent: the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā) Nairātmā, wife of the vajra-holder, who dwells on the summit
Nairātmā speaking: 'I am your wife, the jñānamudrā, Sahajasundarī'

entries.definition: A word of unknown sense in the refrain of song 28, paired with gulī: the mad Śabara is told not to make gulī guhāḍā. Munidatta explains only gulī (cp.28.m3), and the Tibetan line, which keeps gu li, has nothing for it. Kept in source form until its sense is found.

An Old Bengali word of uncertain meaning in the refrain of song 28: 'do not make gulī guhāḍā'. Munidatta explains 'do not make gulī' as 'do not form conceptual thoughts such as joy' (cp.28.m3), without a Sanskrit equivalent. The Tibetan keeps the word as gu li, untranslated, and has nothing for guhāḍā.

symbolic.image: making gulī, which the Śabara is told not to do

readings.referent: conceptual thoughts such as joy (ānandādivikalpa), which the Śabara is told not to form

entries.definition: A guard or customs post on a road (Old Bengali gumā, from Sanskrit gulma, which among other senses means a body of guards or their station). Song 15 says there is none on the road it describes. Munidatta names the gulma among the dangers absent from this path (cp.15.m6); the Tibetan has sho gam, 'customs post'.

A garland of guñjā berries, the glossy red, black-tipped seeds of the rosary-pea vine (Abrus precatorius), worn by the Śabarī at her neck in song 28. Spelled like the rāga Guñjarī of song 5 (গুঞ্জরী) but a different word. The Tibetan has ma ru'i phreng ba, and its commentary glosses ma ru as guñjā (guny+dza).

symbolic.image: the guñjā garland at the Śabarī's neck

readings.referent: the secret mantra (guhyamantra), held at the neck, the wheel of enjoyment (sambhogacakra); the Sanskrit is partly corrupt here, and the Tibetan has 'the secret mantra of guhya'

entries.definition: Guñjarī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 5 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes it gu dz+dza rI, which may point to Gujjarī, a Prakrit form of the rāga name Gurjarī; how the two spellings relate is uncertain.

A spiritual teacher. The refrain of song 1 tells the listener to ask the guru. Munidatta stresses that empowerment and the key instruction come from the true guru, and quotes the Guhyasamāja: without the vajra guru one cannot reach nirvāṇa (cp.01.m3).

readings.referent: the true guru, by whose word the innate echo and conventional bodhicitta are accomplished (Tibetan comment)

entries.definition: The unbroken transmission of practical instruction from teacher to student in tantric practice. Munidatta says Ḍombī's hut is known through it, and that for one who lacks it Ḍombī is the unpurified avadhūtī.

The one who steers a boat (Sanskrit karṇadhāra, 'holder of the helm'; Old Bengali kaṇṇahāra). In the last couplet of song 13 the mind is the helmsman; Munidatta repeats 'the mind as helmsman', set on the boat-path of emptiness (cp.13.m6). The Tibetan has mnyen pa, perhaps 'boatman' or 'rowing'.

A cause (hetu), above all the direct cause from which an effect arises, as against its supporting conditions. Munidatta says that what has been shown to be partless has no cause, so no other cause (hetvantara) of that mind is found (cp.26.m2), words that stand where song 26 (2a) has herua. The Tibetan has rgyu.

Old Bengali gātī, apparently a hole or pit (compare Sanskrit garta), which the mouse digs in song 21 (3a). Munidatta cites the word as gatī and takes it as gati, 'destiny' (cp.21.m3). The Tibetan line instead has the mouse bore through a wall (rtsig pa).

symbolic.image: the holes the mouse digs

readings.referent: the fall into the bad destinies, the animal realm, the hells and the rest, which the mind-mouse brings about by itself; he takes the word as gati, 'destiny', and the Tibetan comment makes the wall (rtsig pa) of its line that fall into the bad destinies (ngan 'gro)

entries.definition: Honey (Sanskrit and Old Bengali madhu; Tibetan sbrang rtsi), the sweet juice bees gather from flowers, above all the lotus. Munidatta has the mind-mouse drink 'the honey of ultimate bodhicitta' after going to the lotus grove of great bliss, and quotes Mīnanātha on the bee drinking the honey of the opened lotus (cp.21.m4).

symbolic.image: honey drunk from a lotus

readings.referent: ultimate bodhicitta: 'the honey of ultimate bodhicitta' (paramārthabodhicittamadhu), which the mind-mouse drinks after going, through the guru's lineage, to the lotus grove of great bliss and returning

entries.definition: A hoof (Old Bengali khūra, Sanskrit khura). In the last couplet the deer's hooves are not seen as it bounds away; the Tibetan translation has rkang, 'foot, leg'. Munidatta's paraphrase puts 'the parts and so on' of the mind-deer in their place: yogis who have realized innate knowledge form no concepts of them (cp.06.m6).

symbolic.image: the deer's hooves, not seen as it bounds away

readings.referent: the parts (avayava) and so on of one's own mind-deer, of which yogis who have realized innate knowledge form no concepts (his paraphrase puts them where the song has the hooves; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: A house or home (Old Bengali ghara, Sanskrit gṛha; Tibetan khang, khyim). In song 2 the refrain's gharapaṇa is not clearly segmented: ghara, "house", with an uncertain second element, is assumed. In song 3 the one liquor-seller is in two houses; in the verse of Kāṇha that Munidatta quotes, the motionless wind stays in the house of the housewife.

symbolic.image: the house of the refrain, where the thief comes at midnight; the two houses of the one liquor-seller

readings.referent: the house of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (viramānandāvadhūtīgṛha), to which the lord of yogis is told first to lead both by the instruction in vajra recitation; the gloss does not quote the song's word
the moon and the sun, left and right, which are joined and made to enter the middle channel; Munidatta glosses ‘the two’ without repeating the word ‘house’

entries.definition: The heart (Old Bengali hia, Sanskrit hṛdaya). In song 28 the heart is the betel chewed with camphor. Munidatta quotes the word as hiem̐ and renders it hṛdaya (cp.28.m6); the Tibetan line has sems, 'mind', where its commentary has snying, 'heart'.

symbolic.image: the heart as betel

readings.referent: clear light (prabhāsvara): 'the heart, clear light', which is resolved upon as the betel

entries.definition: Hunting, the chase. Song 23 opens with Bhusuku going hunting: Old Bengali ahei, perhaps from Sanskrit ākheṭa, 'hunt'; the Tibetan has rngon 'gro, 'go hunting'. Munidatta's comment, surviving only in the Tibetan, cites rngon pa and reads it as setting out in search of the means of making the quarry without intrinsic nature (cp.23.m2).

symbolic.image: Bhusuku going hunting

readings.referent: going in search of the means of making (the quarry) without intrinsic nature; the quarry, in the same comment, is the deer of the body's wind (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: A hunter (Sanskrit ākheṭika). The word is not in song 6, whose refrain has Bhusuku keeping the hunted deer in sight, but Munidatta calls Bhusukupāda the hunter, who strikes 'the other' with the arrow of the true guru's words (cp.06.m3). At that point the Tibetan translation has sor rtog, 'examination', instead.

symbolic.image: a hunter pursuing a deer

readings.referent: Bhusukupāda himself, who strikes 'the other' with the arrow of the true guru's words (sadguruvacanavāṇa); the Tibetan has his 'examination' (sor rtog) and the arrow of the true guru's feet

entries.definition: The husband (Old Bengali bhatāra, from Sanskrit bhartṛ, 'supporter, lord'). In the first line of song 20 the woman who speaks calls hers khamaṇa. Munidatta renders the word svāmin, 'lord, master' (cp.20.m2); the Tibetan has bdag, 'lord', in the line and bdag po in the comment. Compare the other kin of the songs' household, such as the mother-in-law and father-in-law.

symbolic.image: the speaker's husband, khamaṇa

readings.referent: the wholly empty mind (sarvaśūnyaṃ manaḥ) as lord (svāmin): through its attachment to love-play (surata; the syllable ra is Shastri's restoration, and the Tibetan has 'great bliss', shin du bde ba), the speaker's experience of imperishable bliss cannot be told

entries.definition: A small dwelling of thatch, bamboo or mud. In this song it is Ḍombī's hut, standing outside the town.

symbolic.image: Ḍombī's hut outside the town

readings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), beyond the reach of the senses and known through the guru's lineage (he calls it ‘your house’, tavāgāra)

entries.definition: A magic show or conjuring display (Sanskrit indrajāla, 'Indra's net'; Old Bengali indiāla), a stock image for what seems real and is not. In song 30 (3a) the indiāla breaks; the Tibetan line has mig 'phrul, 'magic show'. Munidatta takes the word as the host of the senses (indriyasamūha) and quotes Saraha on the senses dissolving (cp.30.m4).

symbolic.image: the magic show that breaks

readings.referent: the host of the senses (indriyasamūha), which breaks apart and flees on beholding innate joy; he glosses indiālam as if it came from indriya, 'sense', and backs this with Saraha's line on where the senses dissolve; the Tibetan comment agrees (mig 'phrul ni dbang po'i tshogs)

entries.definition: The senses or sense faculties (indriya): eye, ear, nose, tongue and body, with the mind in some lists, each a 'door' through which objects are known. Munidatta says the dwelling of the mind and the wind is not understood through the door of the senses (cp.06.m4).

Birth (Sanskrit janman, Old Bengali jāma), and so one life in the round of rebirth. The refrain of song 8 asks how a birth that is gone will come again. Munidatta says another birth returns to one who does not row the boat of the fourth means (cp.08.m2). The Tibetan has skye ba.

'The city of the Jina' (the Victor, a title of the Buddha): the place the singer says he will reach again through the true guru. The Old Bengali jiṇaurā corresponds to Sanskrit jinapura, the form Munidatta uses.

symbolic.image: the city of the Jina, the goal of the crossing

readings.referent: the city of great bliss (mahāsukhapura)

entries.definition: Living, alive (Old Bengali jībanta, from Sanskrit jīvant). The refrain of song 23 (2a) sets the living against the dead in an obscure line; the Tibetan has 'do not kill the living, do not take the corpse of the dead'. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, reads the living as the entering breath (cp.23.m3).

symbolic.image: the living, set against the dead in the refrain

readings.referent: the entering breath (rab tu zhugs pa'i dbugs), joined with the syllable oṃ and the knowledge of day, and having the nature of the forty natures (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Knowledge (Tibetan ye shes, regularly for Sanskrit jñāna): in tantric usage the nondual awareness that realization reveals, as distinct from ordinary cognition. Munidatta says the lord of yogis pervades the three worlds with the rays of knowledge (cp.24.m4). Compare wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna) and knowledge (vidyā), a different word.

'Wisdom seal': in the yoginī tantras, a partner visualized in meditation, as distinct from a physical partner (karmamudrā) and from Mahāmudrā. Munidatta says hariṇī, 'doe', is twilight language for the jñānamudrā, Nairātmā, who comforts the mind-deer as the meditator's practice matures (cp.06.m5).
A cowrie shell, used as small change in eastern India. In the song the ferrywoman takes no cowrie for the crossing; Munidatta compares the ordinary ferry-master, who takes a cowrie as the fare.

A rope, apparently the boat's mooring line (Old Bengali kācchi; Munidatta has kacchikā; the Tibetan translation nyag thag, 'rope'). In song 8 it is let loose once the stake is pulled up. Munidatta's gloss speaks of loosening a thread of knowledge (vidyāsūtra); the Tibetan commentary has the thread of ignorance (cp.08.m3).

symbolic.image: the rope let loose once the stake is pulled up

readings.referent: a thread of knowledge (vidyāsūtra), to be loosened so that the boat runs swiftly; the Sanskrit reads kacchikāsu vidyāsūtrañ ca, and the Tibetan commentary has instead 'the rope is the thread of ignorance' (ma rig pa'i srad bu), as if reading avidyāsūtra

entries.definition: A code word of the yoginī tantras; in ordinary Sanskrit kakkola is a fragrant berry or a perfume made from it. The Hevajra Tantra's list of code words gives it for the lotus, the female organ, and bola for the vajra. In the verse Munidatta quotes on song 18 it meets 'dear bola' (cp.18.m5), unexplained. The Tibetan transcribes it.

Kāla, 'time', and by extension death: time as the destroyer. In song 1 it enters the restless mind. Munidatta identifies it with Rāhu, the eclipse demon, and supports this with a verse of Kṛṣṇācārya in which the pure water dries up when the fire of time (kālāgni) enters (cp.01.m2).

symbolic.image: Kāla, time or death, entering the restless mind

readings.referent: Rāhu, who from the first day of the dark fortnight dries up the moon of conventional bodhicitta through the sequence of lunar days

entries.definition: 'The Man of Time': time personified, or a servant of Yama, lord of the dead. Munidatta says the young wife fears the kāyakālapuruṣa, perhaps 'the Man of Time in the body' (the compound is unclear), glossing the word the Tibetan translation takes as 'crow' (cp.02.m5).

The series of Sanskrit consonants. Munidatta glosses the camaṇa of song 1 as kāli, with the purification of the sun, and quotes the union of āli and kāli as Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6). In song 7 he pairs it instead with (ā)lokābhāsa, the spreading of light, as āli with the light (cp.07.m2). Not to be confused with kāla or the goddess Kālī.

A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the fit (bhavya) is called 'great kāliñjara' and the unfit ḍiṇḍima (cp.04.m3); in his own sentence the Tibetan translation renders the word by its sense, skal ba dang ldan pa, 'fortunate'. As an ordinary name, Kāliñjara is a hill fort in central India.

symbolic.image: kāliñjara, in ordinary use the name of a hill fort

readings.referent: the fit (bhavya)
readings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

entries.definition: The juice or nectar (rasa) of the lotus, which the poet says he drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth. The Tibetan translation has chu skyes khu ba, 'lotus juice'.

symbolic.image: the lotus nectar the poet drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth

readings.referent: ultimate (paramārtha) bodhicitta, described as the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus

entries.definition: A lotus plant, or a cluster or pond of lotuses (Sanskrit kamalinī, from kamala, 'lotus'). In song 27 (3b) the kamalinī carries the lotus along a conduit. Munidatta explains the word as 'she who has the lotus juice', the juice of great bliss (cp.27.m4); the Tibetan has pad+ma can, 'the one with the lotus'.

symbolic.image: the lotus plant (kamalinī) that carries the lotus along the conduit

readings.referent: the naturally purified avadhūtikā, Nairātmā, so called because she has the lotus juice, the juice of great bliss; with that juice, bodhicitta, she gladdens the vajra of body and carries it to the region of the wheel of great bliss

entries.definition: Kāmoda, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 13 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody 'dod pa sbyin pa, 'giving what is desired', as if the name were Sanskrit kāmada, 'granting wishes'; how the two forms relate is uncertain.

A word of uncertain sense closing the refrain of song 15, after rājapatha, 'royal road'. Munidatta's simile has a king keeping to the golden road (kanakapathadhārayā), and the Tibetan line has 'golden road' (gser lam), as if kaṇḍhārā held kanaka, 'gold'; a link with Bengali kāṇḍārī, 'helmsman' (Sanskrit karṇadhāra), is also possible.

An object the thief takes at midnight, apparently an ear ornament (Old Bengali kāna, 'ear'), though the literal sense is not certain and Munidatta does not give it. The Tibetan translation has mdo phugs khang logs, which seems to describe a part of the house rather than an ornament.

symbolic.image: the earring the thief takes at midnight

readings.referent: the vibhava ('wealth' or 'unfolding') of the faults of the winds beginning with entering, stolen by the thief, innate joy
the fault of the winds beginning with entering, carried off by the thief, the clear light; with the grasped and the rest absent, the lord of yogis then asks for nothing anywhere in the ten directions

entries.definition: The neck or throat (Sanskrit kaṇṭha). In song 18 the wise do not let go of Ḍombī's neck, apparently keeping her in their embrace; the Tibetan line has mgul, 'neck', and 'khyud, 'embrace'. Munidatta reads the word as the wheel of enjoyment (sambhogacakra), the wheel at the throat (cp.18.m5).

symbolic.image: Ḍombī's neck, which the wise do not let go of

readings.referent: the wheel of enjoyment (sambhogacakra), named in apposition to the throat (kaṇṭhe sambhogacakre), which the lords of yogis who know Ḍombī do not abandon day and night; the Tibetan has 'gul ba, apparently for mgul ba, 'neck', beside 'the wheel of complete enjoyment'

entries.definition: An ascetic who carries a skull-bowl, wears ornaments of bone, keeps to cremation grounds and ignores the rules of caste purity; the observance is found in Śaiva and Buddhist tantric circles alike. Kāṇha calls himself one and puts on a garland of bones for Ḍombī.

readings.referent: one who protects ka, conventional bodhicitta (kaṃ saṃvṛtibodhicittaṃ pālayati), by setting the vajra of mind (cittavajra) in place

entries.definition: Words of uncertain sense in song 17 (4a): when karahā and karahaka are, it seems, pressed, the thirty-two strings sound, so they may be parts of the vīṇā; the Tibetan line has 'wood and little wood' (shing dang shing bu). Munidatta explains karaha as the heat of the mind and karahakala as clear light (cp.17.m4).

symbolic.image: the karahā and karahaka, pressed as the thirty-two strings sound

readings.referent: karaha: the heat of the mind (cittauṣṇya), to be understood by reflection; the Tibetan comment has instead 'the camel of the mind' (sems kyi rnga mong)

karahakala: clear light (prabhāsvara), called 'the fruit carried by compassion' (karuṇāvahata phalaṃ, apparently corrupt; the Tibetan has 'the unstruck portion of compassion', snying rje gzhom du med pa'i cha), which, as 'the clear-light Rāhu' (prabhāsvararāhuka), presses down the heat of the mind at the moment of vilakṣaṇa

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in song 19 (1b), where mind and wind are 'karaṇḍa and kaśālā', apparently instruments of the wedding band, like the drums of line 1a. In Sanskrit karaṇḍa is a basket or box; which instrument is meant is unclear. The Tibetan names one instrument, khar rnga, 'bronze drum', for the pair; Munidatta does not gloss it.

A female elephant (Sanskrit kariṇī). In song 9 the elephant is in rut for the she-elephant, and in the same way suchness-ichor flows. The Tibetan translation has glang mo. Munidatta sets the outer she-elephant beside the Blessed Lady Nairātmā (cp.09.m3).

symbolic.image: the she-elephant for whom the elephant is in rut

readings.referent: the Blessed Lady Nairātmā: as an outer elephant bears the ichor of passion toward a she-elephant, so the mind-elephant Kṛṣṇācārya, through union with Nairātmā, rains the ichor of suchness (a correspondence made by the simile, not an explicit gloss)

entries.definition: Action or deed (Sanskrit karman; Tibetan las), and the force of past deeds that brings rebirth. Song 22 asks whether kāma comes from birth or birth from kāma (6a); Munidatta and the Tibetan read kāma as karman, though the same spelling means 'desire'. Munidatta calls the lord of yogis free of agent and action (cp.22.m7).

'Action seal': in the yoginī tantras, a physical woman partner in the yoga of sexual union, as distinct from an imagined partner and from Mahāmudrā. Munidatta says conventional bodhicitta is 'milked' through the sequence of joys in the course of union with a karmamudrā (cp.02.m2).

Compassion: the wish that beings be free of suffering, paired in Mahāyāna and tantric thought with wisdom. Munidatta says Virūpa speaks with a mind moved again and again by supreme compassion (cp.03.m1); the Sekoddeśa verse he quotes speaks of the lord's strength of wisdom and compassion (cp.03.m5).

readings.referent: the self-blessing mind (svādhiṣṭhānacitta): in song 12 the karuṇā of the game is the mind in that form
with the cloud, the purified enjoyment body
conventional bodhicitta

entries.definition: Effect and cause: Old Bengali kāja (Sanskrit kārya, 'what is to be done, work, effect') and kāraṇa, 'cause'. Song 26 (5a) says there is neither. Munidatta says Śānti, being free of effect and cause, speaks the unsurpassed state (cp.26.m5). The Tibetan has bya ba and byed pa, 'act and agent'.

Apparently a bell-metal percussion instrument, cymbals or a gong (compare Sanskrit kāṃsyatāla, 'bell-metal cymbal', and Bengali kā̃sar, 'gong'). In song 19 mind and wind are the karaṇḍa and kaśālā of Kāṇha's wedding music. The Tibetan line has khar rnga, 'bronze drum', probably a gong. Munidatta does not gloss the word.

Body, speech and mind (kāya, vāc, citta): the three doors of action, and in the tantras the three aspects of a buddha that practice makes one's own (compare the three vajras). Munidatta reads the song's three refuges as body, speech and mind, which dissolve in a fourth, the body of great bliss (cp.13.m2); Tibetan lus dang ngag dang yid.
An oar, or perhaps a steering paddle, of a boat. In this song there are five of them; what exactly is done with them in the line is uncertain.

symbolic.image: five oars

readings.referent: the instruction of the Five Stages (pañcakrama), which the yogī takes up

entries.definition: A key (Sanskrit kuñcikā, Old Bengali koñcā). In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has lde kyog, 'hooked key', both in the line and in Munidatta's comment.

symbolic.image: the key put, with the lock, in the mother-in-law's house

readings.referent: with the lock: closing the lock, explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense naming the speaker's husband in the first line of song 20 (khamaṇabhatāre). It can be divided as kha, 'sky', and maṇa, 'mind', as the Tibetan does (nam mkha'i yid, 'sky-mind'); Prakrit khamaṇa can also mean a Jain ascetic (Sanskrit kṣapaṇa). Munidatta explains it as the wholly empty mind (cp.20.m2).

symbolic.image: khamaṇa, the speaker's husband

readings.referent: the mind, wholly empty (sarvaśūnyaṃ manaḥ), as the lord (svāmin) of the speaker, whom he takes to be the Blessed Lady Nairātmā; the Tibetan comment has 'having a sky-mind' (nam mkha'i yid can) and 'the lord of the mind, in the all-empty'

entries.definition: A pillar or post (Old Bengali khambha, Sanskrit stambha). In song 16 khambhāṭhāṇā, 'the pillar's place', is apparently where the elephant is tethered. Munidatta reads it as the pillar of ignorance, which the mind-elephant crushes (cp.16.m4); the Tibetan has ka ba, 'pillar'. Compare the post (bākhoṛa) of song 9.

symbolic.image: the pillar where the elephant is tied

readings.referent: the pillar of ignorance (avidyāstambha), which the mind-elephant crushes

entries.definition: A staff topped with a skull, carried by kāpālika ascetics and held by many tantric deities. Munidatta (khaṭṭāṅga) and the Tibetan translation (kha T+wAM ga) read the khaṭṭe of song 11 as this staff; but khaṭṭa can also mean 'bed, cot', so the literal sense of the line is not certain.

symbolic.image: the khaṭvāṅga, the skull-topped staff

readings.referent: emptiness: he explains kha as emptiness and adds 'having touched the innate with the clear light'; the rest of the word is not explained, and Shastri notes a variant śūratā, 'heroism', for śūnyatā

entries.definition: A stake or post (Old Bengali khuṇṭi), apparently the one the boat is moored to: in song 8 it is pulled up before the boat sets off. Munidatta writes khuṇṭikā; the Tibetan translation has brtod phur, 'tethering stake', in the song and the comment. Munidatta reads it as the fault of appearance (cp.08.m3).

symbolic.image: the stake pulled up before the boat sets off

readings.referent: the fault of appearance (ābhāsadoṣa), which the best of yogis is to pull up once he has made the guru's word firm; the Tibetan commentary has the guru's word producing firmness against the fault of appearance, without the pulling up

entries.definition: The mind spoken of as a king (Tibetan sems kyi rgyal po; the Bengali original is lost). In song 24 the king of mind is stainless once the full moon has risen. Munidatta names the lord of yogis and the king of mind together, as the one who becomes utterly stainless when the moon-disc of bodhicitta rises (cp.24.m2).

symbolic.image: the king of mind, stainless when the full moon has risen

readings.referent: the lord of yogis (rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug), named in apposition with it, who becomes utterly stainless when the moon-disc of bodhicitta rises by the guru's kindness
the jewel of mind (cittaratna)

entries.definition: The afflictions: disturbing mental states such as desire, hatred and delusion that keep beings in saṃsāra. In the Guhyasamāja verse Munidatta quotes, nirvāṇa is the state that removes all afflictions, reached only with the vajra guru (cp.01.m3).

A compartment or chamber (Old Bengali koṭhā; compare Sanskrit koṣṭha, koṣṭhaka). In the last line of song 12 Kāṇha counts sixty-four of them, the squares of the game board; the Tibetan translation has re mig, 'squares'. Munidatta speaks of the wheel of emanation 'with sixty-four compartments' (catuḥṣaṣṭikoṣṭaka).

symbolic.image: the sixty-four squares Kāṇha counts

readings.referent: the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), with its sixty-four compartments, in which Kṛṣṇācārya, having made it steady, takes his own mind, clear light by nature

entries.definition: Throwing or casting (Sanskrit kṣepa; Old Bengali khem̐pa-, here an imperative). In song 4 the yoginī is told to throw; what she throws is not said. The Tibetan translation has 'phangs nas, ‘having thrown’, in the song and the comment. Munidatta takes the throw as union in her own place (svasthānayoga).

symbolic.image: the yoginī told to throw

readings.referent: union in her own place (svasthānayoga), from which she, the Nairātmā yoginī in the form of bodhicitta, enjoys play at the root of the jewel and rises to be absorbed into the wheel of great bliss

entries.definition: The bank or shore of a river (Sanskrit kūla; the manuscript writes kula). The last line has someone sinking at the shore, or 'shore after shore'. The spelling coincides with kula, 'family, clan', a different word that needs its own entry.

symbolic.image: the river bank at which those who climbed into the chariot sink

readings.referent: the body (śarīra), in which yogis proud of outer treatises, not knowing selflessness, wander
each individual body (pratyekaśarīra)

entries.definition: High-born, of good family (Sanskrit kulīna, from kula, 'family'): people of respectable caste, bound by purity rules that forbid contact with outcastes. The refrain of song 18 sets the kuliṇajaṇa, 'high-born people', at the edge or outside (ante) and the kāpālī in the middle. Munidatta does not comment; the Tibetan has mtha' rigs skye ba, of unclear division.

In yoga, holding the breath after drawing it in, named from kumbha, 'pot', since the body is held full like a jar. Munidatta speaks of the absorption (samādhi) of kumbhaka purified by vilakṣaṇa and reads the song's crocodile (kumbhīra) through it (cp.02.m2); the Tibetan transcribes the word.

Jasmine (Sanskrit kunda, transliterated in the Tibetan as kun+da), a white flower. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes on the stainless cloth, the conventional is like jasmine and the ultimate has the form of bliss (cp.25.m2). In the tantras its whiteness makes it a stock simile for conventional bodhicitta, the white vital essence.

Earrings (kuṇḍala), often large rings, worn by yogis and kāpālika ascetics as part of their regalia. In song 11 the sun and the moon are made into the poet's earrings. The Tibetan has rna ba'i rgyan, 'ear ornament'. A different word from kāneṭa in song 2, which the glossary also renders 'earring'.

symbolic.image: the sun and the moon made into earrings

entries.definition: A word the tantras use for the sexual union of yogic practice, usually spelled kunduru; in ordinary Sanskrit kunduru is olibanum, a fragrant resin. The poet calls himself a hero in kundura. Munidatta explains it as the imperishable bliss of uniting the two organs (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan translation keeps the word.

symbolic.image: kundura, in which the poet says he is a hero

readings.referent: the union of the two organs (dvīndriyasamāpatti) and the imperishable bliss of that yoga, by which he crushes the enemy, the afflictions

entries.definition: Virtue, the wholesome (kuśala): actions and states that lead to happiness and awakening; their accumulated force is called the roots of virtue. Munidatta says the last couplet of song 9 shows the mark of ripened virtue (cp.09.m5); the Tibetan has 'fully ripened roots of virtue' (dge ba'i rtsa ba).
A lake or large pond, typically one where lotuses grow. In this song Ḍombī breaks the lake and eats the lotus root.

symbolic.image: the lake that Ḍombī breaks

readings.referent: the body, as a lotus pool (kāyapuṣkara)

forms.translit: dpe byad bzang po brgyad cu

entries.definition: The thirty-two major marks (lakṣaṇa) and eighty minor signs (vyañjana) on the body of a buddha or universal monarch, such as the uṣṇīṣa and the wheels on palms and soles. Munidatta says that by the power of fresh youth the practitioner has become beautiful with the great Vajradhara's body, which bears them (cp.20.m5). Tibetan mtshan, dpe byad bzang po.

In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the left of the central channel (avadhūtī). Munidatta names lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed and made free of appearance (cp.04.m2).

Play or sport (Sanskrit līlā, Old Bengali līṛa): effortless, spontaneous activity, a favourite word of the siddhas for how the realized act. In song 18 Kāṇha falls asleep in the play of great bliss; Munidatta renders the word krīḍā, 'play', and says he went into yogic sleep in play (cp.18.m2). The Tibetan has rol, 'revel, play'.

A lock (compare Bengali tālā); the word tāla also means palm tree and musical time. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house; in Kāṇha's verse quoted by Munidatta a firm lock is set at the door of the sky (cp.04.m5). The Tibetan translation of the line has lde mig, usually 'key'.

symbolic.image: the lock put, with the key, in the mother-in-law's house

readings.referent: sealing the lock shut (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa), explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

entries.definition: Worldly custom (Old Bengali loācāra, Sanskrit lokācāra; Tibetan 'jig rten spyod pa, 'worldly conduct'): the accepted conventions of society, which siddha conduct openly sets aside. In song 31 (4a) the poet gives it up together with fear and disgust; Munidatta speaks of 'the conduct of the world', fear, shame and the like, given up by the siddha master (cp.31.m5).
The water flower that rises unstained from the mud, a pervasive image in Indian religious poetry. In this song there is one lotus with sixty-four petals, on which Ḍombī climbs and dances.

symbolic.image: one lotus with sixty-four petals

readings.referent: the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), which has sixty-four petals

entries.definition: The edible root and stalk of the lotus (Sanskrit mṛṇāla), gathered from the bed of a pond. In this song Ḍombī breaks the lake and eats it.

symbolic.image: the lotus root that Ḍombī eats

readings.referent: bodhicitta, which in its conventional aspect has the form of semen (he calls it the lake's ‘root’, mūla)

entries.definition: Ichor: the fluid that flows from a bull elephant's temples in rut (musth), a stock image of Indian poetry; mada also means intoxication and pride. In song 9 suchness-ichor flows as the elephant desires the she-elephant. Munidatta speaks of the ichor of passion and the ichor of suchness (cp.09.m3); the Tibetan renders these 'intoxication' and 'liquor of suchness'.

symbolic.image: the ichor that flows from the elephant in rut

readings.referent: the ichor of suchness (tathatāmada), which the mind-elephant Kṛṣṇācārya rains through union with the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, as an outer elephant bears the ichor of passion (īrṣyāmada) toward a she-elephant

entries.definition: A drum (Old Bengali mādala, from Sanskrit mardala), barrel-shaped with two heads and played with the hands; the name survives in the madal of eastern India. In song 19 it is named with the paṭaha as the drums that existence and nirvāṇa are at Kāṇha's wedding. The Tibetan line has rnga bo che, 'great drum'.

‘The middle one’ (madhyamā): a name for the central channel of the subtle body, which runs between the left and right channels and which the tantras also call avadhūtī. Munidatta says the moon and the sun, left and right, are joined and made to enter the middle one (cp.03.m2).

The great elements (Sanskrit mahābhūta, Tibetan 'byung ba chen po): earth, water, fire and wind, with space as a fifth in tantric lists, of which bodies and the world are made. Couplet 4 of song 23 names earth, water and fire; Munidatta speaks of the substances become the five great elements, to be eaten from the body-vessel (cp.23.m5).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘Great Seal’: in the yoginī tantras, the highest accomplishment (siddhi), the realization of the nature of mind and reality. Munidatta has Kāṇha say that through union with Nairātmā he attains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, whose nature is wisdom and means.

Great passion (mahārāga): desire not suppressed but taken up as the means of awakening; it gives its name to what Munidatta calls the way of great passion. He speaks of the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion seen at Vairocana's door (cp.03.m4) and, in the Tibetan, of the blazing fire of great passion (cp.03.m6).

Munidatta's name for the path of the songs, in which passion is itself the means of freedom rather than something to be suppressed by austerity. He contrasts it with ascetic observances and cites the Hevajra: the world is bound by passion and freed by passion itself (cp.01.m4).

The great juice or essence (mahārasa; rasa is juice, flavour or essence). In song 16 drinking it makes one drunk, and the three worlds are disregarded. Munidatta calls it the juice of great bliss, the oneness of being and nonbeing (cp.16.m5). The Tibetan has bcud chen, 'great essence' or 'great elixir'.

symbolic.image: the great essence, drunk until one is drunk

readings.referent: the juice of great bliss (mahāsukharasa), which is the oneness of being and nonbeing (bhāva and abhāva); the Tibetan comment lacks 'great bliss' here

entries.definition: Great bliss: the highest bliss, which the tantric path of the songs takes as its goal. Munidatta equates it with the fourth joy and speaks of the great bliss of innate joy, to be known day and night after questioning the guru (cp.01.m3).

In the yoginī-tantra map of the subtle body, the highest of the four wheels (cakra), at the crown of the head, pictured as a lotus of thirty-two petals. Munidatta identifies Ḍombī's hut outside the town with it.

The body of great bliss (mahāsukhakāya): in some tantric systems a fourth buddha body, beside the emanation, enjoyment and dharma bodies, associated with the wheel of great bliss. Munidatta calls it the fourth refuge, in which body, speech and mind dissolve, and says the song's boat is to be understood as it in twilight language (cp.13.m2).

forms.translit: bde ba chen po'i grong khyer

entries.definition: The city of great bliss (mahāsukhapura), a figure for the goal of the path. Munidatta, citing Saraha, says the path of the avadhūtī is excellent and not crooked for going to the city of great bliss (cp.32.m6); the Tibetan gives Saraha's words as verse. Elsewhere he reads the city of the Jina of song 14 as this city (cp.14.m3).

'Great Vehicle': the Buddhist way that takes buddhahood for the sake of all beings as its goal; the tantras present themselves as part of it. In the Rativajra verse Munidatta quotes, this excellent path is 'the great rise of the Mahāyāna', by which you will become tathāgatas (cp.15.m2).

A stain or impurity (Tibetan dri ma, regularly for Sanskrit mala): in Buddhist usage the defilements that cloud the mind; a mind free of them is stainless (dri ma med). In song 24 the king of mind is stainless and the guru's word cuts the stain of delusion; Munidatta says the lord of yogis becomes utterly stainless (cp.24.m2).

Mallārī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 30 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name as mal la re instead of translating it. Later Indian music knows a rāga Mallār (Malhār) sung in the rainy season; whether it is the same melody is uncertain.

Flesh or meat (Old Bengali mām̐sa, Sanskrit māṃsa; Tibetan sha). The refrain of song 23 (2b) seems to say Bhusuku will not enter the lotus grove without flesh (Shastri prints haṇabiṇu: perhaps haṇa, 'kill', and biṇu, 'without'); the Tibetan has 'without flesh, do not enter the house'. Munidatta calls the flesh twilight language for the joy of cessation (cp.23.m3).

symbolic.image: flesh, without which Bhusuku does not enter

readings.referent: in twilight language, the joy of cessation (khyad par gyi dga' ba), whose nature is self-blessing: unless it is purified by the fourth joy, Bhusuku does not enter the house of great bliss (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Mind and wind (Old Bengali maṇa pabaṇa; Sanskrit manas, pavana): in tantric yoga, the mind and the vital wind, or breath, that carries it, so that stilling the wind stills the mind. In song 19 the two are the karaṇḍa and kaśālā of Kāṇha's wedding music. Munidatta speaks of the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest (cp.19.m2).

Pride or conceit (Sanskrit māna, Tibetan nga rgyal): an inflated sense of oneself, which Buddhist lists count among the root afflictions. Munidatta says the mind-mouse stays puffed up with delusion and pride only until the device of the true guru's word is at hand (cp.21.m5).

A circle or disc; in the tantras, the circular arrangement of a deity with its retinue and palace, and by extension a bounded sphere of practice or of the body. In a caryā verse Munidatta quotes, there is no difference among the three maṇḍalas (cp.07.m4); the three are not named.

A word of uncertain sense in song 8: in 4a the rower climbs onto the māṅga and looks in four directions; 5a has māgā. Munidatta renders both as mārga, 'path'; the Tibetan translation takes them as the boat's stern (gru yi mjug) and prow (gru sna). The source form is kept for now.

symbolic.image: the māṅga the rower climbs onto before looking in four directions

readings.referent: the path (mārga) that is the joy of cessation (viramānanda): one who, lacking the guru's lineage, goes on it and looks in the four directions at the grasped and the rest falls into saṃsāra
for māgā in 5a: the path, the joy of cessation, to which bodhicitta has gone, purified by one's own knowledge, once left and right have entered the middle channel

entries.definition: A jewel or gem (Tibetan nor bu, regularly for Sanskrit maṇi); distinct from ratna. Line 5a of song 25 opens nor bus son pa, of unclear sense ('sown with the jewel'?). Munidatta also cites 'abiding in the jewel' (nor bur gnas), which the line lacks, and glosses it: I, Tha ga'i zhabs, have obtained the way of weaving (cp.25.m6).

A word of uncertain sense in song 4: where the yoginī flows before reaching Oḍḍiyāna. Maṇi is 'jewel'; kula may be 'family' or, as elsewhere in the songs, kūla, 'bank'. The Tibetan translation has ma Ni kuN+Da li, perhaps from a different reading. Munidatta's paraphrase has the root of the jewel (maṇimūla) in its place.

symbolic.image: the maṇikula through which the yoginī flows

readings.referent: the root of the jewel (maṇimūla), from which, having enjoyed the taste of play, she rises up and up to the wheel of great bliss (his paraphrase puts maṇimūla where the song has maṇikula; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: ‘Root of the jewel’: a point in the lower body named in the code language of the yoginī tantras, where the ‘jewel’ (maṇi) usually stands for the male organ. Munidatta says bodhicitta goes to the kacchikā, the root of the jewel, and, opened by innate joy, is to be rowed by way of the wheels (cp.14.m4).

The range or field of the mind (Sanskrit manogocara; Tibetan yid kyi spyod yul): whatever thought can reach. In the refrain of song 7 whatever lies within it is uāsa, 'indifferent'. Munidatta applies the word to yogins in whom understanding through the mind-sense predominates, and quotes Saraha on a place where mind and wind do not move (cp.07.m3).

symbolic.image: whatever lies within the mind's range

readings.referent: yogins who stay within the mind's range, in whom understanding through the mind-sense predominates; they too stand indifferent to this teaching, far removed from it

entries.definition: A mantra: a formula of sacred syllables recited in ritual and meditation, central to tantric practice. Munidatta says some novice yogins reach the heaven of the gods by the power of mantras, herbs and the like, yet do not attain deathlessness, since they lack the guru's path (cp.22.m6). The Tibetan has sngags.

The way of mantra (mantranaya): the tantric path of Buddhism, the Vajrayāna, as distinct from the way of the perfections (pāramitānaya). Munidatta glosses the naa of song 12's first line as naya, 'the secret of the way of mantra' (cp.12.m2); the Tibetan has sngags kyi tshul.

Māra, 'the killer': in Buddhist myth the tempter whose army tried to stop the Buddha's awakening, and by extension whatever binds beings to saṃsāra, often counted as four Māras. In song 16 Māra is named when the unstruck roar is heard. Munidatta takes the Māras as the adventitious aggregates, afflictions and the like (cp.16.m2).

symbolic.image: Māra, when the unstruck roar is heard

readings.referent: the Māras: the adventitious aggregates, afflictions and the like, which make saṃsāra fearful, broken on hearing the unstruck sound; he then quotes the Rativajra on the buddhas breaking Māra's army

entries.definition: Death (Sanskrit maraṇa; Tibetan 'chi ba). Song 22 pairs it with birth (jāma) throughout: it asks how birth, death and existence come about, and says birth and death are alike (2b, 3a). Munidatta says a yogin who fears death and the like turns to alchemy, while 'we' are without doubt or concepts about that fear (cp.22.m5).

Path (mārga): the way of practice that leads to awakening, a basic Buddhist term. Munidatta uses it for what the songs call the road: the excellent path of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (cp.15.m2), apart from which no other path leads toward the goal (cp.15.m3). The Tibetan has lam for both road and path.

A woman of the Mātaṅga, a community ranked outside caste society, comparable to the Ḍom. In this song she is the one who ferries across, between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. The word can also mean a female elephant, a sense that does not seem to be meant here.

symbolic.image: an outcaste woman who ferries people across the river

entries.definition: Intelligence or understanding (Sanskrit mati), by which, in couplet 4 of song 12, the king is brought to parinirvāṇa. Munidatta glosses it as understanding in accord with the perfection of wisdom (cp.12.m5); the Tibetan translation has blo, 'mind, intelligence', in the line and blo gros in the comment.

symbolic.image: the intelligence by which the king is brought to parinirvāṇa

readings.referent: understanding that follows the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitānubuddhi); the Tibetan says intelligence (blo gros) is to touch the perfection of wisdom

entries.definition: Mātsarya: selfish possessiveness, envy or avarice; Buddhist lists of secondary afflictions count it as avarice, the Tibetan ser sna. Munidatta says the mind-deer, restless through the faults of ignorance and avarice that it has itself made, is the sworn enemy of all (cp.06.m3).

Drunk, intoxicated (Sanskrit matta, Old Bengali mātela); of an elephant, also maddened or in rut. In song 16 the mind-elephant runs drunk in the refrain, and in couplet 4 drinking the great essence makes one drunk. Munidatta speaks of intoxication with the drink of knowledge (cp.16.m1, cp.16.m2).

symbolic.image: the drunk elephant; drunkenness from the great essence

readings.referent: intoxication with the drink, or honey-liquor, of knowledge (jñānapāna, jñānamadhupāna), both of the siddha master Mahīdhara and of his mind-elephant; the Tibetan of the comment on the refrain has 'drunk on reality' (de kho na nyid)

entries.definition: Illusion (māyā): a conjured appearance, like a magician's show, that seems real but is not; Mahāyāna texts use it for the way all things appear. Munidatta calls ignorance something that has the form of illusion (cp.11.m5); the Tibetan has sgyu ma'i tshul, 'in the manner of an illusion'.

A doe made of illusion (Old Bengali māā, Sanskrit māyā, 'illusion', with hariṇī, 'doe'), which in song 23 (3a) is bound once the net of illusion is spread. The Tibetan line has sgyu ma'i ri dgas, 'illusory deer', to be killed rather than bound. Munidatta's comment speaks of the net binding the deer of the body (cp.23.m4).

symbolic.image: a doe of illusion, bound in the net of illusion

readings.referent: the deer of the body (lus kyi ri dgas), which the net binds; a paraphrase in the place of the song's words, not an explicit gloss (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

the wind of the body: he calls the quarry 'the deer of body-wind, the nature of the body's wind' and 'the deer of the body, whose nature is wind', without quoting this line (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: A net of illusion (māyājāla): the world pictured as a web of conjured appearances, like a magician's show; also the name of a group of tantras. In 13.3b it stands beside Kāṇha and the body, in unclear syntax. Munidatta has 'like a net of illusion' (cp.13.m4); the Tibetan has sgyu 'phrul, and sgyu ma'i dra ba in the comment.

symbolic.image: the net of illusion, named with Kāṇha and the body

readings.referent: a simile for the ocean of objects, the aggregates, elements and the rest, which Kṛṣṇācārya, addressing himself, is told to stop (his paraphrase makes 'like a net of illusion' qualify that ocean; there is no explicit gloss)
the net laid on the body in the bliss of the moments beginning with vicitra; illusion is the action seal (karmāṅganā) (Tibetan comment)

forms.translit: sgyu ma la rmongs rgya mtsho
sgyu ma la rmongs pa rgya mtsho

entries.definition: An ocean made of illusion (māyā) and delusion (moha), or of delusion about illusion, as the Tibetan (sgyu ma la rmongs) and Munidatta take it. In song 15 the fool knows neither its end nor its bottom, and sees no boat or raft on it. Munidatta says māyā is also called wisdom, and attachment to it is delusion (cp.15.m4).

symbolic.image: an ocean of illusion and delusion, whose end and bottom the fool does not know

readings.referent: attachment (abhiṣvaṅga) to māyā, which is also called wisdom (prajñā): that attachment is delusion, the great ocean whose end, its measure, the novice yogin does not reach

entries.definition: A cloud (Old Bengali meha, from Sanskrit megha; Tibetan sprin). Song 30 opens with a cloud of compassion that spreads without cease; Mahāyāna writing sometimes likens compassion to a rain cloud that waters all alike. Munidatta's gloss on the phrase speaks instead of the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreading forth by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2).

symbolic.image: a cloud of compassion that spreads without cease

readings.referent: the purified enjoyment body (pariśuddhasambhogakāya) of the lord of yogis, which spreads forth (prasphurita) by the guru's grace once being and nonbeing, the conceptualization of the grasped and the rest, have been split and made without intrinsic nature; the gloss stands under karuṇa and does not name the cloud; the Tibetan comment agrees (longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku ... 'phro ba)

entries.definition: Meeting, union (Old Bengali mela; Sanskrit melā, melaka). In the last couplet of song 27 Bhusuku says he understood 'in union' (melem̐). Munidatta renders it melaka, in 'the union of wisdom and means' (cp.27.m6); the Tibetan line has tshogs pa, 'gathering, assembly', and the Tibetan comment sbyor ba, 'joining'.

symbolic.image: the union (melem̐) in which Bhusuku says he understood

readings.referent: the union of wisdom and means (prajñopāyamelaka), in which Bhusuku, by the true guru's grace, playfully understood innate joy, great bliss

entries.definition: A mirror (Old Bengali dāpaṇa, Sanskrit darpaṇa; Tibetan me long). In song 32 (3a) one is told not to take a mirror to look at the bracelet on one's hand; Munidatta repeats the question and turns to knowing the true nature of bodhicitta with one's own mind, by the vajra guru's grace (cp.32.m4). Compare mirror-like wisdom.

False or mistaken knowledge (mithyājñāna): cognition that takes things for what they are not, close to confusion (bhrānti) and ignorance. Munidatta says that Ḍombī, the unpurified avadhūtī, has destroyed the whole threefold world of gods, asuras and humans through false knowledge (cp.18.m4). The Tibetan has log pa'i shes pa.

Delusion or bewilderment (moha): with desire and hatred, one of the three root afflictions of Buddhist teaching, the confusion that hides how things are. Munidatta speaks of the stain of delusion (mohamala) in describing the yoginī (cp.04.m4); the Tibetan has rmongs pa.

The net of delusion (Tibetan gti mug dra ba). In the last line of song 25 the weaver, having found the taste of the weave, is freed from it. Munidatta's comment speaks instead of the binding by the thread of delusion's clinging embrace, torn apart (cp.25.m6). Not the net of illusion (mayajala), nor the hunter's net of song 23.

The tree of delusion (moha), which in song 5 is split so that its planks can be joined into the bridge. The Tibetan translation has 'tree of ignorance' (ma rig ljon shing), both in the line and in Munidatta's comment.

symbolic.image: a tree of delusion, split for the planks of the bridge

readings.referent: the tree of conventional bodhicitta, split so as to cut off its grasping of sense objects; the gloss first sets the tree of delusion beside the sense object (viṣaya), and its syntax is loose

entries.definition: Liberation (mokṣa): release from saṃsāra, the round of birth and death. Munidatta speaks of yogins eager for liberation who, by the siddha's means, reach the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, and quotes Saraha: one who meditates on compassion alone does not gain liberation in a thousand births (cp.05.m3). The Tibetan has thar pa.
The moon. In song 14 the moon and the sun are the two wheels; in the commentary on song 1 Munidatta speaks of the moon of conventional bodhicitta, which Rāhu swallows.

symbolic.image: the moon

readings.referent: conventional bodhicitta
the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna)
with the sun and the pulinda, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that bring about the making and unmaking of saṃsāra, which practice brings to a stop
the moon of innate joy, which destroys the darkness of delusion
the king of mind, in the simile of the moon and its light

entries.definition: The disc of the moon (Sanskrit śaśimaṇḍala). In tantric meditation a moon disc, often with a sun disc, is visualized as the seat on which a seed syllable or deity arises. Song 32 (1a) names it last among the things that are not there; the Tibetan line has 'the disc of sun and moon' (nyi zla'i dkyil 'khor).

Moonlight (Old Bengali cāndakānti, Sanskrit candrakānti, 'the moon's lustre'; Munidatta's candrikā; Tibetan zla ba'i 'od zer, 'the moon's rays'). In song 31 (3a) moonlight shows in the moon, an image for the mind's transformations entering 'there' (3b). Munidatta speaks of moonlight going back into the moon once it has set (cp.31.m4).

symbolic.image: moonlight in the moon

readings.referent: the series of conceptual thoughts (vikalpāvalī) of the king of mind, which dissolves right there when the king of mind goes to no-mind and enters clear light, as moonlight goes back into the moon once it has set: a correspondence drawn by his simile (yathā … tathā), not an explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment agrees (rnam par rtog pa thim)

entries.definition: The mother (Old Bengali māa, from Sanskrit mātṛ). In the last couplet of song 11 Kāṇha becomes a kāpālika by killing the mother. Munidatta's paraphrase puts ignorance, which has the form of illusion (māyā), in her place (cp.11.m5), perhaps hearing māa as māyā. The Tibetan has ma.

symbolic.image: the mother whom Kāṇha kills to become a kāpālika

readings.referent: ignorance, which has the form of illusion (māyā), made without intrinsic nature by the practice of the nondifference of wisdom and means (his paraphrase puts avidyāṃ māyārūpām where the song has māa; there is no explicit gloss)
Nairātmā, as the speaker addresses herself ("O mother, Nairātmā"); the Tibetan line has no mother

entries.definition: A mountain (Old Bengali pābata, from Sanskrit parvata; also giribara, 'finest of mountains'). The Śabarī of song 28 lives on a high mountain, and in the last couplet the Śabara enters the cleft of the great mountain's peak. The Tibetan has ri bo. Munidatta reads the mountain as the yogi's body and as Sumeru.

symbolic.image: the high mountain where the Śabarī lives; the peak of the great mountain

readings.referent: the raised staff of the skeleton of the lord of yogis' own body (the Tibetan says the spine, sgal tshigs), at the tip of Sumeru's peak, in the wheel of great bliss
the body, as 'this body-Sumeru' (kāyasumeru) and 'the forest of the body-mountain' (kāyaparvatavana) where the Śabarī roams

entries.definition: A mouse (Old Bengali musā, muṣā; Sanskrit mūṣaka), the central image of song 21: in the dark night it eats nectar, digs holes and runs restlessly until its movement is cut off; the refrain sets it beside pabaṇā, 'wind'. Munidatta says the poet speaks in the twilight language of 'mouse' (cp.21.m1) and derives mūṣaka from muṣṇāti, 'steals' (cp.21.m2).

symbolic.image: a restless mouse that roams in the dark night, eats nectar and digs, until its movement is cut off

readings.referent: the mind-wind (cittapavana): mūṣaka, 'the stealer' (from muṣṇāti, 'steals'), is in twilight language the mind-wind, which itself makes its meal of the taste of the nectar of bodhicitta in the union of vajra and lotus; the Tibetan has 'mind and wind' (sems dang rlung)
the mind, which Munidatta calls 'the mind-mouse' (cittamūṣaka, mūṣakacitta) throughout his comments on the later couplets

the mind-mouse that, through its natural restlessness, tears apart existence, which he explains as one's own body, and itself brings about the fall into the bad destinies; knowing this natural fault, the yogin is not to impute real existence to it

kāla (the word means both 'black' and 'time, death'): the mind-mouse is kāla because it destroys conventional bodhicitta; the Tibetan comment makes it Rāhu (sgra gcan), which destroys the moon of conventional bodhicitta

entries.definition: Dead (Old Bengali maela, apparently a past form of mar-, 'die'). The refrain of song 23 (2a) sets the dead against the living; the Tibetan has shi ba'i ro, 'the corpse of the dead', which is not to be taken up. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, reads the dead as the outgoing breath (cp.23.m3).

symbolic.image: the dead, or the corpse of the dead, set against the living in the refrain

readings.referent: the outgoing breath (dbyung ba'i dbugs), joined with the syllable hūṃ and the knowledge of night, and having the nature of the thirty-three natures; he then adds the abiding breath, with āḥ, the knowledge of the neuter and seven natures (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Death as Māra, the 'killer' and tempter of Buddhist myth; one of the four Māras, with those of the aggregates, the afflictions and the divine son. Munidatta says that from beginningless time, through lack of vigilance, 'my mind-deer', wrapped in the poison of the Māra of death, heard the cry 'kill! kill!' (māra māra) (cp.06.m2).

A fool, someone deluded (Old Bengali mūṛha, Sanskrit mūḍha). In the last line Bhusuku says it does not enter the hearts of fools. Munidatta identifies them with scholars proud of outer treatises and scriptures, who are thoroughly deluded about this teaching and far from it (cp.06.m6). The Tibetan translation has blun, 'fool'.

symbolic.image: fools, into whose hearts it does not enter

readings.referent: scholars (paṇḍita) proud of outer treatises and scriptures, thoroughly deluded about this teaching and far from it, in whose hearts not even a glimmer of reality opens
the novice yogin (bālayogin), addressed as fool

entries.definition: Nāda, 'sound, resonance': in tantric yoga and mantra meditation, the subtle sound into which a seed syllable is said to dissolve, often drawn as a fine stroke above its bindu, the dot of the nasal. Song 32 (1a) says there is no nāda, no bindu, no sun and no moon disc. The Tibetan keeps the word (nA da).

symbolic.image: nāda, the first of the things the song says are not there

readings.referent: conceptual thought (vikalpa): 'the concepts of nāda, bindu and the rest' (nādabindvādivikalpa), by abandoning which the jewel of mind of those who know the ultimate is freed by its own nature, through the power of the waves of nectar from the true guru's mouth; the Tibetan agrees (nA da dang thig le la sogs pa'i rnam par rtog pa)

entries.definition: A channel of the subtle body. In tantric yoga the vital winds move through a network of channels, of which the chief three are lalanā, rasanā and the central avadhūtī. Munidatta speaks of pressing these three (cp.04.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan name of the goddess; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: Selflessness, the absence of an inherent self in persons and phenomena, personified in the Hevajra tradition as a goddess, Nairātmā, ‘She who is without self’. Munidatta uses the word both for the goddess, whom he addresses in place of Ḍombī, and for selflessness as a doctrine.

Selflessness: the absence of a self. Munidatta uses the term in glossing lines 4a-4b of song 1, and quotes a verse in which the vajra of realizing selflessness splits the mountains of the view of a real self (cp.01.m5). The Hevajra tradition personifies it as the goddess Nairātmyā.

A grove or bed of lotuses (Sanskrit nalinīvana; nalinī is the lotus plant). In the refrain of song 9 Kāṇha enters the lotus grove of the innate. The Tibetan translation has chu skyes tshal, 'lotus grove'. Munidatta's comment on song 6 also speaks of a lotus grove of great bliss (cp.06.m5).

symbolic.image: the lotus grove of the innate, which Kāṇha enters

readings.referent: the lotus of great bliss (mahāsukhakamala): having made the lotus grove the lotus of great bliss, Kṛṣṇācārya plays in a form free of concepts; the Tibetan has 'having gone to the lotus grove of great bliss'
the wheel of great bliss, entered by the guru's grace once vajra and lotus are joined (Tibetan comment)

entries.definition: The husband's sister (Old Bengali naṇanda, Sanskrit nanāndṛ), who in the joint household shares with the mother-in-law authority over a young wife. In song 11 she is among those killed at home. The Tibetan has a ne, 'aunt'. Munidatta does not gloss her by name.

symbolic.image: the husband's sister, killed at home

entries.definition: The neuter (Sanskrit napuṃsaka, Tibetan ma ning): neither male nor female. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, joins the abiding breath and the syllable āḥ to 'the knowledge of the neuter' and seven natures, beside the knowledges of day and night (cp.23.m3); the glossary also records his reading of song 14's pulinda as 'the neuter' (cp.14.m5).

A drama (nāṭaka), the Sanskrit genre of staged play with music and dance. Song 17 ends with 'the Buddha drama' becoming bisamā, 'uneven' or 'extraordinary'. Munidatta calls it distinguished and surpassing and speaks of nirvāṇa for beings (cp.17.m5); the Tibetan has 'the Buddha's dance' (sangs rgyas gar), 'especially difficult'.

symbolic.image: the Buddha drama, which becomes bisamā

readings.referent: his paraphrase: the Buddha drama, distinguished and surpassing, becomes nirvāṇa, alike (samaṃ) for beings; the Tibetan: the Buddha's dance, especially exalted, makes beings pass beyond sorrow (a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss, and its syntax is loose)

entries.definition: Lord or protector (Sanskrit nātha, Old Bengali nāhā): a title for a master, a deity or a teacher. In song 15 the fool, in his confusion, does not ask the lord. The Tibetan has mgon, 'protector'. Munidatta identifies the lord as the true guru (sadgurunātha) (cp.15.m4).

symbolic.image: the lord whom the fool does not ask

readings.referent: the true guru (sadgurunātha), from whose mouth the novice yogin is to take the means of the fourth joy

entries.definition: Leader, chief (Sanskrit nāyaka). In song 16 the one drunk on the great essence is the leader of the five sense objects and sees no adversary. Munidatta says that as their leader he is himself the sixth, the great Vajradhara (cp.16.m5); the Tibetan has 'dren byed, 'one who leads'.

symbolic.image: the leader of the five sense objects

readings.referent: he himself, as the sixth, the great Vajradhara; the Tibetan comment likewise has 'the sixth, the great Vajradhara'

entries.definition: The near bank of a river, where the traveller stands (Old Bengali uāra, Sanskrit avāra; Tibetan tshu rol), set against the far shore (pāra). Song 32 (4a) names the two together. Munidatta's citation of the word is corrupt (deāra?); he places it in existence (bhava), where ordinary people follow, as against the far shore, the ultimate (cp.32.m5).

symbolic.image: the near shore, named with the far shore

readings.referent: existence (bhava), where it is followed by ordinary people (pṛthagjana), as against the far shore, glossed 'by the ultimate' (paramārthena), where the best of yogins follow bodhicitta; his citation of the word is corrupt (deāra?), and the Tibetan comment has 'in saṃsāric existence it is understood by ordinary beings' ('khor ba'i srid par de so so'i skye bos khong du chud par 'gyur)

entries.definition: A hunter's net or trap (Tibetan rgya; the Old Bengali is lost). In couplet 5 of song 23, which survives only in the Tibetan, the deer escapes though there is no net, stone or rope. Munidatta takes the three as twilight language for conceptual thought about the joys of body, speech and mind (cp.23.m6). Not the net of illusion (mayajala).

symbolic.image: the net, absent as the deer escapes

readings.referent: in twilight language, conceptual thought about the joy of body (sku'i dga' ba); the gloss opens with 'the joy of great bliss', loosely attached (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Sleep (Sanskrit nidrā; Old Bengali niṃda; Tibetan gnyid). With dream, a stock comparison for how things appear without being real. Song 13 speaks of a dream without sleep, and Munidatta says one free of sleep and torpor sees things in the waking state as in a dream (cp.13.m5). Distinct from yogic sleep (yoganidrā).

Night (Old Bengali nisi; Sanskrit niś, niśā; Tibetan mtshan mo). Song 21 opens with the dark night in which the mouse roams. Munidatta reads the night as prajñā, 'wisdom', a name also given to the female partner, or as the action-woman (karmāṅganā) (cp.21.m2).

symbolic.image: the dark night in which the mouse roams

readings.referent: prajñā ('wisdom', also a name for the female partner) or the action-woman (karmāṅganā), with whom, in the union of vajra and lotus, the mind-wind makes its meal of the nectar of bodhicitta; the Tibetan has 'the limb of the wisdom action seal' (shes rab las kyi phyag rgya'i yan lag)
Bhusuku's night, its darkness of ignorance cleared (Tibetan comment)

forms.translit: ngo bo nyid mi gnas pa'o
forms.lemma: ngo bo nyid mi gnas pa

entries.definition: Lacking intrinsic nature (svabhāva): the Madhyamaka teaching that nothing exists by its own nature, another way of stating emptiness. Munidatta opens his comment on song 4 by saying that Guṇḍarīpāda, through understanding the conduct of Heruka, teaches others that things are without intrinsic nature (cp.04.m1).

Without support or object (Sanskrit nirālamba; Tibetan dmigs pa med pa): resting on nothing and taking nothing as an object, a Mahāyāna description of realized mind. In the refrain of song 31 Āryadeva shines ṇirāse; Munidatta renders it nirālamba, through the yoga of not apprehending any phenomenon (cp.31.m3). The Old Bengali might also reflect nirāśraya, or nirāśa, 'without hope'.

forms.translit: dmigs pa med pa'i ngo bo

entries.definition: 'Without añjana' (eye-black, hence stain): in siddha and dohā poetry, the unstained, unconditioned state of mind. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya that Munidatta quotes, hardly one in ten million becomes absorbed in the stainless (cp.02.m6). The Tibetan translates literally, 'without eye-salve'.

Partless (Sanskrit niravayava): having no parts, as the atom was claimed to be. Munidatta glosses the ṇirabara of song 26 (1b) as niravayava: carded down, the whole is shown to be partless (cp.26.m2). The Old Bengali word is of uncertain derivation, and the Tibetan line has lhag ma med, 'without remainder', for ṇirabara sesu.

Free of revulsion: untroubled by the disgust that caste purity attaches to impure people, places and substances. Kāṇha uses the word of himself, and Munidatta explains it as being free of faults such as shame.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: In the yoginī-tantra map of the subtle body, the wheel (cakra) at the navel, the lowest of four along the central channel, pictured as a lotus of sixty-four petals. Munidatta identifies the song's lotus with it.

The cessation of suffering and its causes; freedom from saṃsāra. Munidatta quotes the Guhyasamāja: without the vajra guru one cannot reach nirvāṇa, the peaceful, irreversible state that removes all afflictions (cp.01.m3).

The completion stage: the phase of tantric yoga that follows the visualization of the deity and works with the subtle body toward realization. Munidatta cites Āryadeva: its awakening cannot be realized without passing through the five stages in order (cp.01.m2).

A dwelling or place to live (Old Bengali nibāsa, Sanskrit nivāsa). In the refrain of song 7 Kāṇha asks where he is to go and make his dwelling. Munidatta says the refrain breaks down the imputing of a dwelling of one's own, since the world is pervaded by bliss (cp.07.m3). The Tibetan has gnas.

symbolic.image: the dwelling Kāṇha asks where to make

readings.referent: the imputing (āropaṇa) of a dwelling of one's own, which the refrain is said to break down: since the world is pervaded by bliss, there is no place where a dwelling is to be made

entries.definition: A noose or snare (Sanskrit pāśa), used to catch and bind, and in tantric art an emblem held by deities. In song 1, on this draft's reading of pāsa, the listener is told to take up the noose; the Tibetan translation reads 'noose' (zhags pa) there, and Munidatta's gloss mentions it (cp.01.m5).

symbolic.image: a noose, taken up on the side of emptiness

readings.referent: the nature of selflessness (nairātmadharma), which the listener is to embrace closely; the Tibetan translation of the comment says 'the dharma of selflessness is the noose' (the division of the Sanskrit is uncertain)

entries.definition: Dance (Old Bengali nāc-, Sanskrit nṛtya). In the last couplet of song 17 someone dances while a goddess sings. Munidatta says that, in joy at attaining the fruit, Vīṇāpāda dances the vajra-step dance with the step of Vajradhara (cp.17.m5), and quotes the Dvikalpa: if joy has arisen, one dances for the sake of liberation.

symbolic.image: dancing while the goddess sings

readings.referent: the dance Vīṇāpāda performs with the step of Vajradhara (vajradharapadena; the Tibetan has 'the dance of the state of Vajradhara', rdo rje 'dzin pa'i go 'phang gi gar), a vajra-step dance done out of joy at attaining the fruit

entries.definition: The ocean or sea (Sanskrit samudra, jaladhi; Tibetan rgya mtsho). The songs speak of rivers, but Munidatta often speaks of an ocean: in song 8 the boat goes to ‘the ocean, the wheel of great bliss’ (cp.08.m2, cp.08.m5), and whoever seeks bliss by the true guru's word crosses the ocean of existence (cp.08.m4).

symbolic.image: an ocean, which the boat goes to or crosses

readings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), named in apposition as the ocean the boat goes to; the song itself rows toward the sky
existence (bhava): the ocean of existence, crossed by one who seeks the bliss of vajra and lotus by the true guru's word

entries.definition: Teacher whom Munidatta quotes as saying that the awakening of the completion stage cannot be realized without passing through the five stages in order (cp.01.m2). Tantric tradition places an Āryadeva in the Guhyasamāja lineage as a disciple of Nāgārjuna.

'The Blessed One', a common epithet of the Buddha, used in the tantras also of the buddha who teaches them. Munidatta speaks of the Blessed One's five stages (cp.01.m2) and of the countless absorptions the Blessed One taught (cp.01.m4).

'The Blessed Lady' (bhagavatī), feminine of bhagavat, 'Blessed One', an epithet of goddesses in the tantras. Munidatta gives it to Nairātmā, through union with whom the mind-elephant rains the ichor of suchness (cp.09.m3). The Tibetan uses bcom ldan 'das, its word for the Blessed One.

Bhusukupāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript and the Tibetan translation attribute song 6. He names himself Bhusuku in its last couplet, and Munidatta and the Tibetan also read his name in the refrain, where Shastri's text has bhukua. Munidatta calls him a siddha master (cp.06.m6). Shastri's edition identifies him with Śāntideva, whose Bodhicaryāvatāra Munidatta quotes here (cp.06.m3).

Cāṭilapāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 5. He names himself Cāṭila in its refrain, where he builds a bridge, and in its last couplet. The commentary also spells the name Cāṭilla; the Tibetan translation has tsA TI la and tsA TI li pa. Munidatta calls him a siddhācārya (cp.05.m3).

Teacher whom Munidatta quotes at the end of his comment on song 11, for a verse in which the living being is a vajra-holder and the women of the world are like the kāpālika's consort (cp.11.m5). The Tibetan translation names him da u Da'i zhabs, which suggests a different reading of the name. Not otherwise identified here.

Teacher whom Munidatta quotes at the end of his comment on song 27, for a verse beginning gavāṃ yūtha, 'a herd of cows' (cp.27.m5). The Tibetan translation names him rdo rje Da DI zhabs, which suggests a name like Ḍaḍī. Possibly the same teacher as Daṛatīpāda, quoted on song 11; not otherwise identified here.

Ḍombīpāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes this song. Munidatta introduces him as the siddhācārya Ḍombī, steeped in supreme compassion, who sets out the teaching under the guise of a boat journey. The name is the word for a Ḍom woman with the honorific -pāda.

Guṇḍarīpāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 4. He names himself Guḍarī in its last couplet; the manuscript also spells the name Guṇḍarī and Guḍḍarī, and the Tibetan translation guN+Da rI. Munidatta calls him a siddha master who has directly realized the vajra-like samādhi (cp.04.m6).

forms.where: standard Tibetan transcription; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: A wrathful tantric deity, and a title of Hevajra and related male deities of the yoginī tantras. In the Hevajra Tantra verse Munidatta quotes, the practitioner is told to dance in Heruka's form.

'Victor', a title of a buddha as one who has conquered the afflictions (the Jains use it of their teachers). Munidatta calls the unity of self-blessing and clear light the bridge of the Jina, for carrying beings across the ocean of saṃsāra (cp.05.m5); the Tibetan translation has no word for 'Jina' there.

forms.translit: la ba'i na bza' can gyi zhabs

entries.definition: Kambalāmbarapāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 8; the name means 'he whose garment is a blanket'. In the refrain and couplet 3 he calls himself Kāmali, an Old Bengali form of kambala, 'blanket'. Munidatta calls him a siddha master (cp.08.m2). The Tibetan has la ba'i na bza' can, 'wearer of a woollen garment', and la ba pa.

forms.where: standard Tibetan name for Kṛṣṇācārya; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: nag po spyod pa pa'i zhabs

entries.definition: Siddha poet, called Kṛṣṇācārya in Sanskrit, to whom songs of this collection are attributed. Munidatta quotes a verse of his in which the pure water dries up when the fire of time (kālāgni) enters (cp.01.m2).

Siddha poet to whom song 2 is attributed; he names himself in its last couplet. The name joins kukkurī, 'female dog', with the honorific -pāda. Munidatta introduces him as setting out the king of great bliss in twilight language, his mind delighted by drinking the liquor of his own bliss (cp.02.m1).

Siddha poet of eastern India to whom song 1 is attributed; he names himself in its refrain and last couplet. Munidatta names him first among the siddhas who composed the songs (cp.01.m1) and calls him 'the first siddha master', ādisiddhācārya (cp.01.m6).

Mahīdharapāda, the siddha to whom song 16 is ascribed; in its last couplet he calls himself Mahittā. Munidatta calls him the siddha master Mahīdhara, drunk on the drink of knowledge (cp.16.m1). The Tibetan translation names him sa 'dzin ('earth-holder', for Mahīdhara) in the heading and comment, but Mahendra (ma hen+d+ra) in the last line.

Teacher whom Munidatta quotes 'in another school' (paradarśane) for an Old Bengali verse: the guru tells of the road of the ultimate, and the bee drinks the honey of the opened lotus (cp.21.m4). The Tibetan calls him a holder of an outsider's view (phyi rol gyi lta ba pa). The Nāth tradition honours a Mīnanātha among its first gurus.

Teacher to whom Munidatta attributes a verse on vajra recitation (vajrajāpa): one who falls from a mountaintop falls though unwilling, and one who has the guru's instruction is freed though not seeking freedom (cp.01.m3). Tantric tradition credits a Nāgārjuna with Guhyasamāja works; whether he is the Madhyamaka philosopher is disputed.

In Indian myth, the demon who swallows the sun or moon and so causes eclipses. Munidatta identifies the Kāla of song 1 with Rāhu, who from the first day of the dark fortnight dries up the moon of conventional bodhicitta through the sequence of lunar days (cp.01.m2).

Siddha poet to whom the Nepal manuscript attributes song 28; in its last couplet he calls himself the mad Śabara. Munidatta calls him a siddha master who, pierced by the flavour of great compassion, teaches for the good of the world (cp.28.m1). The Tibetan commentary calls him sa wa ri pa, though its heading names Saraha.

'Lion of the Śākyas', an epithet of the historical Buddha, Śākyamuni. In the Rativajra verse Munidatta quotes, Śākyasiṃha and the other buddhas broke the mighty, dreadful army of Māra (cp.16.m2). The Tibetan has shAkya seng ge, but credits the victory to 'the wise' (mkhas rnams) where the Sanskrit has 'buddhas'.

Śāntipāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript and the Tibetan translation attribute song 15; he names himself Śānti in its last couplet. Munidatta calls him a siddhācārya, delighted with full supreme joy (cp.15.m1, cp.15.m2). Tibetan tradition counts a Śāntipa among the eighty-four siddhas, often identified with the scholar Ratnākaraśānti; whether he is this poet is uncertain.

Siddha poet famous for his dohās, rhymed couplet songs. Munidatta quotes him praising the true guru (cp.01.m3) and asking how the tender sprout of mind, if not watered with the pure juices of sense objects, could become the wish-granting tree (cp.01.m4).

Siddha poet of song 25, known in Sanskrit as Tantrīpāda. The song survives only in the Tibetan translation, whose heading calls him thag pa'i zhabs; Munidatta's comment calls him the siddhācārya Tha ga pa'i zhabs, tha ga pa being 'weaver' (cp.25.m1). In the refrain and the last couplet the poet calls himself a weaver (tha ga).

‘The Illuminator’, one of the five buddhas who head the families of tantric deities, often placed at the centre of the maṇḍala. Munidatta calls the tenth door of song 3 ‘the door of Vairocana’ (vairocanadvāra), where the sign of the bliss of great passion is seen (cp.03.m4); he does not say where in the body it lies.

'Vajra-holder': a name of the buddha who teaches the tantras, in some systems the primordial buddha. In the verse of Daṛatīpāda that Munidatta quotes, the living being is vajradhara (cp.11.m5), whether as that buddha's name or as an epithet is not certain. The Tibetan has rdo rje 'dzin.

Vajrapāṇi ('vajra in hand'), the bodhisattva who in many tantras questions the teacher and gathers the teaching; Indian authors also bore the name. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, quotes Vajrapāṇi for verses tying the syllables oṃ, hūṃ and āḥ to beings entering, going out and abiding (cp.23.m3). Which Vajrapāṇi is meant is not said.
'Vajra being', a buddha form central to many tantric systems. Munidatta ends his comment on song 1 with a verse from the Dvikalpa: the union of āli and kāli is Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6).

Vīṇāpāda, 'he of the vīṇā', the siddha to whom the manuscript and the Tibetan translation attribute song 17. Munidatta says that, having understood the meaning of Heruka, he teaches through the word 'vīṇā' (cp.17.m1), and pictures him dancing with the step of Vajradhara (cp.17.m5). Tibetan tradition counts a Vīṇāpa among the eighty-four siddhas; whether he is this poet is uncertain.
