Siddha poet to whom song 3 is attributed; he names himself Biruā in its last couplet, and the manuscript heads the song ‘of Virūpāda’. Munidatta calls him Viruāpāda and says he spoke out of supreme compassion to make the avadhūtī plain (cp.03.m1). Tibetan tradition counts a Virūpa among the eighty-four siddhas.

Munidatta's word for a couplet of a song, used when he turns to comment on it ('with the next verse', 'the third verse'). In song 1 he calls couplets 4 and 5 the third and fourth, so he counts the opening couplet as the first and leaves the refrain out of the count.

Wing, side or flank (Sanskrit pakṣa, Old Bengali pakhā); also half of a lunar month, and a party in a dispute. In song 4 the sides of the braid of moon and sun are to be split; the Tibetan translation renders the word there as sgo glegs, 'door-panel'. Munidatta speaks of the 'taking of sides' (pakṣagraha).

symbolic.image: the sides of the braid of moon and sun, which are to be split

readings.referent: the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) by the moon and the sun, which the lord of yogis breaks through the instruction in vajra recitation, so steadying the vajra of speech

entries.definition: Five people (Old Bengali pāñcajanā; Sanskrit pañca jana), who in couplet 3 of song 12 are gholiu, perhaps 'churned up', once the elephant is brought out; apparently pieces in the game, though in Bengali 'five people' can also mean people at large. The Tibetan translation has skye bo lnga, 'five persons'.

symbolic.image: the five people, churned up once the elephant is brought out

readings.referent: the five sense objects, which consist of the five aggregates, whose ornament of I-making, mine-making and the rest the suchness-mind elephant strikes down, leaving them without pride (his paraphrase puts these where the song has pāñcajanā; there is no explicit gloss)
the five sense objects, become the aggregate of form, the mirror-like knowledge, the earth element, the eye faculty and so on, killed by withdrawing the maṇḍalas (Tibetan comment)

entries.definition: The five wisdoms (Tibetan ye shes lnga, Sanskrit pañcajñāna) of a buddha: mirror-like, of equality, discriminating, all-accomplishing, and of the dharmadhātu. Munidatta says conventional bodhicitta, in the lotus of wisdom, has the nature of the five wisdoms beginning with the mirror-like (cp.25.m2). He does not tie them explicitly to the line's 'five times'.

A graded sequence of five stages of tantric yoga, associated with the Guhyasamāja tradition and with a work of the same name. Munidatta says those who seek innate joy through the Blessed One's five stages realize the vajra-like absorption, and cites Āryadeva: without them completion-stage awakening cannot be realized (cp.01.m2).

The five seals (mudrā): bone ornaments worn as emblems by tantric yogis and yoginīs. Munidatta says the Śabarī puts on the five seals, beginning with earrings, as her ornament (cp.28.m4); the Tibetan calls them bone ornaments (rus pa'i rgyan) and begins the list with the wheel ('khor lo).

Sin and merit (pāpa, puṇya): harmful and wholesome deeds and the bad and good results they store up. Tantric and siddha teaching often treats both as bonds to be left behind. In song 16 both are broken; Munidatta calls them the two nooses of saṃsāra (cp.16.m4). The Tibetan has dge sdig, 'virtue and sin'.

symbolic.image: sin and merit, both broken

readings.referent: the two nooses (pāśa) of saṃsāra, which the mind-elephant cuts

entries.definition: The far bank of a river, used in the phrase pāra kar-, 'take across, ferry over'. Crossing to the far shore is a widespread Buddhist image; Munidatta places the crossing in this song on the ocean of saṃsāra.

symbolic.image: ferrying someone over to the far bank

readings.referent: crossing the ocean of saṃsāra (cp.14.m2), the sea of becoming (cp.14.m6)
the ultimate (paramārtha): the far shore

entries.definition: Supreme joy (paramānanda): in the yoginī tantras, the second of the four joys of yogic union, after joy and before the joy of cessation and innate joy (systems order the last two differently); also, loosely, the highest joy. Munidatta opens his comment on song 15 by calling Śānti delighted with full supreme joy (cp.15.m1).

Atom (paramāṇu): the smallest particle of matter, which some Indian schools held to be partless and real. Buddhist critics, notably Vasubandhu, argued that an atom joined to others on six sides must have six parts, and so cannot be partless. Munidatta runs this argument on the heap of atoms that make up the parts, speaking of six parts (ṣaḍaṃśa) (cp.26.m2).

The ultimate (paramārtha): how things really are, as against the conventional (saṃvṛti); together they are the two truths. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya that Munidatta quotes, people swell with pride, thinking themselves skilled in the ultimate (cp.02.m6).

forms.translit: yongs su mya ngan las 'da' bar

entries.definition: Complete or final nirvāṇa (parinirvāṇa), classically a buddha's passing at death. In couplet 4 of song 12 the king becomes parinibittā, which the Tibetan translation renders yongs su mya ngan 'das and Munidatta takes as parinirvāṇa (cp.12.m5). The Old Bengali might instead reflect parinivṛtta, 'brought wholly to a stop', which would suit the game.

Goods spread out for sale, or the stall that displays them (Sanskrit prasāra, ‘spreading out’). In song 3 the liquor-seller sets out her wares in sixty-four pots. The Tibetan translation has stegs bu, ‘platform, stall’.

symbolic.image: the wares, or stall, that the liquor-seller sets out

readings.referent: a seat (gdan), apparently the wheel of emanation itself, into which the gandharva being enters from the blazing fire of great passion; the stall (stegs bu) is called twilight language here (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: An Old Bengali word of uncertain sense in the first line of song 16, where three pāṭas are 'attached' (lāgeli). It may go back to Sanskrit paṭṭa, 'slab, seat, band'. The Tibetan line has only 'the three' (rnam gsum). Munidatta takes the three pāṭas as the joys beginning with the joy of the body (cp.16.m2).

symbolic.image: three pāṭas

readings.referent: the joys beginning with the joy of the body (kāyānanda), taken together by treating them as non-different (abhedopacāra); the Tibetan comment has 'the three are the joy of the body and so on'

entries.definition: A drum (Sanskrit paṭaha, Old Bengali paṛaha) beaten in processions, festivals and public proclamations. In the first line of song 19, existence and nirvāṇa are the paṭaha and the mādala of Kāṇha's wedding music. Munidatta speaks of 'the instruments beginning with the paṭaha' (cp.19.m2); the Tibetan keeps the word (pa Ta ha).

symbolic.image: the paṭaha, which the song says existence and nirvāṇa are

readings.referent: with the other instruments, existence and nirvāṇa as the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest, imagined (utprekṣya) as 'the instruments beginning with the paṭaha' (paṭahādibhāṇḍa); the Tibetan takes bhāṇḍa as 'vessel' (snod)

entries.definition: Paṭamañjarī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 1 is sung, given in its heading and repeated at the start of Munidatta's comment (cp.01.m2).

Peacock feathers (Old Bengali moraṅgi pīccha), which the Śabarī of song 28 wears as her dress. Munidatta renders the word mayūrāṅga, 'peacock's limb', and his gloss perhaps plays on pakṣa, both 'wing' and 'side'. The Tibetan has rma bya'i mdongs, 'peacock plumes'.

symbolic.image: the peacock feathers the Śabarī wears as her dress

readings.referent: the many and varied forms of conceptual thought about sides (pakṣavikalpa), made into her garment and ornament as they rest in their own nature

entries.definition: A necklace of pearls (Old Bengali muttihāra, Sanskrit muktāhāra), one of the yogi's ornaments in song 11, where the poet takes supreme liberation as his pearl necklace; Munidatta repeats the phrase (cp.11.m4). Muktā, 'pearl', sounds like mukta, 'freed', a play the line may intend. The Tibetan has mu tig do shal.

The fruit or result (phala; Tibetan 'bras bu) of the path, as against the path itself; in Munidatta's comments often innate joy or coupled union. He speaks of the arising of the fruit, wondrous coupled union (cp.30.m3), and introduces the last couplet of song 30 as stating the power of that joy once the fruit is attained (cp.30.m6).

A word of uncertain sense in the first line of song 12, joined to compassion (karuṇā) at the opening of Kāṇha's game; it may name the board (compare Bengali piṛi, 'low wooden seat'). Munidatta explains it as the seven faults, stains of samādhi; the Tibetan translation has rgyal mtshan, 'banner', in the line and rgyal in the comment.

symbolic.image: the pihāṛi of compassion on which Kāṇha plays

readings.referent: the seven faults, stains of samādhi, connected with the mind's support (āśraya; the construction is unclear), which are split and removed; the Tibetan calls them obscurations of samādhi and adds that victory over them is called non-apprehension

forms.translit: phung po za bas dbye bas

entries.definition: Apparently the two meditations of the Guhyasamāja completion stage for dissolving into clear light: piṇḍagrāha, 'holding as a whole', and anubheda, 'successive dissolution', in which the body, the world and oneself are withdrawn in stages. Munidatta says that when the mind-mouse is examined in them no colour is found to apprehend (cp.21.m4). The Tibetan reads the compound differently.

'Condensed sequence' (piṇḍī, 'lump, compact whole'; krama, 'sequence, stage'), a term of the Guhyasamāja tradition, in which a sādhana ascribed to Nāgārjuna is known as the Piṇḍīkrama. Munidatta says that when the body, whose channels are the thirty-two goddesses, is examined in the order of the piṇḍīkrama on the authority of the true guru's words, vāsanā is not found (cp.20.m4).

The piṭā of the first line of song 2, which cannot hold, or be held. Munidatta renders it pīṭhaka, 'little seat, stool', and the Tibetan translation stegs bu, 'stand, platform'; both point to a seat or stand rather than a vessel. The syntax of the line, and so the object's role in the milking, is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the stool (or stand) in the milking scene

readings.referent: the vajra jewel (vajramaṇi): conventional bodhicitta falling into it cannot be held, and novice yogis are unable to hold it

entries.definition: The Ganges, the chief river of northern India, sacred in Indian religion. In this song a boat moves between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the two rivers that meet at Prayāga.

symbolic.image: the river Gaṅgā, one of the two rivers the boat moves between

readings.referent: together with the Yamunā, the 'moon-appearance' and the 'sun-appearance' (candrābhāsa, sūryābhāsa), which are the grasped object and the grasping subject; pairing the Gaṅgā with the moon and the grasped follows word order only

entries.definition: Jambudvīpa, 'Rose-apple Island': in Indian and Buddhist cosmology the southern continent, the world of humans, often meaning India. Munidatta says novice yogins wander in the great places (mahāsthāna) of Jambudvīpa, among the moving and the unmoving (cp.22.m6). The Tibetan has 'dzam bu'i gling.

Kāmaru, a vernacular form of Kāmarūpa, the ancient kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley in present-day Assam, known in tantric tradition as a seat of the goddess and a land of adepts. In song 2 the young wife goes there at night; the Tibetan translation transcribes the name.

symbolic.image: Kāmaru, where the young wife goes at night

readings.referent: her own place (svasthāna) in the wheel of great bliss, to which the naturally purified avadhūtī goes of itself, free of concepts

entries.definition: Oḍḍiyāna (also Uḍḍiyāna), a land celebrated in tantric Buddhism as a seat of yoginīs and a source of tantras, usually placed in the Swat valley in the northwest, though some locate it in Orissa. In song 4 the yoginī's course ends there; Munidatta's paraphrase has the wheel of great bliss in its place (cp.04.m4).

symbolic.image: Oḍḍiyāna, where the yoginī's course ends

readings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), into which she is absorbed (his paraphrase puts it where the song has Oḍḍiyāna; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: The mountain at the centre of the world in Indian cosmology, also called Meru; tantric texts also locate it within the body. Munidatta says the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā to the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru (cp.04.m5).
The Yamunā (Jumna), the great river that joins the Ganges at Prayāga. The song uses the vernacular form Jaunā; Munidatta has the Sanskrit Yamunā.

symbolic.image: the river Yamunā, one of the two rivers the boat moves between

readings.referent: together with the Gaṅgā, the 'moon-appearance' and the 'sun-appearance' (candrābhāsa, sūryābhāsa), which are the grasped object and the grasping subject; pairing the Yamunā with the sun and the grasper follows word order only

entries.definition: A plank or board (Old Bengali paṭi). In song 5 the tree of delusion is split and its planks joined to build the bridge. Munidatta's word is pāṭaka; the Tibetan translation has spang leb, 'plank', in the line and in the comment.

symbolic.image: the planks joined after the tree is split

readings.referent: joined in one with the constant light (satatāloka); the Tibetan translation says 'the constant clear light is the plank'

entries.definition: A pot or jar for liquor. In song 3 sixty-four pots (ghaṛi) hold the liquor-seller's wares, and one pot (ḍulī) has a narrow spout. Old Bengali ghaṛi can also mean a period of about twenty-four minutes, and the Tibetan translation renders it both ways (chu tshod and g+ha ṭā). Munidatta's word is ghaṭī, which he links with ghaṭati, ‘joins’.

symbolic.image: the sixty-four pots of wares, and the one pot with a narrow spout

readings.referent: the one pot with the narrow spout: the avadhūtī, called ghaṭī because it joins (ghaṭati) the two truths, conventional and ultimate, and subtle in form because it stops the two appearances

the sixty-four pots: the sixty-four lotus petals of the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), for which ghaṭī is twilight language (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation, and its syntax is loose)

entries.definition: 'Radiant, clear light': in the completion-stage yoga of the tantras, the luminous nature of mind that dawns when the winds and concepts have dissolved. Munidatta calls the thief of the refrain 'the thief, clear light', who carries off the fault of the winds (cp.02.m4).

Power or efficacy (prabhāva; Tibetan mthu). Munidatta uses the word to introduce couplets: in song 30 the refrain, his second verse and his fourth verse each set out 'its power' (tasya prabhāva), in cp.30.m4 the power of innate joy (cp.30.m3, cp.30.m4, cp.30.m6). Compare his other framing words, such as praise (anuśaṃsā).

Wisdom (prajñā): discernment of how things really are, above all insight into emptiness; in the tantras it is paired with means (upāya) and pictured as female. In the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse Munidatta quotes, the flesh is to be freed from the cage of bones with the knife of wisdom (cp.06.m3).

The knowledge arising from wisdom (prajñā) in tantric union; it also names the third empowerment. Munidatta says that at night the naturally purified avadhūtī, through wisdom-knowledge, empowers the five aggregates (cp.02.m5); he names the wisdom-knowledge empowerment in song 1 (cp.01.m3).

forms.translit: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin mar
forms.lemma: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa

forms.translit: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa
forms.lemma: shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa

entries.definition: The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of all things, chief of the bodhisattva's perfections, also personified as a goddess and the name of a class of Mahāyāna sūtras. Munidatta glosses the mati of song 12 as understanding in accord with it (cp.12.m5); the Tibetan uses the feminine phyin ma.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The pairing of wisdom (prajñā), the understanding of emptiness, with means (upāya), compassionate method. In the yoginī tantras the two are pictured as female and male and their union is the goal. Munidatta describes Mahāmudrā, and the Hevajra Tantra itself, as having the nature of wisdom and means.

forms.translit: drug cu lhag pa brgya'i rang bzhin
drug cu lhag pa'i brgya'i rang bzhin

entries.definition: Natures (prakṛti): in the completion-stage yoga of the Guhyasamāja tradition, the natural states of conceptual mind, commonly counted as eighty and linked with the three luminous appearances, which cease as the winds dissolve. Munidatta speaks of a hundred and sixty, made without intrinsic nature by vajra recitation, and reads the song's pawns as them (cp.12.m4).

Faults belonging to nature (prakṛti), apparently the impurities of the body. Munidatta says the river of existence is deep because of them, since urine, excrement and the like flow out through six openings, and that its two banks are smeared with their mud (cp.05.m2). The Tibetan has rang bzhin gyi skyon.

Valid cognition, or a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa; Tibetan tshad ma): in Indian epistemology a reliable source of knowledge, such as perception or inference. Munidatta speaks of examination by valid cognition (cp.26.m3) and of reasoning established by it (cp.26.m5); the Tibetan line of song 26 has tshad ma where the Bengali has tulā, 'cotton'. The word also means 'measure'.

A conduit or channel for water, a spout or drain (Old Bengali paṇāla, Sanskrit praṇāla, praṇālī). In song 27 (3b) the lotus plant carries the lotus 'by the conduit' (paṇālem̐). Munidatta does not gloss the word; the Tibetan line has 'bab pa'i chu, 'flowing water', perhaps for it.

Prāṇāyāma, yogic control of the breath and vital wind, a limb of yoga in Indian and tantric systems; the Tibetan renders it srog rtsol, 'life' and 'exertion', and the comment on song 25 treats the two as a pair. Munidatta says prāṇa and āyāma have the nature of means and wisdom, and explains the fine weave through them (cp.25.m5).

Elaboration or proliferation (prapañca): the spreading out of the world in concepts and words, and in conduct, outward ritual complexity. Munidatta calls the conduct of song 2 'utterly free of elaboration' (niṣprapañca) (cp.02.m6); the conduct entry notes conduct 'with elaboration' (saprapañca) elsewhere.

Grace or favour (Sanskrit prasāda; Tibetan drin): the kindness of a teacher or deity through which realization comes. Munidatta often speaks of what is gained by the guru's grace; in song 19 he introduces the last couplet as the conduct of the lord of yogis that comes from the yoginī's grace (cp.19.m5).

Love (Old Bengali pehma, Sanskrit preman), the love in which the Śabara and Nairātmā pass the night until dawn in song 28. The Tibetan line has dga' bas, 'with joy'. Munidatta glosses it as the incomparable flavour of play (krīḍārasa), made to grow (cp.28.m5).

symbolic.image: the love in which the lovers pass the night until dawn

readings.referent: the incomparable flavour of play (krīḍārasa), which is made to grow; the Tibetan comment has 'the incomparable play increases' (rol pa'i dpe med pa 'phel bar 'gyur ro)

entries.definition: An ordinary person (Sanskrit pṛthagjana; Tibetan so so'i skye bo): in Buddhist usage, anyone who has not yet directly seen the truth, as distinct from the noble ones (ārya). Munidatta asks to whom, and saying what, he could give a settled doctrine for an ordinary person, since what appears is like the moon in water (cp.29.m5).

A word of uncertain sense in this song, set with 'creation and destruction' after the moon and sun are named as the two wheels. In Sanskrit Pulinda is the name of a forest-dwelling people; what it denotes in the boat scene is unclear, so the source form is kept for now.

symbolic.image: pulinda (literal sense uncertain)

readings.referent: 'the neuter' (napuṃsaka), in twilight language; the phrase 'nondual knowledge' just before it in the gloss may also belong to it
with the moon and the sun, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that make and unmake saṃsāra

entries.definition: A melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung; song 1 is in Paṭamañjarī. In the commentary the same word rāga also means 'passion', a different term (see way of great passion).

Passion or desire (rāga), with hatred and delusion one of the three root afflictions of Buddhist teaching. In song 11 the three are the ash the poet smears on; Munidatta says the fire of the passion of great bliss burns them (cp.11.m4). The same word names a song's melody, which has its own entry (raga).

Night (Old Bengali raeṇi, from Sanskrit rajanī). In song 19 the night passes, or dawns (pohāa), in the net of yoginīs; the Tibetan line has 'dawn broke' (nams langs). Munidatta takes its passing as the flight of the darkness of the afflictions (cp.19.m4). Compare the entries for midnight and evening.

symbolic.image: the night that passes, or turns to dawn, in the net of yoginīs

readings.referent: the darkness of the afflictions (kleśāndhakāra), which flees; the Tibetan: 'the darkness of the afflictions is cleared' (nyon mongs pa'i mun pa sangs pa)
the darkness of the conceptual thought of wisdom and means
the darkness of the afflictions of one’s own body

forms.translit: rgyal po yi ni gser lam

entries.definition: The royal road or king's highway (rājapatha), the main road of a kingdom. In the refrain of song 15 it follows a warning not to swerve by even a hair's breadth. The Tibetan has 'the king's golden road'; Munidatta compares a universal monarch entering his pleasure garden by the golden road (cp.15.m3).

symbolic.image: the royal road

readings.referent: the path of the avadhūtī, by which the lord of yogis playfully enters the lotus garden of the wheel of great bliss, as a universal monarch enters his pleasure garden by the golden road (a simile; he does not quote rājapatha)

entries.definition: Rāmakrī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 15 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody dga' bar byed pa, 'making joyful', as if the name were built from Sanskrit rāma, 'delighting', and kṛ, 'make'; how the name is formed is uncertain.

In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the right of the central channel (avadhūtī); the word also means 'tongue'. Munidatta names it with lalanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed (cp.04.m2).

Rasāyana: in Indian medicine, rejuvenating treatment; in alchemy, the making of elixirs, often of mercury (rasa), meant to make the body ageless and deathless. In song 22 the one who fears birth and death pursues rasa and rasāyana (4b); Munidatta speaks of various procedures of rasāyana (cp.22.m5). The Tibetan has bcud len, 'extracting essence', and gser 'gyur, 'turning to gold'.

A jewel or gem (Sanskrit ratna, Old Bengali raaṇa), a common image of worth in Buddhist writing. Song 9 speaks of the jewel of the ten powers in the ten directions; Munidatta calls it the jewel of suchness (cp.09.m5). Distinct from maṇi, 'jewel', in the code phrases 'root of the jewel' and 'vajra jewel'.

symbolic.image: the jewel of the ten powers, in the ten directions

readings.referent: the jewel of suchness (tathatāratna), endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses and other qualities, which pervades the ten directions and is 'taken' (hāritam) by us through the force of repeated experience (the Tibetan has 'radiates'); by its power the lord-elephant of ignorance is to be tamed

entries.definition: A river (Old Bengali ṇaī, Sanskrit nadī). Song 5 opens with the river of existence, deep and swift, muddy on both sides and without footing in the middle; the poet's bridge crosses it. Rivers, their banks and their crossings recur throughout the songs.

symbolic.image: the river of existence, deep and swift, with mud on both sides and no footing in the middle

readings.referent: the three appearances (ābhāsatraya), lalanā, rasanā and the rest, which are to be understood as the river in twilight language because of the depth of its near and far banks; in it the surge of sense objects rises and perishes by day, by night and at twilight
the river of great delusion that is the three appearances, which the yogis wish to cross; the Tibetan translation has rtsa, 'channel', where the Sanskrit has 'river', apparently reading nāḍī for nadī

entries.definition: A road or way (Old Bengali bāṭa). In the first line of song 7 āli and kāli block the road, and seeing it Kāṇha is downcast. The Tibetan translation has lam, 'road, path'.

symbolic.image: the road that āli and kāli block

readings.referent: the path of the avadhūtī (avadhūtīmārga), which Kṛṣṇācārya, having received the instruction in vajra recitation, firmly blocks, unifying by means of āli and kāli; the Tibetan has āli and kāli made one and then held firm and stopped in the avadhūtī's path
the path of the joy of cessation in the purified avadhūtī, on which no fear of toll-house or guard-post remains

entries.definition: A root (Sanskrit and Old Bengali mūla). In song 20 (4b) the speaker does something to the root (nakhali, of uncertain sense; Munidatta has nikṛtti, 'cutting') before the father is destroyed; the Tibetan line seems to say 'gathers what fell at the root'. Munidatta glosses the root as conventional bodhicitta (cp.20.m5). Not the root of the jewel.

symbolic.image: the root that the speaker cuts

readings.referent: conventional bodhicitta (saṃvṛtibodhicitta), whose cutting (nikṛtti) was done by Kukkurīpāda, meditating on selflessness, at the root of the jewel, inside the jewel

entries.definition: A rope (Tibetan thag pa), the third of the things the deer escapes without in couplet 5 of song 23, which survives only in the Tibetan. Munidatta takes it as twilight language for conceptual thought about the joy of mind (cp.23.m6). Not the boat's mooring rope (kācchi), which the glossary also renders 'rope'.

symbolic.image: a rope, absent as the deer escapes

readings.referent: in twilight language, conceptual thought about the joy of mind (thugs kyi dga' ba) (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Rage, anger (Sanskrit roṣa). In the last couplet of song 28 the mad Śabara, in great rage (garuā roṣe), enters the cleft of the mountain's peak; the Tibetan has cher khros, 'greatly enraged'. Munidatta reads the rage as the impulse of the scent of the joy of knowledge (cp.28.m8).

symbolic.image: the mad Śabara's great rage as he enters the cleft of the peak

readings.referent: being impelled by the scent of the joy of knowledge (jñānānandagandha) and set moving toward the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss; the Tibetan comment agrees (ye shes kyi dga' ba'i dris bskul bar gyur pa)

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense closing the refrain of song 17: the sound of the string bilasai ruṇā, 'plays ruṇā'. The Tibetan line has 'proclaims compassion' (snying rje), as if reading karuṇā; the word may instead echo the ringing of the strings. Munidatta's comment does not take it up (cp.17.m2).

Form (Sanskrit rūpa, Old Bengali rūba; Tibetan gzugs): visible shape and appearance, and in Buddhist analysis the first of the five aggregates. Song 29 says the colour, mark and form of what it speaks of are not known (3a), and Munidatta repeats the three (cp.29.m4). Not silver (rūpā), on which Munidatta puns elsewhere.

A Śabara, one of a forest and hill people of eastern and central India whom caste society treated as outsiders; a Śabara woman, the Śabarī, is a figure of the songs. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya's Dohākoṣa that Munidatta quotes, the Śabaras dwell on a high mountain peak (cp.06.m4). The Tibetan renders the word sha ba, 'deer'.

forms.translit: sa wa ri yi bu mo

entries.definition: A woman or girl of the Śabaras, a forest and hill people (Old Bengali sabarī). In song 28 the young Śabarī lives on a high mountain, dressed in peacock feathers with a guñjā garland at her neck, and roams the forest alone wearing earrings and a vajra. The Tibetan transcribes the word sa wa ri, as for the man.

symbolic.image: the Śabara girl who lives on the high mountain and roams the forest alone

readings.referent: Nairātmā, the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā) born of the letter aṃ: the vajra-holder's wife, who dwells at the summit of Sumeru in the wheel of great bliss
Nairātmā alone: 'the Śabarī alone' is glossed 'that Nairātmā is alone' (sā nairātmā ekakā)

alt: all that moves and does not move

forms.lemma: g.yo ba dang mi g.yo ba

forms.translit: g.yo ba dang mi g.yo ba
forms.lemma: g.yo ba dang mi g.yo ba

entries.definition: Sacarācara, 'with the moving and the unmoving': beings that move and things that do not, a stock Sanskrit phrase for the whole world. In song 22 some roam sacarācara (5a); Munidatta places them in the great places of Jambudvīpa (cp.22.m6). The Tibetan has g.yo dang mi g.yo, 'moving and unmoving'.

The six destinies or realms of rebirth (Sanskrit ṣaḍgati, Old Bengali chaṛagai): gods, asuras, humans, animals, hungry ghosts and hell beings. Song 9 says all six are pure by nature. Munidatta lists the four kinds of birth, from eggs, wombs, moisture and spontaneously, and beings 'of the nature of gods, asuras and the rest' (cp.09.m4).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The innate: what is inborn and unfabricated, a central idea of the siddhas' songs. Munidatta speaks of 'the fruit, innate joy', in the form of coupled union (cp.01.m2) and of 'the great bliss of innate joy' (cp.01.m3).

forms.translit: lhan cig skyes pa ni mdzes pa can
forms.lemma: lhan cig skyes pa mdzes pa can

entries.definition: Sahaja Sundarī, 'the innate beauty', the name the refrain of song 28 gives the Śabara's own wife. The Tibetan translates it lhan skyes mdzes ldan ma, 'the beautiful one, innate'. Munidatta puts the refrain in the mouth of the Blessed Lady Nairātmā.

symbolic.image: the Śabara's wife, named Sahaja Sundarī

readings.referent: the jñānamudrā, the name the Blessed Lady Nairātmā gives herself when she comforts the Śabara

forms.translit: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba
lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas
forms.lemma: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba
lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba

entries.definition: 'Innate joy', one of the four joys of tantric yoga (joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation, innate joy); traditions differ over the order of the last two. Munidatta says bodhicitta is opened by it.

A woman's female friend or confidante (Sanskrit sakhī, Old Bengali sahi), a stock addressee of Indian love poetry. The refrain of song 17 calls 'O friend' as Heruka's vīṇā plays. Munidatta's paraphrase addresses her as Nairātmā ('bho sakhi nairātme', cp.17.m2); the Tibetan has grogs and grogs mo, 'friend'.

symbolic.image: the friend addressed in the refrain

readings.referent: Nairātmā, addressed as 'O friend, Nairātmā' (bho sakhi nairātme); the Tibetan has kye'i grogs mo bdag med ma

entries.definition: Direct realization (sākṣātkāra, 'making before the eyes'): knowing something by immediate experience rather than by inference or report. Munidatta introduces the last couplet of song 20, his 'fourth verse', as stating direct realization (cp.20.m6), and says Guḍḍarī has directly realized the vajra-like samādhi (cp.04.m6). The Tibetan has mngon sum du byas pa.

Power or potency (śakti), which tantric traditions often personify as the female energy of a deity. Song 11 speaks of the nāṛi śakti that the poet holds firm; Munidatta takes the śakti as the chief of the thirty-two channels, the avadhūtikā (cp.11.m2). The Tibetan translation renders it nus ldan, 'the potent one'.

symbolic.image: the śakti of the channels, which the poet holds firm

readings.referent: the chief of the thirty-two channels, the avadhūtikā, whose form is the joy of cessation, held firm at the root of the jewel by the guru's grace; the Tibetan has 'the channel of the potent one is the chief, the avadhūtī'

entries.definition: The wife's sister (Old Bengali śālī; compare Sanskrit śyālī), named in song 11 among those killed at home, beside the husband's mother and sister, which makes the household hard to picture. The Tibetan has skud po, a brother-in-law. Munidatta does not gloss her by name.

symbolic.image: the wife's sister, killed at home

entries.definition: Meditative absorption: a settled, one-pointed state of mind. Song 1 asks what all the samādhis are for. Munidatta explains that the absorptions taught for restraining the senses, like harsh fasting observances, achieve nothing on the way of great passion, because they lack bliss (cp.01.m4).

‘Same taste’ (samarasa): the state in which what seemed separate, such as bliss and emptiness or the partners in union, is known as a single savour; a key word of the siddhas' songs, close to ‘one taste’ (ekarasa). In the Sekoddeśa verse Munidatta quotes, the luminous stream becomes of the same taste with the hosts of Jinas (cp.03.m5).

The commitments a tantric initiate takes on, and by extension the ritual substances bound up with them. Munidatta says the yogin pleases the true guru with an offering of pledge substances before receiving the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (cp.01.m3).

In the yoginī-tantra map of the subtle body, the wheel (cakra) at the throat, between the wheel at the heart and the wheel of great bliss at the crown; usually pictured as a lotus of sixteen petals. Munidatta reads the neck of song 18 as this wheel (cp.18.m5). The Tibetan has longs spyod rdzogs pa'i 'khor lo.

The enjoyment body (sambhogakāya; Tibetan longs spyod rdzogs pa'i sku): in Mahāyāna accounts of a buddha's bodies, the glorious form in which a buddha appears to bodhisattvas, between the dharma body and the emanation body. Munidatta, glossing the cloud of compassion, speaks of the purified enjoyment body of the lord of yogis spreading forth by the guru's grace (cp.30.m2).

Vigilance (saṃprajanya): watchful awareness of what one's body, speech and mind are doing, a key virtue of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, which Munidatta quotes in this song. He blames its lack (asaṃprajanya) for the plight of 'my mind-deer', wrapped from beginningless time in the poison of the Māra of death (cp.06.m2). The Tibetan has shes bzhin ma yin pa.

The round of birth and death in which beings wander, driven by ignorance and craving. In a verse Munidatta quotes from the Sampuṭodbhava, the Vajra-holder calls the mind itself saṃsāra when it is clouded by concepts, restless as lightning and stained by passion (cp.01.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The conventional or relative level of truth, things as they appear and are spoken of, as opposed to the ultimate. Munidatta uses it for the conventional aspect of bodhicitta, which he describes as having the form of semen.

The coded idiom of the songs, in which ordinary images such as an outcaste woman, a boat or a lotus carry a hidden sense disclosed by a teacher. Munidatta says Kāṇha speaks here ‘in the twilight language of the word Ḍombī’. Whether sandhyā ‘twilight’ or sandhā ‘intention’ is meant is debated.

A continuum or stream (Sanskrit santāna; Tibetan rgyud): in Buddhist thought, the unbroken succession of moments that makes up a person or a mind, in place of a lasting self. On song 29's refrain Munidatta says he cannot make out its continuum, long, short, round or otherwise, nor where it stays (cp.29.m3).

A fret of a vīṇā, if Old Bengali sāri goes back to Sanskrit sārikā, the word musical treatises use for frets. In song 17 āli and kāli are both sāri. The Tibetan has gnya' non, literally 'neck-presser'. Bengali sāri also means 'row', which would suit the two series of letters.

symbolic.image: frets of the vīṇā, which the song says are āli and kāli

readings.referent: the essential syllable (sārākṣara), the letter a, among the letters of āli and kāli; his paraphrase puts sāra where the song has sāri, without an explicit gloss

entries.en: emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects

forms.translit: rnam pa thams cad dang ldan pa'i stong pa nyid
forms.lemma: rnam pa thams cad dang ldan pa'i stong pa nyid

forms.translit: rnam pa thams cad kyi mchog dang ldan pa'i stong pa nyid

entries.definition: Emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (sarvākāravaropetā śūnyatā): emptiness understood not as a bare absence but as bearing every excellent quality, a phrase of Mahāyāna and especially Kālacakra literature. Munidatta says the boat, bodhicitta, is filled, through identity with this emptiness, with the essence of the true guru's grace (cp.08.m2).

A husband's mother, in the joint household the figure of authority over a young wife. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law'.

symbolic.image: the mother-in-law's house, where key and lock are put

readings.referent: the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru, to which the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā; his words śvāsam āgāraṃ ('breath', 'house') seem to echo sāsu gharem̐, and the Tibetan has dbugs kyi khyim, 'house of breath'
breath (śvāsa): the mind-wind spoken of before, understood as the wind of the consciousnesses of the eye and the other senses, which Kāṇha makes without nature of its own

entries.definition: 'Constant light' (satatāloka): in Munidatta's gloss on the planks of song 5, what is made one with the plank (cp.05.m4). The Tibetan renders it 'constant clear light' (rtag tu 'od gsal), linking it with clear light (prabhāsvara); Munidatta does not explain the phrase.

The two truths of Mahāyāna thought: conventional truth (saṃvṛti), how things appear and function, and ultimate truth, their emptiness. Munidatta pictures beings sunk in an ocean of great delusion about the two truths, whom Lūyī wished to rescue (cp.01.m2).

A seed (Tibetan sa bon, regularly for Sanskrit bīja); in Buddhist thought also a latent potential, and in the tantras the syllable from which a deity arises. Song 24 speaks of a seed like the sky. Munidatta calls the verse a teaching on the power of the seed of dharma, born from the mind whose nature is clear light (cp.24.m4).

symbolic.image: a seed like the sky

readings.referent: the seed of dharma (chos kyi sa bon), whose power the verse teaches: the seed equal to the sky, born from the mind whose nature is clear light

entries.definition: Shade or shadow (Tibetan grib ma). In song 24 the three worlds are pervaded by shade from one's own tree. Munidatta equates the shade of one's own tree with the sky-like seed's own nature, utterly luminous, and speaks of the lord of yogis pervading the three worlds with rays of knowledge (cp.24.m4).

symbolic.image: the shade from one's own tree, which pervades the three worlds

readings.referent: the nature of the sky-like seed, utterly luminous ('od rab tu gsal ba); its pervading the three worlds is the lord of yogis pervading them with the rays of knowledge (ye shes kyi 'od zer)

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: 'Accomplished one': a tantric adept who has gained accomplishment (siddhi). The poets of the songs are siddhas; Munidatta calls Lūyī a siddha master, siddhācārya (cp.01.m2), and 'the first siddha master' (cp.01.m6).

A settled doctrine or conclusion (Sanskrit siddhānta, 'established end'; Tibetan grub mtha', 'tenet'): what a school holds as proven. Munidatta's paraphrase of song 29 (4a) puts it where the song has piricchā: to whom, saying what, should he give a settled doctrine to an ordinary person (cp.29.m5)? The Tibetan line has dri ba, 'ask'.

Accomplishment: a power or attainment won through practice, above all the supreme accomplishment of awakening. Munidatta quotes the Rativajra calling bodhicitta 'the treasury of all accomplishments' (cp.01.m2), and the Guhyasamāja on harsh austerities that disturb the mind and so defeat accomplishment (cp.01.m4).

Silver (Old Bengali rūpā, Sanskrit rūpya). In song 8 the boat is so full of gold that there is no place to put silver; the Tibetan translation has dngul. Munidatta takes rūpā as rūpa, 'form', the first of the aggregates, which have no separate place (cp.08.m2); the Tibetan commentary keeps the sound, rU pa.

symbolic.image: silver, for which there is no place in the boat full of gold

readings.referent: form (rūpa) and the other aggregates, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, which have no separate place, since everything is made of that (a play on rūpā, 'silver', and rūpa, 'form')

entries.definition: The lion's roar (siṃhanāda): in Buddhist texts, the Buddha's fearless proclamation of the teaching, which silences opponents as a lion's roar silences other animals. Munidatta sets 'the lion's roar of emptiness' beside the hero's sound of Kāṇha's unstruck ḍamaru (cp.11.m2); the Tibetan has stong pa nyid seng ge'i sgra.

Śīvarī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 26 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name sha ba ri, which points rather to a form like Śabarī or Śavarī (compare the Śabara people); which spelling is original, and how the two relate, is uncertain.

In Indian tradition the moon has sixteen digits (Sanskrit kalā), the portions by which it waxes; all are present at the full moon. Munidatta speaks of the moon-disc of bodhicitta 'endowed with sixteen digits' (cha bcu drug dang ldan pa), rising at the time of the full moon of song 24 (cp.24.m2).

The five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness) into which Buddhist analysis divides a person. Munidatta reads the five branches of the tree in song 1 as these aggregates, 'beginning with form' (cp.01.m2).

The pair creation (sṛṣṭi) and destruction or withdrawal (saṃhāra): the coming into being and dissolution of a world. In this song the phrase stands beside the pulinda after the moon and sun are named as two wheels; Munidatta says the moon, the sun and the pulinda bring about the creation and destruction of saṃsāra.

Steady, still (Old Bengali thira, Sanskrit sthira): in the siddhas' songs, often the steadiness a yogi gives to mind, breath or vital essence so that it neither wavers nor falls. In song 3 the refrain and the last couplet both speak of making something steady; Munidatta names innate joy (cp.03.m3) and the unfallen bodhicitta (cp.03.m5).

symbolic.image: making something steady (the object is unstated in the song)

readings.referent: innate joy, made steady through the joy of cessation by the grace of the vajra guru
the unfallen bodhicitta, made steady through the channel of semen and moved without waves

entries.definition: A stone (Tibetan rdo), the second of the three things the deer escapes without in couplet 5 of song 23, which survives only in the Tibetan. The line reads rdo lcags, perhaps 'stone and iron' or one device; Munidatta cites only rdo, as twilight language for conceptual thought about the joy of speech (cp.23.m6).

symbolic.image: a stone, absent as the deer escapes

readings.referent: in twilight language, conceptual thought about the joy of speech (gsung gi dga' ba) (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Torpor or dullness (styāna): heaviness of body and mind, a secondary affliction and, with drowsiness, one of the five hindrances to meditation. Munidatta says that one who understands the true nature of all things, and so is free of sleep and torpor, sees things in the waking state as in a dream (cp.13.m5). The Tibetan has rmugs pa.

'Well-gone' (sugata), an epithet of a buddha. In the verse Munidatta attributes to Nāgārjuna, the very mind by which fools are bound in saṃsāra brings yogins to the state (gati) of the sugatas (cp.12.m5); the Tibetan has bde bar gshegs pa.

Bliss, happiness (sukha). In the tantras the songs draw on, the bliss that arises in yogic union is itself the path, and great bliss (mahāsukha) its goal. Munidatta says the world is pervaded by bliss, as pervader and pervaded (cp.07.m3); the Tibetan has 'great bliss' there.

A channel of the subtle body through which semen, the bodily form of bodhicitta, is said to move. Munidatta apparently gives this name to the avadhūtī here: by it, through the guru's instruction, bodhicitta is made steady and moved without waves (cp.03.m5).

A woman who distils and sells liquor (Sanskrit śuṇḍinī), a trade that caste society ranked low. In song 3 she is one woman in two houses who brews liquor with bark and sets out her wares for customers. The Tibetan translation calls her chang ma, ‘beer woman’.

symbolic.image: a woman who brews and sells liquor, one woman in two houses

readings.referent: the avadhūtī, the central channel (‘she, the avadhūtikā, is the liquor-seller’); in the same gloss the mature yogī joins the moon and the sun, left and right, and makes them enter the middle channel (the syntax is loose)

entries.definition: Emptiness: the absence of intrinsic existence in all things, a central idea of Mahāyāna thought. In song 1 it appears in the Old Bengali compound sunupākha, which Munidatta renders śūnyatāpakṣa, 'the side (or wing) of emptiness' (cp.01.m5).

readings.referent: the mind made to enter clear light (prabhāsvara)

forms.translit: shin du mngon par dga' ba
forms.lemma: shin tu mngon par dga' ba

entries.definition: Sexual pleasure, lovemaking (Sanskrit surata, Old Bengali suraa). In song 19 day and night pass in lovemaking (suraapasaṅga). Munidatta speaks of attachment to lovemaking (suratābhiṣvaṅga) with the jñānamudrā (cp.19.m4) and with Ḍombī, whom he calls the jñānamudrā (cp.19.m5); the Tibetan line has shin tu dga' ba, 'great delight'.

symbolic.image: lovemaking, in which day and night pass

readings.referent: lovemaking 'with this jñānamudrā' (the wisdom seal), to which the lord of yogis is attached day and night

attachment to lovemaking with Ḍombī as the naturally radiant, purified avadhūtikā, the jñānamudrā, whom the yogins who delight in it never abandon for a moment, since she is the support of the joy of great bliss

entries.definition: The sun. In this song the sun and the moon are called 'the two wheels'. The pair recurs throughout the songs.

symbolic.image: the sun, one of 'the two wheels'

readings.referent: with the moon and the pulinda, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that bring about the making and unmaking of saṃsāra, which practice brings to a stop

entries.definition: Own-being or nature (Sanskrit svabhāva, Old Bengali sahāba): what a thing is of itself. Madhyamaka thought denies that anything has such an intrinsic nature. Song 9 says all beings are pure by nature; the verse Munidatta quotes calls outer things unreal because they lack intrinsic nature (cp.09.m2, cp.09.m4). Compare 'without intrinsic nature' and 'true nature'.

‘Self-blessing’ or self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), also the name of the third of the five stages (pañcakrama) of the Guhyasamāja completion stage. Munidatta says that joining moon and sun in the middle channel makes self-blessing firm (cp.03.m2), and speaks of bodhicitta ‘gone to self-blessing’ (cp.03.m3); he does not explain the term.

A dream (Sanskrit svapna, Old Bengali suinā; Tibetan rmi lam). With illusion, a standard Mahāyāna comparison for how things appear without being real. The refrain of song 13 makes the ocean of existence like illusion and dream, and its fourth couplet speaks of a dream without sleep; Munidatta says things then appear like a dream in the waking state (cp.13.m5).

One's own form: what a thing really is, as against how it appears. Munidatta glosses Kāṇha's ‘in good faith’ as ‘with an intention set on the true nature’ and quotes the Hevajra: the innate is called the true nature, and the true nature itself is nirvāṇa (cp.10.m5).

forms.translit: rang gis yang dag par rig pa

entries.definition: Self-awareness (svasaṃvedana): in Buddhist epistemology, the mind's awareness of itself in the very act of knowing; in the siddhas' songs, a knowing that needs no object beyond itself. Song 15 opens by examining its true nature. Munidatta calls Śānti a siddhācārya whose nature is the experience of self-awareness in the union of vajra and lotus (cp.15.m2).

‘One's own place’ (svasthāna): a phrase in Munidatta's glosses for the proper seat of the yoginī or avadhūtī. He explains the yoginī's throw in song 4 as union in her own place (cp.04.m4); the Kāmaru entry records her own place in the wheel of great bliss (cp.02.m5).

forms.translit: dang pa'i rgyal pos (apparently an error for ngang pa'i rgyal pos)

entries.definition: The king of swans (Tibetan ngang pa'i rgyal po; ngang pa regularly renders Sanskrit haṃsa, a goose or swan). Indian poetry credits the bird with separating milk from water and drinking only the milk. Munidatta gives this outward example for song 24's swan king, then turns to the supreme yogin who eats existence without taking it up (cp.24.m6).

symbolic.image: the swan king that separates milk from water

readings.referent: outwardly, the swan king separates water mixed with milk and drinks the milk; so the supreme yogin (the comment addresses Kāṇha himself), understanding the nature of existence through reality itself, is to eat existence and not take it up

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in song 16 (gaaṇa ṭākali, 'the sky's ṭākali'), just before the mind enters nirvāṇa. Munidatta repeats it as gaganaṭaka and explains it as being driven on by the unstruck sound (cp.16.m4). The Tibetan line has 'the sky became the unstruck sound'; the Tibetan comment only transliterates the word (ṭa ge).

symbolic.image: the sky's ṭākali

readings.referent: being impelled by the unstruck sound (anāhataśabda), so that the mind-elephant goes to the lake of nirvāṇa

entries.definition: The tamarind (Old Bengali tentali; Sanskrit tintiḍī or ciñcā), a tree with curved, sour pods. Munidatta likens bodhicitta, the fruit of the body-tree, to a tamarind pod for its crookedness. The Tibetan translation renders it bse yab, a fruit name whose identification is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the tamarind of the tree, which the crocodile eats

readings.referent: bodhicitta, the fruit of the body-tree, crooked like a tamarind pod

entries.definition: Cord or string (Sanskrit tantrī), which Ḍombī sells in song 10. Whether cord, an instrument string, thread or even a loom is meant is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the cord that Ḍombī sells

readings.referent: the bhaga (female organ), 'the place of the lotus', which has the form of ignorance

entries.definition: 'Finest of trees', from taru, tree, and vara, excellent. Song 1 opens by calling the body such a tree, with five branches. Munidatta defends the comparison as a poetic figure (utprekṣā) that states a likeness resting on some difference (cp.01.m2).

symbolic.image: a fine tree with five branches

readings.referent: the five aggregates, beginning with form, as the five branches
the six senses, the elements and the sense objects, taken together as the body-tree, its leaves being the grasped, the grasper and the grasping
ignorance (avidyārūpa)

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘Thus-gone’: an epithet of a buddha. The tantras arrange their deities in families headed by five or six tathāgatas, and Munidatta links six tathāgatas with the wheel, earrings, necklace and other ornaments of tantric conduct.

Suchness (tathatā): things just as they are, their real nature beyond conceptual construction; in Mahāyāna thought a synonym of emptiness and of reality. In song 9 the elephant's ichor is suchness-ichor, and Munidatta speaks of the ichor and the jewel of suchness (cp.09.m3, cp.09.m5). The Tibetan has de nyid in the song, de bzhin nyid in the comment.

Reality, 'thatness' (tattva): things as they truly are, which the path aims to know directly. Munidatta says that in the hearts of scholars proud of outer treatises not even a glimmer of reality opens, and quotes a tantra: for those who do not know reality, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit (cp.06.m6).

Footing, or a bottom within reach in deep water (Old Bengali thāha; compare Hindi thāh, 'bottom', and Bengali athai, 'bottomless'). In song 5 the river of existence has none in the middle. Munidatta repeats the word without a Sanskrit equivalent; the Tibetan translation has 'no place to stay' ('dug gnas med).

symbolic.image: the middle of the river, where there is no footing

readings.referent: the avadhūtī, whose measure (pramāṇa) a novice yogi cannot take

entries.definition: Lord, master (Old Bengali ṭhākura; Sanskrit ṭhakkura), a title of rank also used of gods. In the refrain and fourth couplet of song 12 it names the chief piece of Kāṇha's game, which the Tibetan translation calls rgyal po, 'king'. Munidatta reads it as the mind (cp.12.m3, cp.12.m5).

symbolic.image: the king (ṭhākura) of the game, brought to parinirvāṇa by intelligence

readings.referent: the mind of ignorance (avidyācitta), named with 'the helpful instruction' in a gloss that has no verb; the Tibetan construes it as 'by the means of one who benefits the mind of ignorance'
the mind on which affliction (saṃkleśa) had been superimposed, made one on which parinirvāṇa is superimposed

entries.definition: A thief, who in the refrain of song 2 takes the earring at midnight while the household sleeps. The refrain's cauri may be the agent case or a feminine, 'thief-woman'; the Tibetan rkun ma does not decide it. Munidatta names the thief differently in two comments.

symbolic.image: the thief who takes the earring at midnight

readings.referent: innate joy (sahajānanda), the thief who steals the 'wealth' of the faults of the winds
the clear light (prabhāsvara), the thief who carries off the fault of the winds

entries.definition: Thread or yarn (Tibetan srad bu, which regularly renders Sanskrit sūtra). In the Tibetan comment on the last couplet of song 25, Munidatta says that by 'his grace' the binding by the thread of delusion's clinging embrace is torn apart (cp.25.m6), where the line has the weaver freed from the net of delusion. Compare cord (tanti) and rope.

A measure: three cubits and a half (Tibetan khru, 'cubit', the forearm's length, regularly renders Sanskrit hasta). It opens couplet 3 of song 25, perhaps as the length of the cloth or the loom. Munidatta explains the phrase as one's own body, in which one is released into the house of meditation and the third joy arises (cp.25.m4).

symbolic.image: three and a half cubits

readings.referent: one's own body (rang gi lus), in which one is released into the house of meditation (bsam gtan gyi khang pa) and the third joy is produced; the gloss covers the phrase and what follows it (Tibetan comment only)

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in the first line of song 4: the thing the yoginī is asked to press. Its first part is probably ti-, 'three'. Munidatta cites it as tiyaṛa; the Tibetan translation has ka mgo, whose sense here is unclear.

symbolic.image: the tiaḍḍā that the yoginī is asked to press

readings.referent: the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā, which are pressed and made free of appearance

entries.definition: Time and non-time (Tibetan dus dang dus min; the Old Bengali is lost): a pair named in couplet 4 of song 23, which survives only in the Tibetan, in an obscure line about the path of the wind. Munidatta explains the pair as the moon and the sun, with the wind of the avadhūtī as a third (cp.23.m5).

symbolic.image: time and non-time, the two named with the path of the wind

readings.referent: the moon and the sun; he adds a third, the wind of the avadhūtī, and says the fourth joy destroys them all (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: 'Ford-maker': a follower of a non-Buddhist religious path. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, buddhatīrthika most likely means 'Buddhists and tīrthikas', those who do not know the reversed meditation in which passion frees (cp.01.m4).

A tortoise: the Old Bengali duli, which the Tibetan translation renders rus sbal. Song 2 opens with the paradox of milking one. Munidatta's gloss echoes the word's syllables (dvaya, 'dual'; līna, 'dissolved'), a division the Tibetan commentary spells out.

symbolic.image: a tortoise that is milked

readings.referent: the lotus of great bliss (mahāsukhakamala), in which the dual aspect has dissolved; duli is to be understood in the convention of twilight language
its milking: conventional bodhicitta, drawn out through the sequence of joys beginning with joy in the course of union with a karmamudrā, which travels the path of the avadhūtī

entries.definition: A town or city, the settled world of caste society. Untouchable communities such as the Ḍoms lived outside it, and in this song Ḍombī's hut stands beyond it.

symbolic.image: the town, outside which Ḍombī's hut stands

readings.referent: the mass of sense objects, beginning with visible form

entries.definition: The three worlds or realms into which Buddhist cosmology divides saṃsāra: the realm of desire, the realm of form and the formless realm; also used loosely for the whole world. Munidatta says the avadhūtī, in its conventional aspect as semen, creates the three worlds (cp.02.m5).

readings.referent: body, speech and mind (kāyavākcitta), which Kāṇha says he has rowed with ease

entries.definition: A tree (Old Bengali rukha, from Sanskrit vṛkṣa). In song 2 a crocodile eats the tamarind of the tree. The plain word is distinct from taruvara, 'fine tree', in song 1, though Munidatta reads both trees as the body.

symbolic.image: the tree whose tamarind the crocodile eats

readings.referent: the body, as 'the body-tree' (kāyavṛkṣa), whose fruit is bodhicitta

entries.definition: The Thirty (Sanskrit tridaśa, Old Bengali tiasa): the gods, thirty in round numbers (strictly thirty-three), and their heaven. Munidatta takes the tiasa of song 22 (5a) as tridaśa, the abode of the gods, reached by mantras and herbs (cp.22.m6); the Tibetan comment has 'the Thirty-three'. The Tibetan line has no equivalent, and tiasa might instead mean 'thirst' (tṛṣā).

The three refuges: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, in which Buddhists take refuge. Song 13 opens by making the three refuges a boat. Munidatta takes 'the three' as body, speech and mind, and speaks of a fourth refuge in which they dissolve, the body of great bliss (cp.13.m2). The Tibetan has skyabs gsum.

symbolic.image: the three refuges, made into a boat

readings.referent: body, speech and mind (kāyavākcitta), 'the three'; the fourth refuge, in which they have dissolved, is the body of great bliss, which in twilight language is to be understood as the boat

entries.definition: The vajra of body, of speech and of mind: a buddha's body, speech and mind, which tantric practice aims to make the practitioner's own. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes the vajra of body firm through deity yoga, steadies the vajra of speech by vajra recitation, then works to make the vajra of mind firm (cp.04.m5).

Cotton (Old Bengali tulā; Sanskrit tūla), here raw cotton being carded: song 26 cards it again and again until nothing is left (1a, 3a). Munidatta, citing the word, plays on tulā, 'balance', calling body, speech and mind 'fit for weighing' (cp.26.m2). The Tibetan line has tshad ma, 'valid cognition' or 'measure', in its place; its comment transcribes tu la.

symbolic.image: cotton, carded again and again

readings.referent: the three worlds, that is, body, speech and mind, which because of the faults of nature (prakṛtidoṣa) are 'fit for weighing' (tulanayogya): a play on tulā, 'balance, weighing', set beside the cited word without an explicit equation; the Tibetan comment has 'what is to be measured by valid cognition' (tshad mas gzhal bar rig pa)

entries.definition: Two places or two states (Tibetan gnas gnyis). In couplet 4 of song 25 the two places are cut before the strands are tightened and stretched firm, apparently work on the loom. Munidatta, citing the phrase as gnas gnyis chad gyur, explains it as cutting off the grasping at things and non-things (cp.25.m5).

symbolic.image: the two places that are cut

readings.referent: the grasping at things and non-things (dngos po dngos po med par 'dzin pa), which is cut off before the right union of vajra and lotus is taught (Tibetan comment only)

forms.translit: gnyis su med pa sgrub pa
forms.lemma: gnyis su med pa sgrub pa

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Advayasiddhi ('Accomplishment of the Nondual'; Tibetan gnyis su med pa sgrub pa), quoting its verse: what has no arising by its own nature, and no destruction to be seen, is nondual knowledge, free of all conceptions (cp.22.m4). A work of this name is ascribed to Lakṣmīṅkarā; that the verse is from it is unchecked.

forms.translit: bla na med pa'i mtshams sbyor
forms.lemma: bla na med pa'i mtshams sbyor

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Anuttarasandhi (Tibetan bla na med pa'i mtshams sbyor); it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse: of all illusions, the illusion of woman is the most distinguished, and in it the distinction of the three knowledges is clearly seen (cp.15.m4).

forms.translit: rab tu mi gnas pa gsal bar mdzad pa
forms.lemma: rab tu mi gnas pa gsal bar mdzad pa

forms.translit: rab tu mi gnas pa gsal ba

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Non-abiding'; Shastri restores the syllable pra); it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse: every concept arising in the mind is to be given up; blissful joy and dispassion alike are mere conception; nirvāṇa is nothing other than the mind free of concepts (cp.08.m2).

forms.translit: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa
forms.lemma: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa

entries.definition: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Conduct of Awakening'), Śāntideva's verse treatise on the bodhisattva path. Munidatta quotes its verses on separating skin, flesh and bones with the knife of wisdom and asking what core there is in the body (cp.06.m3). The Tibetan translation names it byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa.

forms.translit: lha mo bzhis zhus pa rnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud

entries.definition: The Caturdevīparipṛcchā ('Questions of the Four Goddesses'), a mahāyoga tantra usually counted among the explanatory tantras of the Guhyasamāja. Munidatta quotes its verse: for those who do not know reality, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit (cp.06.m6). The Tibetan has lha mo bzhis zhus pa.

Dohākoṣa ('Treasury of Dohās'), a title given to collections of dohā couplets by several siddhas, among them Saraha and Kāṇha. Here Munidatta quotes the one by Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha): Kāṇha clearly knows the one path of the innate, while those who read and recite the many scriptures know nothing (cp.05.m6).

forms.translit: tshigs su bcad pa gcig gis bcom ldan 'das ma

entries.definition: A source Munidatta cites as ekaślokā bhagavatī, apparently a praise of the Blessed Lady (perhaps the Perfection of Wisdom as goddess) in a single verse. He quotes its opening, 'free of the faults of arising, abiding and perishing' (cp.22.m3). The Tibetan reads 'with one verse, to the Blessed Lady'. Not otherwise identified here.

The Guhyasamāja ('Secret Assembly') Tantra, a major Buddhist tantra, which Munidatta cites as the Śrī Samāja. Here he quotes it on the need for the vajra guru (cp.01.m3) and against harsh austerities, urging that awakening be accomplished through bliss (cp.01.m4).

forms.translit: dpal ldan he ru ka'i rgyud kyi rgyal po

entries.definition: A tantra Munidatta cites as the Śrī Heruka Tantra, for an analysis in which nothing is found, taught in its chapter on reality (tattvapaṭala) (cp.05.m3). Which work is meant is uncertain: Heruka is a name both of Hevajra and of Cakrasaṃvara, so a tantra of either cycle may be intended.

forms.where: standard Tibetan title; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The Hevajra Tantra, a major Buddhist yoginī tantra, also called the Dvikalpa after its two parts. Munidatta quotes it on passion: the world is bound by passion and freed by passion itself (cp.01.m4); and on the union of āli and kāli as Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6).

forms.translit: ye shes yang dag par byang chub pa

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Jñānasaṃbodhi ('Full Awakening of Knowledge'), not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse: mind alone is the great seed of both existence and nirvāṇa; in the conventional it becomes the conventional, in nirvāṇa, lack of intrinsic nature (cp.18.m6). The Tibetan renders the title ye shes yang dag par byang chub pa.

The Kālacakra ('Wheel of Time'), a late Indian Buddhist tantra and the tradition built on it, to which the Sekoddeśa also belongs. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, cites 'the glorious Kālacakra' for a line about the falling of the white drop, day and night (cp.23.m5). Whether he means the tantra itself or another work of its cycle is not said.

'Treatise of the Middle Way': the source Munidatta names for a verse on seeing the real as it is: nothing is to be removed, nothing added; whoever sees the real is freed (cp.09.m4). Whether he means one particular work or Madhyamaka writing in general is unclear. The Tibetan has dbu ma'i bstan bcos.

forms.translit: mtshan yang dag par brjod pa
forms.lemma: mtshan yang dag par brjod pa

entries.definition: The Nāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting of the Names'), in full the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, a tantric hymn of the names of Mañjuśrī, widely recited and commented on. Munidatta quotes its line 'a is the foremost of all letters' (cp.17.m3); the Tibetan names it mtshan yang dag par brjod pa, 'Correct Utterance of the Names'.

A 'chapter on wisdom' (prajñā, 'wisdom'; pariccheda, 'section, chapter') that Munidatta cites at the end of his comment on the first couplet of song 26, for a passage beginning vicārite, 'when examined' (cp.26.m2); the Tibetan has shes rab le'u. He does not name the work, and the phrase may describe a chapter rather than give a title.

A tantric work that Munidatta cites by the name Rativajra; it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse asking how there can be flawless accomplishment once bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen and the consciousness of the aggregates has swooned (cp.01.m2).

forms.translit: lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa
forms.lemma: lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Sahajasaṃvara (Tibetan lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa); it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse in which emptiness, like a woman in desire, at once embraces the mind that is all-pervading, free of appearance and of one taste with compassion (cp.06.m5).

A Buddhist tantra, cited by Munidatta as 'the king of tantras, Sampuṭodbhava', probably the Saṃpuṭa Tantra of the Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara traditions. He quotes its verse in which the Vajra-holder calls the mind, clouded by concepts and restless as windblown lightning, saṃsāra (cp.01.m2).

A 'chapter on empowerment' (seka, 'consecration, empowerment'; paṭala, 'chapter'), whose prescribed rite Munidatta follows when he sets the empowerment at midnight (cp.27.m2); the Tibetan has dbang gi le'u. He does not say which tantra's chapter he means, and the phrase may describe a chapter rather than give a title.

The Sekoddeśa (‘Summary of Empowerment’), a work of the Kālacakra tradition on tantric empowerment. Munidatta quotes from it a verse on the luminous stream of the moon that must not fall, and on knowing the innate form of the lord (cp.03.m5). The Tibetan translation names it dbang bshad pa.

A work Munidatta cites twice in his comment on song 13 as the Sūtaka, not otherwise identified here. He quotes from it verses on aggregates, elements and senses, each fivefold and blessed by a tathāgata (cp.13.m4), and on sleeping and waking as no different (cp.13.m5). The Tibetan transcribes the title once (sU ta ke) and once renders it mdo, 'sūtra'.

The Veda: the oldest scriptures of Brahmanical religion, hymns and ritual texts held to be revealed and taught by brahmins. Song 29 asks how what has no colour, mark or form is explained by scripture and Veda (3b); Munidatta names the Veda after poetry, Vinaya, scripture and treatises (cp.29.m4). The Tibetan has rig byed.

The Vinaya ('discipline'): the part of the Buddhist canon that lays down the rules of monastic life with the stories behind them. Munidatta asks how what has no colour, mark or form could be explained in poetry, the Vinaya, scripture, treatises or the Veda (cp.29.m4); the Tibetan has 'dul ba.

forms.translit: rnal 'byor rin po che'i phreng ba
forms.lemma: rnal 'byor rin po che'i phreng ba

entries.definition: The Yogaratnamālā (‘Garland of Yoga Jewels’), probably the commentary on the Hevajra Tantra of that name ascribed to Kṛṣṇa (Kāṇha). Munidatta quotes from it a verse calling emptiness the vajra: firm, solid, not hollow, uncuttable, unbreakable, unburnable and indestructible (cp.03.m3).

Annihilation (uccheda): the view that things, or the self, are simply cut off and cease to be, one of the two extremes, with eternalism, that the Middle Way avoids. Munidatta warns the fool who has reached the path not to take clear light as empty and so fall into annihilation (cp.15.m5).

The moon reflected in water: a stock Mahāyāna image for what appears vividly but has no substance of its own. Song 29 says what it speaks of is like it, neither true nor false (4b); Munidatta applies the image to how the host of things appears to the lord of yogis (cp.29.m5). The Tibetan has chu yi zla ba.

symbolic.image: the moon in water, neither true nor false

readings.referent: the appearance (pratibhāsa) of the host of things (bhāvagrāma) to the lord of yogis, which, like the moon in water, is neither true nor false, so that it is not fit to be put into words; the Tibetan comment has 'the reflection of the town of meditation of the lord of yogis' (rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug sgom pa'i grong khyer gyi gzugs brnyan), as if reading bhāvanā for bhāva

entries.definition: Indifferent, standing apart (Sanskrit udāsa, udāsīna; the Old Bengali uāsa drops the d, as Prakrit regularly does between vowels). In the refrain of song 7 whatever lies in the mind's range is uāsa. Munidatta adds sudūratara, 'very far removed' (cp.07.m3); the Tibetan has btang snyoms, 'equanimity, indifference', in the song and the commentary.

The straight road (Old Bengali ujū, 'straight', from Sanskrit ṛju, and bāṭa, 'road'), the governing image of song 15: those who went by it became anābāṭā, the refrain names it with saṃsāra, and going by it the eight great accomplishments are gained. The Tibetan has drang po'i lam. Munidatta reads it as the excellent path of the avadhūtī (cp.15.m2).

symbolic.image: the straight road, by which those who went became anābāṭā and by which the eight great accomplishments are gained

readings.referent: the excellent path of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation, by which the lords of yogis of the past have gone
the path that is the means of the joy of cessation (viramānandopāyamārga), apart from which no other path leads toward the goal

entries.definition: Delight or elation (Sanskrit ullāsa, 'brightening, rising up'; Old Bengali ulāsa): a surge of joy. In song 30 (3b) one's own mind 'does not give' ulāsa; Munidatta's paraphrase has the mind give the delight of the innate (sahajollāsa) (cp.30.m4), and the Tibetan line has joy (dga' ba) given to one's own mind.

Mad, out of one's mind (Old Bengali umata, from Sanskrit unmatta; also pāgala, 'crazy'): the Śabara's epithet in the refrain of song 28 and again in its last couplet. The Tibetan has smyon pa, 'madman'. Compare the entry for drunk (matta), which lists the related form unmatto.

symbolic.image: the mad Śabara

readings.referent: one whose mind is overwhelmed by sense objects (viṣayavihvalacitta), whom the Blessed Lady Nairātmā addresses and comforts
intoxicated with drinking the innate (sahajapānapramatta): the Śabara is the poet's own mind-vajra

entries.definition: Instruction: the practical, often oral, teaching a guru gives a disciple for yogic practice. Munidatta quotes Nāgārjuna on helpful instruction gained by the guru's grace (cp.01.m3), and says Lūyī saw coupled union by practising the fourth instruction received from the guru (cp.01.m6).

Apprehension (upalambha): taking something as an object, as really there; the opposite of non-apprehension (anupalambha). Munidatta has Śānti ask what is to be meditated on when there is no apprehension of things (cp.26.m2), and introduces the last couplet of song 26 as stating the apprehension of the true nature (cp.26.m5). The Tibetan has dmigs pa.

Gathering up, summing up (Sanskrit upasaṃhāra; Old Bengali saṃkeliu, perhaps from saṃkalita, 'collected'). In the last couplet Śānti speaks saṃkeliu, apparently 'in sum'. The Tibetan nyer sdud and Munidatta's upasaṃhāra both mean summary and also withdrawal; Munidatta takes it as the withdrawal of the objects of existence (cp.15.m6).

symbolic.image: Śānti's summing up

readings.referent: the withdrawal (upasaṃhāra) of the objects of existence (bhāvaviṣaya), which Śānti makes once he has made it plain by avoiding the pair of appearances, left and right

entries.definition: Means or method (upāya): in Mahāyāna thought the skilful, compassionate method by which awakening is reached, paired with wisdom (prajñā); in the tantras it is pictured as male. Munidatta calls the refrain of song 13 praise of 'the fourth means', and the boat 'the boat of the means of the fourth joy' (cp.13.m3). The Tibetan has thabs.

The protuberance on the crown of a buddha's head, one of the marks of a great being; tantric accounts of the body also use the word for the top of the head. Munidatta speaks of the honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus (cp.04.m3).

Arising or origination (utpāda): a thing's coming into being, which Madhyamaka argues never truly takes place. Munidatta uses it for the song's birth (jāma): his second verse states 'the nature of arising', since for one who understands selflessness nothing arises, and what has no arising has no perishing (cp.22.m4). The Tibetan has skye ba, 'birth'.

forms.translit: skye ba dang gnas pa dang 'jig pa
forms.lemma: skye ba dang gnas pa dang 'jig pa

entries.definition: Arising and perishing (utpāda, bhaṅga): the coming into being and destruction of conditioned things. Munidatta's paraphrase of the fourth couplet of song 7 puts it where the song has ‘coming and going’: knowing the nature of conventional truth in the arising and perishing of things, Kāṇha becomes of distinguished mind (cp.07.m5).

The generation stage: the first phase of tantric practice, in which practitioners visualize themselves as the deity with its maṇḍala, in preparation for the completion stage. In the verse Munidatta attributes to Nāgārjuna, a means built like a stairway serves those established in the generation stage who long for the completion stage (cp.07.m6).

Utprekṣā, 'poetic fancy': in Sanskrit poetics, a figure of speech (alaṅkāra) that imagines one thing as if it were another. Munidatta says calling bodhicitta 'boat' in song 8 is such a figure (cp.08.m2), as he does for the body-tree of song 1. The Tibetan here has gzugs kyi rgyan, perhaps for rūpaka, 'metaphor'.

The four fearlessnesses or confidences (vaiśāradya) of a buddha, counted with the ten powers among a buddha's qualities: confidence in claiming full awakening, in having ended the defilements, in naming what obstructs the path, and in teaching the way to freedom. Munidatta names them with the ten powers (cp.09.m5); the Tibetan has mi 'jigs pa.

The thunderbolt-diamond, emblem of the indestructible in tantric Buddhism; as a prefix it marks what belongs to that path (vajra guru, vajra recitation). Munidatta uses vajra and its synonym kuliśa, as in 'the union of vajra and lotus' (cp.01.m3) and 'the vajra of realizing selflessness' (cp.01.m5).

readings.referent: the knowledge of means (upāyajñāna), held by the Śabarī

forms.translit: rdo rje bzlas pa'i rim pas

entries.definition: A breathing practice of the completion stage, associated with the Guhyasamāja and the Five Stages, usually described as joining the syllables oṃ āḥ hūṃ to the breath as it enters, abides and leaves. Munidatta says the lord of yogis is first to lead both into the house by instruction in vajra recitation (cp.02.m3).

'Vajra jewel': in the code language of the yoginī tantras, the tip of the male organ (vajra and maṇi, 'jewel', both stand for it). Munidatta equates the song's stool (pīṭhaka) with it: conventional bodhicitta falling into it cannot be held, and novice yogis cannot hold it (cp.02.m2).

The peak or summit (śikhara) of the vajra. Munidatta says the moon of bodhicitta, moving by the path of the avadhūtī, reaches the vajra peak, and at its tip goes to nirvāṇa, clear light (cp.27.m3, cp.27.m4); the Tibetan has rdo rje'i rtse mo. He does not say here where in the body it lies.

The vajra woman (vajravanitā), apparently a name for the female partner of tantric union. Munidatta has Kṛṣṇācārya say that through attachment to her (abhiṣvaṅga) the faults of the three worlds, body, speech and mind, were overcome with ease (cp.18.m2); whether a visualized or a physical partner is meant is not said. The Tibetan has rdo rje'i btsun mo.

forms.translit: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin
forms.lemma: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin

entries.definition: In Mahāyāna accounts of the path, the final meditative absorption, which like a vajra cuts through the last and subtlest obscurations just before awakening. Munidatta says Guḍḍarī speaks his own praise because he has directly realized it (cp.04.m6).

Crooked, bent (Old Bengali baṅka, Sanskrit vakra). The refrain of song 32 (2a) says not to leave the straight and take the crooked. Munidatta's paraphrase has 'the crooked path' (vakramārga; Shastri prints va(ca)-) and calls the avadhūtī path 'not crooked' (avakra) (cp.32.m3, cp.32.m6). The Tibetan line has gzhan, 'other'; its comment, lam kyog po.

symbolic.image: the crooked, which one is told not to take in place of the straight

readings.referent: the crooked path (vakramārga), set against the path of the avadhūtī, apart from which the lord of yogis has no other means; the novice yogin is told not to resort to it and so become a wanderer in saṃsāra again; the Tibetan has 'having fallen onto the crooked path (lam kyog po), do not take up saṃsāric existence again'

entries.definition: Left and right, the two sides. In song 5 whoever climbs onto the bridge is told not to go right or left. Munidatta pairs left and right with the moon and the sun, here with their 'appearances' (cp.05.m5), and calls the river's two banks left and right (cp.05.m2).

symbolic.image: going right or left on the bridge

readings.referent: the moon-appearance and the sun-appearance (candrasūryābhāsa), left and right, which are first stopped by vajra recitation and are then not to be dwelt on again (the sense of the instruction is not fully clear)

entries.definition: Varāḍī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 21 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes the name (ba rA DI) instead of translating it. Sanskrit music treatises name a rāga Varāṭī, probably the same melody.

Colour (Sanskrit varṇa, Old Bengali bāna; Tibetan kha dog), one of the features by which a thing is singled out; varṇa also means 'letter' and 'caste'.
