Song 29 says the colour, mark and form of what it speaks of are not known (3a); Munidatta quotes Nāgārjuna: no colour, red, yellow or madder, is perceived (cp.29.m4).

Vāruṇī, a strong distilled liquor named after the god Varuṇa; Vāruṇī is also the goddess of wine. In song 3 the liquor-seller brews it, and it returns in the refrain. The Tibetan translation renders it chu bdag chang, ‘Varuṇa's beer’, or simply chang, ‘beer’.

symbolic.image: the liquor the liquor-seller brews

readings.referent: bodhicitta, which she binds, ‘because of the delight of bliss’
conventional bodhicitta: Munidatta calls vāruṇī a twilight word (sandhyāvacana) for it

entries.definition: Habitual tendencies (vāsanā; Tibetan bag chags): latent impressions left by past actions and perceptions, which shape later experience and keep the round of birth turning; a key Yogācāra term. Song 20 (3a) has bāsanapūṛa, which Munidatta renders vāsanāpuṭa, 'casket of tendencies', and the Tibetan 'wrapped in tendencies'; he says examination finds no vāsanā at all (cp.20.m4).

symbolic.image: bāsanapūṛa, the packet (?) of tendencies that the speaker says was her first biāṇa

readings.referent: this body, born at first as a casket (puṭa) of conventional tendencies (saṃvṛtivāsanāpuṭa); when its channels, the thirty-two goddesses, are examined, that wretched vāsanā is not found; the Tibetan line has instead 'my consciousness wrapped in tendencies' (rnam shes bag chags gtums)

entries.definition: A lad or boy (Sanskrit vaṭu, baṭu), especially a young brahmin pupil; as an address it can be fond or scornful ('fellow, fool'). Taken here for Old Bengali baṭa in the refrain of song 29 (2a), where Munidatta's paraphrase has the novice yogin (cp.29.m3) and the Tibetan line rmongs pa, 'fool'. The same spelling can be bāṭa, 'road'.

symbolic.image: a lad the poet addresses

readings.referent: the novice yogin (bālayogin), by whom reality, hard to discern, cannot be discerned: his paraphrase puts the novice yogin where the song has baṭa, without an explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment has byis pa'i rnal 'byor pa

entries.definition: Wind or breath (Sanskrit vāyu, vāta, pavana, prāṇa; Old Bengali pavaṇa; Tibetan rlung): in tantric yoga, the vital winds that move through the channels of the subtle body and carry the mind; stilling them is a central aim. Munidatta speaks of the winds beginning with entering, and of the wind of emergence.

A braid or plait of hair (Sanskrit veṇī); the same word names the meeting of rivers, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga. In song 4 the moon and the sun form a braid whose sides are to be split. The Tibetan translation has gnyis, 'the two', where the Bengali has beṇi.

symbolic.image: a braid made of the moon and the sun

readings.referent: supreme joy (paramānanda): in the middle braid the waves of the self-blessing mind are enjoyed

entries.definition: A vessel or container (Tibetan snod). In couplet 4 of song 23, which survives only in the Tibetan, the body is 'my vessel', in a line naming earth, water, fire and food. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, speaks of the body become the vessel and basis of oneself, from which the substances become the five great elements are eaten (cp.23.m5).

Examination or analysis (vicāra): looking into something by discursive thought; in Buddhist accounts of meditation, the sustained probing of an object. In song 15 the true nature of self-awareness is examined. Munidatta treats such examination of the mark of the unmarkable as conceptual thought, which Śānti does not go into (cp.15.m2). The Tibetan has rnam dpyod.

symbolic.image: examining the true nature of self-awareness

readings.referent: conceptual thought (vikalpa): the examination of the mark of the unmarkable and the rest, into which Śānti, a siddhācārya whose nature is the experience of self-awareness, does not go

entries.definition: 'Variety': in the Hevajra system, the first of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, followed by vipāka, vimarda and vilakṣaṇa. Munidatta says the yoginī gives the sequence of joys through union with the characteristics beginning with vicitra (cp.04.m2).

The wise or learned (Old Bengali bidujaṇa, from Sanskrit vidvajjana). In song 18 some people speak ill of Ḍombī, but the wise do not let go of her neck. The Tibetan has rigs ldan skye bo, 'people of good family', as if reading a word like kulīna. Munidatta's paraphrase has certain lords of yogis in their place (cp.18.m5).

symbolic.image: the wise, who do not let go of Ḍombī's neck

readings.referent: those lords of yogis (prādeśikā yogīndrāḥ, perhaps 'found here and there'; the Tibetan has phyogs gcig tu) who know Ḍombī through the imperishable bliss of the union of vajra and lotus, and who do not abandon the throat, the wheel of enjoyment, day and night (his paraphrase puts them where the song has the wise; there is no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: Knowledge (vidyā): in Buddhist thought the opposite of ignorance (avidyā); in the tantras the word can also name a spell and the yogin's female partner. In song 9 the poet tames 'the elephant of knowledge' (vidyākari); Munidatta reads 'the lord-elephant of ignorance' (cp.09.m5), while the Tibetan song has rig pa'i glang dbang.

Consciousness (vijñāna): awareness arising through a faculty, as eye-consciousness through the eye; Buddhist analysis usually counts six, and consciousness is the fifth aggregate. Munidatta speaks of 'the wind of the consciousnesses of the eye faculty and the rest', of many kinds (cp.11.m5). The Tibetan has rnam par shes pa.

Evening (Sanskrit vikāla, Old Bengali biālī), the time the poet names for the rubbing of lotus and vajra. Munidatta takes the word as vi-kāla, 'without time'. The Tibetan translation gives both dus min, 'not the time', and dgongs mo, 'evening'.

symbolic.image: evening, the time named for the rubbing of lotus and vajra

readings.referent: free of time (kālarahita): the yogi is told to realize directly the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is free of time

forms.translit: rnam par rtog pa med pa
forms.lemma: rnam par rtog pa med pa

entries.definition: Conceptual thought (vikalpa, kalpanā): the mind's construction of things through concepts, which Buddhist tantric teaching treats as what binds. Munidatta speaks of shaking off the concepts of beginningless existence, of going to the wheel of great bliss free of concepts (nirvikalpa), and of the innate wind freed from the net of concepts (cp.02.m4, cp.02.m5).

Transformation or modification (Old Bengali bikaraṇa; compare Sanskrit vikaraṇa, vikāra; Tibetan rnam 'gyur). In song 31 (3b) the mind's bikaraṇa slips and enters 'there', like moonlight in the moon. Munidatta's paraphrase has the mind's series of conceptual thoughts (vikalpāvalī) in its place (cp.31.m4). Whether the word names the mind's changing states or the act of change is unclear.

symbolic.image: the mind's transformations, which slip and enter there

readings.referent: the series of conceptual thoughts (vikalpāvalī) of the king of mind, which dissolves right there when the king of mind goes to no-mind and enters clear light: his paraphrase puts it where the song has cia bikaraṇe, with no explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment cites rnam 'gyur and has the concepts dissolve (rnam par rtog pa thim)

entries.definition: ‘Beyond characteristics’: in the Hevajra system, the last of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, commonly paired with innate joy, though systems differ. Munidatta twice speaks of something ‘purified by vilakṣaṇa’: the boat or the avadhūtī (cp.14.m2), and the bodhicitta that is rowed as a boat (cp.14.m5).

Downcast, dejected (Old Bengali bimana, Sanskrit vimanas, literally 'without mind' or 'of altered mind'). Twice in song 7 Kāṇha becomes bimana. The Tibetan translation of the song takes it as unhappiness (rnam mi dga', yid mi bde); Munidatta's paraphrase, in the Sanskrit and the Tibetan alike, has 'of distinguished mind' (viśiṣṭamanas) in its place.

symbolic.image: Kāṇha becoming bimana: downcast, or literally 'without mind'

readings.referent: becoming of distinguished mind (viśiṣṭamanas): having unified by means of āli and kāli and firmly blocked the path of the avadhūtī, Kṛṣṇācārya, by the true guru's grace, becomes of distinguished mind in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtikā (the paraphrase puts viśiṣṭamanaso bhūtāḥ where the song has bimana bhailā; there is no explicit gloss)
becoming of distinguished mind and purified, through knowing, by the guru's grace, the nature of conventional truth in the arising and perishing of things (again a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss)

entries.definition: The vīṇā, an Indian stringed instrument; the one in song 17 has a gourd, a stick and strings, like the stick zithers of early India. The song makes the sun its gourd and the moon its string, calls its stick unstruck, and names it Heruka's vīṇā. Munidatta says Vīṇāpāda proclaims the unstruck through it (cp.17.m2). The Tibetan has pi wang.

The opposing side, adversary (Sanskrit vipakṣa, Old Bengali bipakha); in Buddhist usage what works against the path, as the afflictions do, set against its remedy (pratipakṣa). In song 16 the leader of the five sense objects sees no adversary at all; Munidatta says he no longer sees affliction acting as an adversary (cp.16.m5).

symbolic.image: no adversary to be seen

readings.referent: affliction (kleśa) acting as an adversary

entries.definition: Hero; in the yoginī tantras also a title of the male adept, the partner of the yoginīs. The poet of song 4 calls himself a hero in kundura; Munidatta says he is one because he has crushed the enemy, the afflictions (cp.04.m6). The Tibetan translation of the line has no separate word for 'hero'.

readings.referent: those who, having made existence steady, crush the enemy, the sense objects

entries.definition: One of the four joys (ānanda) that the yoginī tantras describe in yogic union; viramānanda is the ‘joy of cessation’. Its position among the four differs between systems. Munidatta pairs it with the ‘root of the jewel’ (maṇimūla).

The sound or roar of a hero (vīranāda), with which the unstruck ḍamaru plays in song 11; vīra, 'hero', is also a title of the male tantric adept. Munidatta sets 'the lion's roar of emptiness' beside it (cp.11.m2). The Tibetan has dpa' bo'i gdangs, 'the hero's tone'.

symbolic.image: the hero's sound with which the unstruck ḍamaru plays

readings.referent: the lion's roar of emptiness (śūnyatāsiṃhanāda), named in apposition: with it Kṛṣṇācārya, the kāpālika, sounds the unstruck sound of the ḍamaru

entries.definition: The objects of the senses: visible form, sound, smell, taste and touch, with mental objects in some lists. Munidatta reads the town of song 10 as 'the mass of sense objects beginning with form', and speaks of 'the appearance of objects' (viṣayābhāsa).

Purity or purification (viśuddhi; Tibetan rnam dag): in Buddhist tantra, seeing the sense objects, aggregates and elements as pure by nature, or making them so. Song 30 (4a) speaks of the purity of the sense objects, in which the poet understood in joy; Munidatta likens it to the moon lighting up the sky (cp.30.m5).

Marriage, a wedding (Sanskrit vivāha, Old Bengali bibāha). In song 19 Kāṇha sets out to marry Ḍombī to the sound of drums and cries of victory, and the marriage brings a dowry. Munidatta introduces couplet 3 as stating the fruit of the marriage with Ḍombī (cp.19.m3). The Tibetan has bag ma len pa, 'taking a bride'.

symbolic.image: Kāṇha's marriage to Ḍombī

readings.referent: breaking the flow of Ḍombī, the channel of semen and the unpurified avadhūtikā: his paraphrase has Kṛṣṇācāryapāda set out 'to break her flow' (vāhavabhaṅgārtham; vāhava is odd, perhaps for vāha) where the song has him set out for the wedding (bibāhe), apparently a play on vi-vāha; the Tibetan has 'to destroy her leaking' ('dzag pa gzhom pa'i phyir)
the vivāha of the 'door of going' of Ḍombī, who has the form of wind; the Tibetan explains that through that door her going is to be destroyed ('gro ba gzhom par bya)

forms.translit: khyab par bya ba dang khyab par byed pa

entries.definition: The pervaded (vyāpya) and the pervader (vyāpaka): in Indian logic, the two terms of a relation of invariable concomitance. Munidatta uses the pair for the way bliss fills the world, which he says is pervaded by bliss ‘in the form of pervaded and pervader’ (cp.07.m3). The Tibetan has ‘great bliss’ there.

Emergence or rising (vyutthāna): in yoga, coming out of absorption; in breath practice apparently the outgoing phase of the breath, paired with entering (praveśa). Munidatta reads the courtyard of song 2's refrain as the wind of emergence, together with entering (cp.02.m3); the Tibetan has 'byung ba'i rlung, 'wind of arising'.

The warp: the lengthwise threads stretched on a loom, across which the weft is woven (Tibetan rgyu, which also means 'cause'). In the refrain of song 25 the poet, a weaver by nature, does not know how to mark warp and weft as his own (2a–2b). Munidatta's comment on the pair speaks of the distinction of conventional and ultimate (cp.25.m3).

symbolic.image: warp and weft, which the weaver does not know how to mark as his own

readings.referent: the distinction of conventional and ultimate: the comment says that those who mark (mtshon pa) by apprehending that distinction do not know; the syntax is loose and warp and weft are not explicitly equated with anything (Tibetan comment only)

entries.definition: A wave (Sanskrit taraṅga; Tibetan chu rlabs). The refrain of song 13 has waves in the middle, by the braid, in a line whose syntax is unclear. Munidatta speaks of the wave, the surging bliss, of the self-blessed mind in supreme joy, of which no self-awareness is looked for (cp.13.m3).

symbolic.image: waves in the middle of the crossing, by the braid

readings.referent: the wave, the surging (ullola) bliss, of the self-blessed mind, in supreme joy, in the middle braid; no self-awareness such as 'I have enjoyed it' is looked for there (the Tibetan: 'here even one's own feeling is not apprehended')

entries.definition: A weaver (Tibetan tha ga pa). In the refrain of song 25, which survives only in Tibetan, the poet calls himself a weaver by nature (2a), and in the last couplet names himself simply 'the weaver' (5b). Munidatta reads the refrain's 'I' as Tha ga pa'i zhabs himself, the self of means by nature (cp.25.m3).

symbolic.image: the weaver, the 'I' of the refrain

readings.referent: the poet Tha ga pa'i zhabs himself, 'the self of the means by nature' (ngo bo nyid kyi thabs kyi bdag); the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation

entries.definition: Weaving (Tibetan 'thag pa, 'to weave'; thags, 'woven work', spelled thag in the lines), the governing image of song 25: weaving five times, the poet makes a stainless cloth (1b), weaves at home (3a) and weaves the weave that fills the sky (3b). Munidatta has the poet say he has obtained 'the way of weaving' (cp.25.m6).

symbolic.image: the weave (thag) whose taste the weaver finds

readings.referent: the comment cites thag and glosses: having parted from things that are born, [he] became a vajra-holder (rdo rje 'dzin pa); whether it cites thag, 'weave', or tha ga, 'weaver', is unclear

entries.definition: The weft: the crosswise thread woven through the warp. Song 25's refrain pairs warp (rgyu) with spun dog, Munidatta's comment with spun dag (cp.25.m3). Spun ordinarily means 'siblings'; the weaving sense suits the pair and the song but is a draft reading to be checked, and the line's dog is unexplained.

symbolic.image: warp and weft, which the weaver does not know how to mark as his own

readings.referent: the distinction of conventional and ultimate: the comment says that those who mark (mtshon pa) by apprehending that distinction do not know; the syntax is loose and warp and weft are not explicitly equated with anything (Tibetan comment only)

entries.definition: A wheel. In this song the moon and the sun are called 'the two wheels', though the vehicle is a boat. The same word (Sanskrit cakra) also names the wheels of the subtle body in the tantras, which have their own entries (wheel of emanation, wheel of great bliss).

symbolic.image: the moon and the sun as 'the two wheels'

entries.definition: A class of powerful spirits of Indian religion, sometimes benign, often feared. In the verse Munidatta quotes, a painter draws a terrifying yakṣa and is then frightened by it himself; so is the fool in saṃsāra (cp.02.m5).

Property given with a bride at marriage (Sanskrit yautuka, yautaka; Old Bengali jautuka). In song 19 the dowry of Kāṇha's marriage is the unsurpassed dharma. Munidatta writes jautaka: by the dowry, without affliction, the unsurpassed Dharma was directly realized (cp.19.m3). The Tibetan has zhal mthong ston mo, apparently 'the feast of seeing the face', a wedding feast.

Youth, the prime of life (Old Bengali jaubaṇa, Sanskrit yauvana). In song 20 (4a) the speaker's youth has become full; the Tibetan line has 'my youthful prime became complete'. Munidatta cites the line as navayauvana, 'fresh youth', where Shastri's text has jāṇa jaubaṇa, and says it is made by withdrawing the sphere of sense objects (cp.20.m5).

symbolic.image: the speaker's youth, grown full

readings.referent: fresh youth (navayauvana), made by the withdrawal of the maṇḍala of sense objects (viṣayamaṇḍalopasaṃhāra); by its power, addressing himself as 'body-vajra', the practitioner has become beautiful with the body of the great Vajradhara, with its thirty-two marks and eighty signs

entries.definition: 'Yogic sleep': a state of deep meditative rest, outwardly like sleep. Munidatta equates it with the fourth joy and reads the father-in-law's falling asleep as the breath being led into it (cp.02.m4); the Tibetan translation calls it the yogic sleep of 'the joy of peace'.

A practitioner of yoga; in the songs, a tantric adept on the siddhas' path. Kāṇha calls himself a kāpālika yogi, and Munidatta speaks of yogins who lack the guru's lineage. Distinct from 'lord of yogis' (yogīndra), Munidatta's term for the accomplished practitioner.
'Lord of yogis', Munidatta's usual term for the accomplished practitioner the songs speak of; in this song, the one the Ḍombī ferries across.

A woman practitioner of yoga; in the yoginī tantras also a female deity of the maṇḍala. Munidatta says the yoginīs, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, keep awake day and night, glossing the wakeful young wife (cp.02.m4).

The net or circle of yoginīs (yoginījāla): in the yoginī tantras, the host of female deities of a maṇḍala, pictured as a net. In song 19 the night passes in the net of yoginīs. Munidatta explains it as the rays of knowledge of the lord of yogis (cp.19.m4); the Tibetan has rnal 'byor ma yi dra ba, 'the yoginī's net'.

symbolic.image: the net of yoginīs in which the night passes

readings.referent: the rays of knowledge (jñānaraśmi) of the lord of yogis who is attached day and night to lovemaking with the jñānamudrā; the Tibetan agrees (ye shes kyi 'od zer)

entries.definition: 'Yoked as a pair': the state in which two poles, such as wisdom and method or the two truths, are inseparably joined. Munidatta says the fruit of innate joy has this form (cp.01.m2) and that Lūyī saw it through practising the fourth instruction received from the guru (cp.01.m6).
